bruges-the-port-that-froze-in-time.context_blurb:
Bruges, in Belgium, was one of the richest trading cities of medieval northern Europe, an early home of modern banking and of the first great Flemish painters. Today it looks like a city in a fairy tale, all canals, cobbled lanes and stepped brick gables. That beauty is the strange gift of a disaster.

Over the market square rises the 83-metre Belfry, and 366 steps up hangs its carillon, 47 tuned bronze bells weighing about 27.5 tonnes, played by one musician at a keyboard struck with the hands and fists.

Bruges lived by the sea through the Zwin, a tidal channel that a great storm tore open in 1134. When sand and mud choked the Zwin and cut Bruges off from the sea, the trade moved to Antwerp, which became the leading city of the Low Countries.

Left poor, Bruges could not afford to knock down its old streets and build new ones, so the medieval city simply survived while richer rivals rebuilt theirs. Around 1350 it had held some 46,000 people and the richest money market in the region. In 2000 its historic centre became a World Heritage Site.

bryce-canyon.context_blurb:
High in southern Utah, the edge of a plateau breaks away into giant bowls crowded with stone spires that blaze orange, pink and red at dawn. This is Bryce Canyon, though it is not really a canyon at all. Frost, rain and time carved it, and its strange stone crowds have inspired settlers' jokes and Paiute legends alike.

The spires are hoodoos, tall, thin pillars of rock that bulge and narrow like totem poles, and Bryce holds more of them than anywhere else on Earth. They crowd most thickly inside the Bryce Amphitheater. The most famous single hoodoo is Thor's Hammer, a slab of harder rock perched on a slender stone neck about 150 feet high, the park's most photographed spot.

The park is named after Ebenezer Bryce, a Mormon settler whose cows wandered among the spires after he moved here in 1875, and he reportedly grumbled that the maze was a hell of a spot to lose a cow.

Scrape the rock and it is pale limestone, but iron oxide stains it rose, orange and red, so early mapmakers named this band the Pink Cliffs. The limestone is about 50 to 60 million years old.

No river ever cut Bryce: its bowls are amphitheatres that erosion ate backward into the eastern edge of the high Paunsaugunt Plateau. A real canyon is carved downward by a river, as the Colorado carved the Grand Canyon.

The real sculptor is frost wedging: on over 200 freezing nights each year water seeps into cracks, freezes, swells by about 9 percent and pries the rock apart. Slightly acid rain then dissolves the stone's cement. Wind does little, since the hoodoos do not line up with it. A hoodoo lasts only as long as its caprock, a layer of harder rock on top that shelters the soft mudstone below, so a capped column wears away far more slowly than the rock around it.

To the Paiute people, the hoodoos are the Legend People, creatures with human looks who were really birds, lizards and beasts, whom the trickster Coyote turned to stone for their greed. In one telling he invited them to a feast, and as they sat down in their finest paint he froze every one before a single bite. The Paiute name for the rocks means red painted faces.

Bryce is the top of something much bigger. It crowns the Grand Staircase, a giant flight of coloured cliffs climbing more than 6,000 feet across Utah and northern Arizona, and the bottom step, far to the south, is the Grand Canyon.

budapest.context_blurb:
Budapest, the capital of Hungary, is two cities joined across the Danube: hilly old Buda on the west bank, crowned by its royal castle, and flat, busy Pest on the east. Beneath both lies a hidden world of hot springs and caves, and its grand bathhouses have steamed for centuries.

For a long time no permanent bridge crossed the river there, until the Chain Bridge opened on 20 November 1849, the first fixed crossing of the Danube in Hungary. Buda and Pest formally became one city in 1873.

More than 100 natural thermal springs well up beneath the streets and pour out roughly 70 million litres of warm mineral water every day, which earned Budapest the official title City of Spas in 1934. The biggest bathhouse is the yellow, palace-like Széchenyi Baths, opened in 1913 and said to be Europe's biggest medicinal bath, where bathers play chess on floating boards in the steaming outdoor pool even when snow is falling. Its spring is drilled more than 1,200 metres down.

There is no volcano here. The heat comes from a fault line, a deep crack where the Buda hills drop sharply to the Pest plain, and rainwater that sinks deep along it is warmed by the Earth and climbs back up. That same hot mineral water, rising from deep below, has dissolved more than 200 caves into the limestone under the Buda hills, carving them from the bottom up rather than from the top down like caves made by ordinary rain.

Under the castle hill lies the Hospital in the Rock, built for about 60 patients, which crammed in over 600 wounded during the siege of 1945, and in the Cold War the government secretly refitted it as a nuclear-fallout bunker. Today it is a museum.

On the Pest bank stretches the neo-Gothic Parliament, 268 metres long, exactly 96 metres high to honour 896, the traditional year the Magyars settled the land. By custom nothing in the centre rises higher. St. Stephen's Basilica was built to the very same 96 metres, a match often said to show that worldly and spiritual power stand equal in Hungary.

Deep under József Hill lies a cave found in 1984, lined with glittering needles of aragonite, which formed when hydrogen sulfide gas rising with the hot water turned into sulfuric acid and ate away the limestone. Ordinary caves are dissolved by the weak carbonic acid in rainwater; only a few on Earth, such as Carlsbad Caverns in the United States, formed this rarer way.

buenos-aires.context_blurb:
Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, spreads along a vast brown estuary where the Paraná and Uruguay rivers meet the Atlantic. Between the 1870s and 1930s waves of Italian and Spanish immigrants poured in, and the city grew grand boulevards that earned it the name Paris of the Americas. Its port streets gave the world a dance, and its river is a giant.

The tango was born in the 1880s in the crowded tenements, bars and dance halls of La Boca, the poor port district, danced by immigrants, dockworkers and sailors long before it conquered the ballrooms of Europe. Its aching voice is the bandoneon, a small squeezebox that Heinrich Band invented in Germany around 1840 as a cheap substitute for an organ in poor churches, and German immigrants brought it to the Río de la Plata around 1870.

In La Boca the little street called Caminito is lined with tin-walled houses in clashing colours, because the shipyard workers who built them painted each wall with whatever was left over from painting the boats in the harbour. The painter Benito Quinquela Martín later turned the neighbourhood into an open-air canvas.

Downtown runs Avenida 9 de Julio, which Guinness World Records lists as the widest avenue on Earth, about 110 metres across with up to seven lanes each way, named for 9 July 1816, the day Argentina declared independence. A white obelisk stands at its centre, and crossing on foot can take two or three changes of the lights.

In the wealthy Recoleta district lies La Recoleta Cemetery, a city of the dead where 4,691 marble mausoleums line little streets and squares, and where Eva Perón, Evita, rests in her family's tomb.

Back in La Boca, the Boca Juniors football club plays at La Bombonera, the chocolate box, a stadium named for its odd shape, with three steep tiers and one flat stand like an open box of sweets. When the crowd jumps, the stands really flex, and fans say it does not shake, it beats.

The city faces the Río de la Plata, which separates Argentina from Uruguay. The water is a steady, murky brown all year round because it carries an enormous load of fine silt and mud, washed off the land, that hangs suspended in it. Near Buenos Aires it is already more than 40 kilometres across, and it widens to about 220 where it meets the Atlantic, so if it counts as a river at all, it is the world's widest. Geographers still argue whether something so broad and brackish is a river or an estuary.

bukhara-the-silk-road-museum-city.context_blurb:
Bukhara, in today's Uzbekistan, was for a thousand years one of the great stops of the Silk Road, where camel caravans between China, India, Persia and Europe rested and traded. It was a famous seat of Islamic learning, and the great physician Ibn Sina grew up nearby. Mongols, Timurid emperors and khans all left their mark on its domes and towers.

Over the old city rises the Kalyan, or Great, Minaret, a slender brick tower finished in 1127, and a minaret is the tower beside a mosque from which the call to prayer is sounded. It has called the faithful for close to 900 years.

Legend says that when Genghis Khan rode in to destroy Bukhara in 1220, he tipped his head back so far to see the top that his hat fell off, and the conqueror who bowed to no man was so impressed that he commanded his men to spare the tower while the rest of the city burned. The tale is unproven, but the minaret really did survive the Mongol sack.

The Samanid Mausoleum, a near-perfect cube about 9 metres a side and one of the oldest Islamic monuments in Central Asia, is built of nothing but baked brick, set in woven and chequered patterns whose shadows change from morning to evening. It survived the Mongols by being lost: over the centuries floods had buried it under silt and sand, so the raiders never even saw it. It was dug out again much later.

Caravans slept in a caravanserai, a walled roadside inn whose rooms ringed a great courtyard where traders could stable their camels and lock up their goods. Bukhara also roofed its busiest crossroads with domed markets; the Jewellers' Dome once held 36 goldsmiths' workshops.

The Kalyan had a darker side. For centuries, and into the early 1900s, Bukhara's rulers had condemned prisoners led up to its high gallery and thrown to their deaths on the pavement below, so people called it the Tower of Death.

The Ark, the mud-brick citadel where the emirs ruled until 1920, is perched on a mound some 20 metres high made of its own past: each time it fell or decayed, the rulers flattened the ruins and built again on top. Its walls circle about 790 metres.

In a quiet side street stands Chor Minor, Persian for four minarets, built in 1807 by a rich merchant as the gate of an Islamic school that has since vanished. Each of its four blue-domed turrets is decorated differently. Some scholars read the four designs as hints of four of the world's great religions, pointing to shapes that may suggest a cross and a fish.

With some 140 mosques, tombs, schools and domed markets packed into a lived-in, working town, Bukhara is often called a museum city. UNESCO listed its historic centre as a World Heritage Site in 1993.

byblos-and-the-phoenician-alphabet-that-.context_blurb:
On the coast of Lebanon, a short drive north of Beirut, a little stone harbour has been home to people for about seven thousand years. This is Byblos, a Phoenician port of seafaring traders. Around 1000 BCE its people used and spread a new way of writing so simple that almost the whole world now writes with its descendants.

Byblos gave us the alphabet: its Phoenician sailors carried a set of just 22 letters across the sea, and nearly every alphabet used today comes from it. The Greeks named the town Byblos, but to the Phoenicians it was Gebal, a name thought to mean mountain town or frontier town. The town has been continuously inhabited for some seven thousand years.

The trick was to write only consonant sounds and leave out the vowels, which readers filled in themselves, a system that works because Semitic languages carry most of their meaning in the consonant sounds. Egyptian writing needed hundreds of signs; this needed 22. Centuries later the Greeks borrowed the letters and added signs for vowels.

Because a merchant could learn two dozen letters quickly, the alphabet spread by trade rather than conquest, carried by Phoenician ships along North Africa and southern Europe.

In 1923 the ground slid away at Byblos and exposed a row of royal tombs. Ten metres down one shaft, the French archaeologist Pierre Montet found the stone coffin of King Ahiram of Byblos, carved with 38 words from about 1000 BCE, the longest early text written in Phoenician letters. The words are a curse on any future king who disturbs the coffin: his royal scepter will break in two, his throne will be overturned, and peace will leave Byblos.

The town gave the world another word. Byblos shipped so much Egyptian papyrus that the Greeks called papyrus byblos, a scroll a biblion and a set of scrolls ta biblia, the books, and from that phrase comes the name of the Bible. Words like bibliography come from the same harbour.

Every Phoenician letter began as a little picture of an everyday thing and was named after it. The first letter, aleph, was the head of an ox, and if you turn a capital A upside down you can still see its two horns. Aleph became the Greek alpha and then our A. The letter mem, which became our M, pictured water, and its name lives on almost unchanged in the Hebrew word mayim. In the same way bet was a house, dalet a door and ayin an eye.

The alphabet kept travelling. From Greece it sailed to Italy. There the Etruscans, known for their painted tombs in the countryside above Rome, reshaped the Greek letters and passed them on to the Romans in the 7th century BCE, and so the Latin alphabet was born. Eastward, one branch became Aramaic and then Hebrew, and another passed to the Nabataeans, the traders who carved Petra, whose flowing script grew into Arabic.

cahokia.context_blurb:
A thousand years ago, across the Mississippi from today's St. Louis, stood the greatest city in North America north of Mexico. We call it Cahokia. Its people, of the Mississippian culture, built a planned city of plazas and great earthen pyramids, traded across half a continent and watched the sky with care. Then, by about 1350, they were gone.

Cahokia's builders raised about 120 mounds without a single stone, carrying baskets of packed earth load after load, some 55 million cubic feet of soil in all. The biggest were flat-topped platforms for temples and the halls of chiefs. The greatest, Monks Mound, climbs in four broad terraces to about 30 metres, and its base covers some 13 acres, about the same ground as Egypt's Great Pyramid at Giza, though the stone pyramid rises far higher.

No one knows what its builders called their city, because they left no writing. French explorers in the 1600s named the abandoned mounds after the Cahokia, an Illiniwek people then living nearby, who had arrived centuries after the city emptied and had not built it.

Crowds packed the Grand Plaza to watch chunkey, a game in which a player rolled a polished stone disc and then threw a spear, trying to make it land closest to the spot where the disc came to rest. Fine chunkey stones were buried with the powerful as treasures.

At its peak around 1100 CE, perhaps 10,000 or even 20,000 people lived at Cahokia, probably more than lived in London then, and no American city outgrew it until Philadelphia did in the 1780s. Its traders brought copper from the Great Lakes and big conch and whelk shells up the river from the Gulf of Mexico.

The sacred centre was walled in by a palisade two miles long made of tree trunks, some 15,000 to 20,000 oak and hickory logs about 20 feet tall, with guard towers jutting out along it. It was torn down and rebuilt several times.

Cahokians also built with the sun. West of Monks Mound they raised rings of red-cedar posts, now called Woodhenge, aimed at the points where the sun rises at different times of year. Standing at the centre on the spring or autumn equinox, a watcher sees the dawn sun come up out of the front of Monks Mound, half a mile away, as if the mound itself gave birth to the day.

In Mound 72 archaeologists uncovered a young man of high rank who had been buried on thousands of polished shell beads, perhaps 20,000. The beads were arranged in the shape of a falcon, its head beneath his head and its wings and tail spread beneath his limbs, so he is known as the Birdman. More than 270 other people lay buried nearby, many of them sacrificed, a sign of rulers who held power of life and death.

Why the city emptied is still argued. One old idea said the Cahokians cut down so many trees that they caused the floods that ruined their fields. A 2021 study of the ancient flood layers found little evidence for that self-inflicted collapse, and scholars now point instead to a great flood around 1200 and to drought. Cahokia became a World Heritage Site in 1982.

cairo-and-the-giza-pyramids.context_blurb:
Cairo, on the Nile in Egypt, is the largest city in the Arab world. Its medieval quarter, founded in the 10th century, is crowded with mosques, minarets and bazaars, and on the desert edge of its southwestern suburbs rise the pyramids of Giza and the Great Sphinx. Few cities hold five thousand years of history in a single skyline.

Of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, six have crumbled or vanished, and only the Great Pyramid at Giza survives, some four and a half thousand years old. The pharaoh Khufu had it built around 2600 BC as his royal tomb, piling up some 2.3 million blocks of stone over roughly 26 years. At 146.6 metres it stayed the tallest structure people had ever built for about 3,800 years, until the spire of England's Lincoln Cathedral overtook it around 1311.

Like almost every Egyptian royal tomb, the pyramids stand on the Nile's western side, because the Egyptians watched the sun die in the west each evening and be reborn in the east each dawn, so they gave the west to the dead.

The builders were not slaves but paid, skilled Egyptian workers: archaeologists found their town and their graves, set proudly beside the king's pyramid. Their work gangs had names like Friends of Khufu and Drunkards of Menkaure, and about 10,000 workers ate some 21 cattle and 23 sheep a day.

Beside the pyramids crouches the Great Sphinx, with its nose missing. A popular story blames Napoleon's soldiers, who invaded Egypt in 1798. But a drawing made in 1737, decades before the French arrived, already shows the nose gone, which proves the story false. The nose was most likely chiselled off on purpose centuries earlier.

In medieval Cairo stands the Mosque of al-Azhar, founded around 972 by the Fatimid rulers, whose school has taught students ever since, so it ranks among the world's most ancient universities still at work. Nearby, the emir Jaharkas al-Khalili built a merchants' inn around 1382 that grew into Khan el-Khalili, a maze of covered alleys full of lantern-makers, spice sellers and goldsmiths that has traded for more than 600 years. To the east stretches Cairo's City of the Dead, a cemetery about 6 kilometres long where thousands of families live among the tombs, with schools, running water and electricity.

The city's very name comes from the sky: when the general Jawhar founded it in 969, the planet Mars, which Arabs called the Conquering Star, was rising, so he named his capital al-Qahira, the Victorious.

When new, the Great Pyramid did not look stepped. It was cased in smooth, polished white limestone that dazzled in the sun. After a great earthquake in 1303 shook the casing loose, the people of Cairo hauled the white stone away to build their medieval city. Only the rough core remains.

All of it rests on the river. The Egyptians called their country Kemet, the Black Land, and the desert around it the Red Land. Every year the Nile flooded and spread a fresh layer of black silt across the valley, and that dark soil fed the whole civilization.

cape-town-and-table-mountain.context_blurb:
At the southwestern tip of Africa, where the Atlantic swings round toward the Indian Ocean, Cape Town spreads beneath a mountain with a top as flat as a table. The Dutch East India Company founded it in the 1600s as a supply stop for its ships rounding the Cape of Good Hope. Today it is one of the most dramatically placed cities on Earth, wrapped in a world of flowers found nowhere else.

On many days a white cloud forms along the flat summit and pours slowly over the front edge, and Capetonians call it the tablecloth. It forms when damp sea air is pushed up the slope, cools into cloud at the rim and melts away in the warmer air below.

An old Cape legend tells another story: the retired pirate Jan van Hunks sat smoking on the mountain when a stranger challenged him to a smoking contest, and only too late did he realise his rival was the Devil. Whenever the tablecloth appears, locals joke that the two of them are puffing away again.

Most visitors ride up by cableway, which first opened in 1929. Since 1997 its cars have had a floor that turns a full 360 degrees on the way up, so all 65 passengers see the whole view without moving. Few cableways anywhere do this. The upper station is not quite the top: the true summit is Maclear's Beacon, a stone cairn about 1,086 metres high that Sir Thomas Maclear built in 1865 for mapping, out across the level plateau on foot. On the sunny rocks up there, visitors nearly always meet the dassie, a plump, tailless little mammal also called the rock hyrax, which lives in colonies among the boulders.

The slopes are covered not in forest but in fynbos, an Afrikaans word meaning fine bush: low, tough, fine-leaved shrubs and bright wildflowers. The mountain and its park hold more than 2,200 kinds of flowering plants, more than the roughly 1,490 native species of all Great Britain, and about 90 of them grow nowhere else. Botanists divide the world's plant life into six floral kingdoms, and the Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of them all, yet the richest for its size.

The flat top is armoured with pale, very hard sandstone. It formed roughly 450 to 510 million years ago, when the first land plants were only beginning to green the continents and no animals had yet crawled out of the sea onto dry land. Hundreds of millions of years of erosion then planed the summit flat.

From the top you can see a low island in the bay. Robben Island, Dutch for seal island, was a prison, and the apartheid government held Nelson Mandela there for about 18 of his 27 years behind bars. He was forced to work in a glaring limestone quarry that damaged his eyes. In 1990 he walked free, and he went on to become South Africa's first democratically elected president.

cappadocia.context_blurb:
On the high plateau of central Turkey lies Cappadocia, a land where volcanoes once buried everything in ash. Rain and frost have since carved that ash into valleys full of pale stone cones, and for well over a thousand years people have cut homes, churches and even whole cities straight into the rock. At dawn the sky fills with colour above them.

The cones are known as fairy chimneys, peri bacaları in Turkish, and some stand as tall as 40 metres. In a much-loved folk explanation, the name Cappadocia is Persian and means land of beautiful horses, though modern scholars doubt it.

The rock is tuff, volcanic ash pressed and hardened into stone, laid down by volcanoes such as Mount Hasan and Mount Erciyes, at 3,916 metres the tallest peak in central Anatolia. It is soft enough to carve by hand yet strong enough to stand for centuries. So the people of Cappadocia simply carved their rooms out of the solid rock by hand: kitchens, bedrooms, stables and churches, many of them now cave hotels.

Many cones wear a cap of harder rock, which shields the column beneath it while rain strips away the soft tuff all around, a process called differential erosion. Wind did not blow them into shape; the cap does the work.

Every calm morning dozens of hot-air balloons lift off together and drift over the fairy chimneys as the sunrise lights them up.

The hidden wonders lie below. In 1963 a man fixing up his house in the town of Derinkuyu broke through a wall into a forgotten city carved deep underground, about 18 levels and some 85 metres down. More than 600 tunnel entrances have since been found in the area, and in the Middle Ages Byzantine Christians fled into cities like this one to hide from Arab raids. In times of invasion, Derinkuyu could hold around 20,000 people with their animals, along with stables, wells, wine and oil presses and chapels.

Each level could be sealed with a great round stone door weighing up to 500 kilograms, which could be rolled shut only from the inside, so defenders locked invaders out one floor at a time. More than 50 shafts cut up to the open air brought fresh air to the very bottom, and a well plunged about 55 metres.

Above ground, the valley of Göreme is full of rock-cut chapels painted by Byzantine Christians. One is called the Dark Church because it has just one tiny window. That darkness turned out to be a blessing: no sunlight could reach the paint to fade it, so its 11th-century frescoes still glow in blue, red and gold.

cappadocia-and-the-derinkuyu-underground.context_blurb:
Beneath the high plateau of Cappadocia in central Turkey lie whole cities carved into the rock, level below level, with stables, wine presses, chapels and air shafts. Byzantine Christians hid in them during raids in the Middle Ages. The greatest is Derinkuyu, and it lay forgotten until the 1960s.

Above ground stand the fairy chimneys, tall cones of soft volcanic rock. Each one survives because it wears a boulder of hard rock like a hat, shielding the softer column directly beneath while rain and wind wear away the rock around it.

That soft rock is tuff, made from the ash of three ancient volcanoes. Freshly cut, it is soft enough to carve with hand tools, but once air touches it, the surface hardens into lasting stone, perfect for rooms meant to endure.

In 1963 a resident of Derinkuyu was renovating his home when he knocked through a basement wall and found a passage into a vast underground network that no one had used for centuries. It opened to visitors in 1969.

Derinkuyu reaches about 85 metres down, as deep as an 18-storey building is tall, and its levels could shelter up to 20,000 people with their animals and food. One hand-cut tunnel runs some 8 kilometres through the rock to a second underground city, Kaymaklı, so people could pass between the two without coming up for air.

When raiders broke in, the defenders had a clever door. They rolled a huge round stone, like a millstone about 1.5 metres across and weighing around half a tonne, across the passage from the inside, where no attacker could shift it. A hole through its centre let the defenders jab spears at anyone outside.

More than 50 narrow shafts reaching up to the surface carried fresh air to the lowest floors. One shaft, about 55 metres deep, doubled as a well that could be sealed from below, so an enemy above could not poison the water.

caral.context_blurb:
In the dry Supe Valley of Peru, about 23 kilometres from the Pacific, six great earthen pyramids rise from the desert. This is Caral, built about 2600 BC, in the very centuries when Egyptians were raising their first pyramids, though the two peoples never knew of each other. Its builders made music, traded and kept records, and left no sign of war.

Radiocarbon dates from reed bags used to carry stones place Caral's building around 2627 BC, which makes it the oldest known city anywhere in the Americas. It became a World Heritage Site in 2009.

Archaeologists have found no defensive walls, no weapons and no wounded bodies, so there is no sign of warfare at Caral. That is an absence of evidence, not proof of perfect peace, but it is striking for a city of its size.

Caral's trade ran on cotton, which its people grew for fishing nets and cloth and traded down to the coast for dried anchovies and sardines.

The city loved ceremony. Archaeologists found 32 flutes carved from the wing bones of condors and pelicans, dating to about 2170 BC, along with 37 horns made from deer and llama bone. In front of its two biggest pyramids lie sunken circular plazas, round courts dug below the ground and ringed with low walls, where crowds gathered for rituals.

Thousands of years later, the Inca ran an empire without writing by keeping records on knotted strings. At Caral, diggers uncovered possibly the earliest quipu ever found, a set of knotted cords whose knots recorded numbers and information. Caral had no pottery at all, yet its people kept records this way, and the archaeologist Ruth Shady believes the knotted tradition lasted some 4,500 years in the Andes.

carnac-the-breton-stone-alignments.context_blurb:
On Brittany's Atlantic shore, in the northwest of France, near the village of Carnac, rank after rank of grey granite pillars marches across the fields. Stone Age farmers set them up thousands of years ago, and no one knows for certain why. They are one of the great mysteries of ancient Europe.

More than 3,000 menhirs, each a single upright stone, stand at Carnac in long parallel rows, not in a ring like Stonehenge, and no other place on Earth has so many standing stones together.

Neolithic farmers raised them roughly between 4500 and 3300 BC, long before Stonehenge's great circle or Egypt's pyramids.

The Scottish engineer Alexander Thom surveyed the rows for years and argued that they formed a giant observatory, lined up with key risings of the sun and moon. His idea is famous but disputed, and the true purpose remains unsolved.

At nearby Locmariaquer, people around 4700 BC raised the Grand Menhir, about 20.6 metres tall and 330 tonnes, the largest single stone that prehistoric builders anywhere raised upright, but it now lies on the ground, broken into four huge pieces. Whether people pulled it down or an earthquake threw it over is still argued.

In the great burial mound of Saint-Michel beside Carnac, the most powerful dead were laid with polished axe-heads of green jade carried all the way from the Alps. Moving such stone hundreds of miles shows how rich and organised these farming peoples were.

The rows once seemed explicable only by magic. A Breton legend says Saint Cornelius, chased to the shore by a pagan Roman army, turned the marching soldiers to stone, which is why the menhirs stand in ranks. It is a folk tale, not history.

cartagena-de-indias.context_blurb:
On Colombia's Caribbean coast, behind miles of thick ramparts, lies the old town of Cartagena, a maze of pastel houses with balconies, patios and churches. For centuries it was Spain's chief port on the South American mainland. Pirates, English fleets and French admirals attacked it again and again, so Spain wrapped it in some of the strongest defences in the New World.

Cartagena was Spain's treasure vault on the Caribbean: silver from the mines of the Americas was gathered here to wait for the yearly fleet home, and that hoard drew the pirates.

The walls, built in stages between 1614 and 1796, are so thick that their broad tops became a promenade where people stroll and gather in the evening breeze. The walled town and its forts became a World Heritage Site in 1984.

On a hill above the city rises Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, about 41 metres high and often called the greatest fortress Spain built in the Americas, and much of it is made of coral cut from the local reefs. Its narrow tunnels were shaped to carry sound, so by tradition the defenders could hear the footsteps of an approaching enemy through the stone. Some chambers were even packed with explosives to bury attackers who broke in.

Two channels led into the harbour: broad Bocagrande and slender Bocachica. In 1741 Admiral Edward Vernon sailed in with almost 200 British ships carrying some 25,000 men. The Spanish commander Blas de Lezo sealed the wide gate and forced the fleet through the narrow one, under the guns of his forts. To choke the channel, Blas de Lezo deliberately sank his own ships in it. His garrison of about 3,000 held out, and the British fleet withdrew with heavy losses.

The walls guarded a darker trade as well. The Spanish crown let only a few American ports sell enslaved Africans, and more than a million captives were landed at Cartagena's docks. They were bought and sold in the Plaza de los Coches, a three-cornered square that is now a pleasant spot for tourists. Nearby, the Jesuit priest Pedro Claver met the arriving ships to care for the captives.

cenotes-sinkholes-to-a-flooded-underworl.context_blurb:
Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula is a flat shelf of limestone with hardly a river or lake anywhere above ground. Instead the ground is pocked with round pools of crystal-clear water, some open to the sky and some deep inside caves, linked underground by some of the longest flooded tunnels on Earth. The ancient Maya lived beside them, drew water from them and held them sacred.

These natural wells are cenotes, from the Yucatec Maya word ts'ono'ot, and the region's roughly 10,000 of them were its only reliable drinking water, which is why the Maya built cities such as Chichén Itzá right beside them. A cenote forms when slightly acidic rain dissolves the limestone into flooded caverns until a cave roof collapses and opens the cool groundwater to the sky.

To the Maya, a cenote's still, dark water was a doorway down to Xibalba, the watery land of the dead, and a home of Chaac, the rain god. When the American Edward Thompson began dredging Chichén Itzá's holy well of sacrifice in 1904, he hauled up jade, gold and human bones, offerings the Maya had thrown in to beg Chaac for rain.

Near Tulum two round blue cenotes sit side by side like a pair of eyes, so they are called Dos Ojos, Spanish for Two Eyes, and a flooded passage about 400 metres long joins them. In 2018 cave divers announced that they had found a drowned tunnel connecting the Sac Actun and Dos Ojos cave systems, merging them into one maze of more than 370 kilometres.

Seen from above, most cenotes look scattered at random, but one great curve of them, about 180 kilometres across, forms the Ring of Cenotes. The ring traces the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater, blasted out 66 million years ago by the asteroid linked to the end of the dinosaurs, where the shattered rock gave way most easily. That asteroid was about 10 kilometres wide, so if it were stood on end beside Mount Everest, about 8.8 kilometres high, it would tower over the summit.

The flooded caves hold their own secrets. In a pitch-black pit inside Sac Actun called Hoyo Negro, the Black Hole, divers found the skull of a teenage girl they named Naia. She turned out to have lived about 13,000 years ago, making her one of the oldest humans ever found in the Americas. Bones of an Ice Age mastodon lay deeper in the same pit.

Far to the north, in the state of Tamaulipas, El Zacatón drops about 339 metres, among the deepest flooded sinkholes known anywhere. It takes its name from zacate, the grass that grows in floating islands on its surface and drifts about with the wind. In 2007 NASA lowered a self-guided diving robot into it, as practice for one day exploring the hidden ocean beneath the ice of Europa, a moon of Jupiter. The robot mapped the pit and found new kinds of bacteria.

chaco-canyon.context_blurb:
In the high desert of northwestern New Mexico lies Chaco Canyon, the ceremonial centre of a vast Ancestral Puebloan network between about 850 and 1150 CE. Its people raised great stone houses, cut roads across the desert and lined their walls up with the sky. Then they moved away, and their descendants are the Pueblo peoples of the Southwest today.

The greatest house is Pueblo Bonito, Spanish for beautiful village, which held about 650 rooms in a great D-shaped sweep four storeys high and remained the largest building in North America until the 1800s.

The great houses needed around 200,000 beams of pine and fir, but no big forests grew nearby. With no wheels, no draft animals and no river to float them on, people carried the beams on foot from mountains up to 70 miles away, and the timbers show almost no scrape marks.

Chaco was also a workshop for turquoise: some 200,000 worked pieces have come from its ruins, shaped into beads and mosaics and traded for hundreds of miles.

Its wide roads ran in dead-straight lines, crossing mesas, ridges and canyons instead of curving around them, which suggests they had a ceremonial purpose as much as a practical one. The Great North Road runs about 35 miles almost due north.

Around 1130 CE the building stopped, as the worst drought in a thousand years of tree-ring records settled over the Southwest and lasted about 50 years, until around 1180. In a land where farming always depended on scarce rain, the people moved away to settle elsewhere.

The Chacoans watched the sky closely. High on Fajada Butte, a lone tower of rock inside the canyon, someone carved a spiral into the rock face behind three tall slabs of stone that lean against the cliff. At midday on the summer solstice, a single blade of sunlight slips between the slabs and cuts straight through the centre of the spiral, the effect now called the Sun Dagger. The artist Anna Sofaer noticed it in 1977, and other light patterns mark other turning points of the year.

Researchers have found that the great houses and the great kiva of Casa Rinconada line up not only with the sun but also with the moon's standstill cycle, an 18.6-year swing in how far north and south the moon rises and sets. No one could watch a full cycle quickly, so this knowledge had to be handed down across generations.

chan-chan.context_blurb:
On the dry northern coast of Peru, near the city of Trujillo, lie the vast mud walls of Chan Chan. It was the capital of the Chimú, a seafaring people who flourished from about 900 to 1470 CE and for a time rivalled the Inca. Tens of thousands of people once lived inside its great walled royal compounds.

The whole city, covering about 20 square kilometres, was built of mud brick, and its walls up to ten metres high have survived only because it almost never rains on this desert coast. It was the largest city in South America before Columbus.

The Chimú lived off the rich Pacific fisheries, so they carved fish again and again across their walls, along with waves, pelicans and cross-hatching that may picture a fishing net.

Around 1470 the Inca swept down the coast and conquered Chan Chan, holding the last Chimú king, Minchancaman, prisoner for life in Cuzco and carrying off the city's famous goldsmiths.

chicago.context_blurb:
Chicago rose on the swampy shore of Lake Michigan, at a low gap where two of North America's great water systems almost touch. In the 1800s it exploded into the nation's railway and meatpacking hub, burned in the Great Fire of 1871 and rebuilt itself into a laboratory for the modern city. Its engineers lifted buildings, reversed a river and invented the skyscraper.

In 1861 crews raised the six-storey Tremont House hotel about six feet on a thousand screw-jacks to fit new sewers beneath it, while its guests stayed in their rooms the whole time. In the 1850s and 1860s Chicago jacked up hundreds of buildings this way. Wooden houses that stood in the way were not torn down but put on logs and rolled through the streets to new lots, so often that a visiting Scot said he met moving houses almost every day.

William Le Baron Jenney's Home Insurance Building of 1885, ten storeys high, was held up by an inner skeleton of iron and steel, so the outer walls simply hung like curtains and height was no longer limited by thick walls. It is widely called the first skyscraper, though the claim is argued. In 1897 the elevated trains, the L, completed a rectangle of tracks around the business district, which is why downtown is called the Loop.

The city drank from Lake Michigan while its river poured sewage into the same lake. So engineers dug the Sanitary and Ship Canal, and on 2 January 1900 they broke the last dam and the Chicago River reversed, flowing away from the lake and inland toward the Mississippi. One branch of the river had become so foul with waste from the Union Stock Yards that gases from the rot rose through its surface, and Chicagoans still call it Bubbly Creek.

The lakefront stayed open because Aaron Montgomery Ward, who made his fortune selling by mail, fought four cases in the Illinois Supreme Court from 1890 and won them all, and today a long string of public parks lines the shore.

For the Willis Tower, first called the Sears Tower, the engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan bundled nine square tubes tightly side by side, stopping them at different heights so they brace one another against the wind. Rising 1,451 feet, it stood as the world's tallest building from 1973 until 1998.

Chicago is so flat because it sits on the floor of a huge vanished lake, Glacial Lake Chicago, the meltwater ancestor of Lake Michigan, which emptied some 13,000 years ago. Ridges such as Ridge Road trace its old beaches.

The city grew at the Chicago Portage, a marshy gap called Mud Lake that the explorers Jolliet and Marquette crossed in 1673, passing between the waters of the Great Lakes and those of the Mississippi River, and Jolliet saw that a canal there would join them. The Illinois and Michigan Canal opened in 1848 and made Chicago the hub of the Midwest.

Since 1975 the city has been building the Deep Tunnel, more than 100 miles of tunnels up to 350 feet underground and 33 feet wide, feeding reservoirs able to store upward of 17 billion gallons of sewage and rainwater. It is among the largest engineering works on Earth.

chichen-itza.context_blurb:
On the flat limestone plain of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula rises Chichén Itzá, one of the greatest cities of the Maya world, which flourished from about 600 to 1200 CE. Its builders blended Maya and Toltec styles and wove the sky, the gods and even sound into their stone. Every part of the city seems to hide a calendar, a god or an echo.

At its heart stands the step pyramid El Castillo. Each of its four staircases has 91 steps, which make 364, and the final step onto the top platform makes 365, one for each day of the solar year, so the pyramid is a calendar in stone.

On the spring and autumn equinoxes, the late afternoon sun throws seven triangles of light down the edge of the north staircase, joining them into a rippling body that seems to slither down to the carved head at the bottom: Kukulkan, the Feathered Serpent, descending to earth. The effect lasts about half an hour, and the builders designed it on purpose.

In the Great Ball Court, the biggest ball court built anywhere in the ancient Americas, players had to drive a heavy rubber ball, using only hips, knees and elbows, up and through a stone ring fixed vertically to the wall about 8 metres overhead. A single goal was so hard that it could end the game. Carvings along the court show the deadly stakes: a defeated player kneels headless, and the seven streams gushing from his neck are carved as wriggling serpents, with one sprouting into a flowering plant, so that his blood becomes fresh life.

The court also works as a whispering gallery: a soft word spoken in the little temple at one end carries clearly to the temple at the far end, more than 135 metres away.

On top of the Temple of the Warriors lies a Chac Mool, a stone figure reclining on his elbows with knees raised and head turned sharply aside, holding a dish on his belly for offerings. Figures like it crown temples across old Mexico.

The Yucatán has almost no rivers or lakes at all. Its bedrock is porous limestone, so rain sinks straight down through the rock to the groundwater instead of running across the land. Where a cave roof has collapsed, that hidden water lies open in a round sinkhole, a cenote, and the Maya built their cities beside them. At the edge of Chichén Itzá lies the Sacred Cenote, about 60 metres across with cliffs 27 metres high, and when the rains failed the Maya cast gold, jade, incense and human offerings into it to plead with Chaac, the hook-nosed god of rain.

El Castillo holds a secret: it was built right over an earlier pyramid, which survives intact within. In April 1935 archaeologists tunnelling in found a throne carved as a jaguar, the Maya emblem of kingship, painted bright red, its spots inlaid with jade discs, its eyes made of jade balls and its teeth of white shell.

Nearby stands El Caracol, the snail, a round tower named for its spiral stair, whose narrow windows and corners point to the spots on the horizon where Venus rises and sets at the extremes of its eight-year cycle. The Maya watched Venus to time planting and war.

A single handclap below the pyramid's main stairway comes back as a chirp that drops from a high note to a low one, which the acoustic engineer David Lubman found in 1998 sounds strikingly like the call of the quetzal, a bird sacred to the Maya. The evenly spaced steps reflect the clap back as a rapid run of falling notes.

chocolate-hills-of-bohol.context_blurb:
On the island of Bohol in the central Philippines, a flat plain is covered with grassy cones so alike in size and shape that they look laid out by a giant's hand. They are green after the rains and brown as chocolate in the dry months. They are among the strangest landscapes in Asia.

Around 1,270 of the cones, about 1,268 by careful count, crowd more than 50 square kilometres of the plain, most of them between 30 and 120 metres high. A local legend says two feuding giants made them by hurling sand and boulders at each other until they tired and made peace.

The rock is pale grey limestone, and the famous colour comes from the blanket of coarse cogon grass that covers the hills and dries brown in the dry months. When the rains return, the hills turn green again.

The limestone is packed with fossils, the shells of tiny ocean animals such as foraminifera, along with coral and algae, proof that a shallow sea once covered Bohol. Rain dissolving that limestone over ages carved the cones, a landform called cone karst. Bohol became the Philippines' first UNESCO Global Geopark in 2023.

classic-karst-the-land-that-named-itself.context_blurb:
Above the Adriatic port of Trieste, along the border of Slovenia and Italy, stretches a dry, stony plateau where rivers vanish into holes and lakes come and go with the seasons. Scientists first studied this kind of country here in the 1800s, and the plateau's name now labels such landscapes all over the world.

The plateau is the Kras, Karst in German, and geographers adopted its name, karst, for limestone country everywhere that drains underground, a word whose ancient root simply means bare, stony rock.

Falling rain absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and becomes weak carbonic acid, which slowly dissolves limestone and tunnels downward. That is why karst has so few streams or lakes on its surface.

The Reka, a river that rises on Mount Snežnik, flows along the surface like any other until, at the village of Škocjan, it plunges into the rock and disappears into the Škocjan Caves. The caves have been a World Heritage Site since 1986. Inside, the river roars through Hanke's Channel, a canyon underground about 3.5 kilometres long and over 140 metres high, and after heavy storms a narrow choke point downstream backs the flood up so that it can climb more than 100 metres up the walls.

After some 34 kilometres in the dark, the Reka bursts back into daylight near the Adriatic coast as the springs of the Timavo, which runs only about 2 kilometres before it reaches the sea. The Roman poet Virgil described it bursting from the mountain through many mouths.

Lake Cerknica, Slovenia's largest lake in the wet season, fills a polje, a flat-floored karst basin, and every summer it drains away through holes in its own bed, leaving ground where farmers cut hay. Locals fish it when it is full and farm it when it is empty.

Karst has its own vocabulary, and the spot where a whole surface stream gulps down into the rock, as the Reka does at Škocjan, is called a ponor. The Serbian geographer Jovan Cvijić turned the words of this corner of Slovenia into a world science in 1893.

cloud-forests-the-forests-in-the-clouds.context_blurb:
On certain tropical mountainsides, usually between about 1,500 and 3,000 metres up, warm damp air rising from the lowlands cools into cloud and wraps the trees in mist nearly every day. These are the cloud forests, dripping, green and crowded with life found nowhere else, from the quetzal to the olinguito.

At Monteverde, high on a ridge in Costa Rica, the passing clouds soak the leaves so constantly that they drip even when no rain falls, the mark of a cloud forest, a tropical mountain forest bathed in almost permanent cloud.

Mosses, orchids and bromeliads crowd the branches there, growing with no soil at all, plants called epiphytes, from Greek words meaning upon a plant. At Monteverde about 878 species, nearly a third of all the plants, live this way.

The leaves also catch the fine droplets of the drifting cloud and let them drip to the ground, water called fog drip, which keeps mountain streams flowing through dry weeks. No rain gauge catches it, and in one study in eastern Mexico the fog delivered far more water than the rain.

The Inca built Machu Picchu about 2,430 metres up on the eastern side of the Andes, in a cloud forest kept damp by moisture rising from the Amazon basin below. Morning mist wraps the ruins almost every day.

Higher still, the trees suddenly give out. Above the cloud forest in the northern Andes spreads the páramo, a cold, wet, treeless grassland between about 3,000 and 4,800 metres, frozen on many nights and thawed and soaked by day. Its signature plant is the frailejón, a giant rosette of leaves on a thick trunk wrapped in shaggy dead leaves, so that whole slopes look dotted with woolly statues in the fog. Spongy plants like it soak up rain and release it slowly, feeding the water supplies of Bogotá and Quito.

coastal-forests-mangroves-and-kelp.context_blurb:
Two of the world's most remarkable forests grow along the edge of the sea, and neither is made of ordinary trees. In the tropics, salt-loving mangroves stand on stilt-like roots in muddy tidal water. In cold seas, golden kelp sways upward from the seabed in underwater woods. Both rank among the richest living places on Earth.

Where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet the Bay of Bengal spreads the Sundarbans, the beautiful forest, a maze of tidal channels and islands across India and Bangladesh, and no mangrove forest anywhere is bigger. Mangroves are among the very few woody plants that grow rooted in salt water, and the forest can be crossed only by boat.

The land is so low and flat that roughly one third of the forest floor disappears under the sea and comes back with the tides every day. The mangrove roots slow the tide and comb silt from the water, so the forest steadily builds new land out into the sea, and the same tangle of roots blunts the storm surges of cyclones.

The mangroves also bury carbon deep in soggy mud with no oxygen, which keeps it out of the air for hundreds of years, and scientists call carbon trapped this way by coastal ecosystems blue carbon. Acre for acre they store several times more than a tropical rainforest.

Far to the south, off Cape Town, grows the Great African Sea Forest, made famous by the film My Octopus Teacher. Its tall, tree-like fronds belong to kelp, which is a giant brown alga, a seaweed, and not a plant with true roots, stems and leaves at all. It runs more than 1,000 kilometres up the cold coast toward Namibia.

Off California, giant kelp forests rise from the seabed toward the light. Few living things grow faster than giant kelp, and a single frond can stretch as much as two feet, some 30 to 60 centimetres, in one day. Its root-like holdfast grips the rock, and rows of gas-filled floats along the fronds hold the whole tower upright, as high as 45 metres. It grows only in cool water, which is why kelp forests cling to coasts washed by cold currents.

cold-currents-and-the-coastal-deserts-th.context_blurb:
Along the western shores of several continents, icy currents flow toward the equator from the polar seas. They chill the air just above the water so that its moisture turns to fog instead of rain, and the land beside them stays parched. That is why some of the driest deserts on Earth sit right beside the ocean, in Chile and in Namibia.

Off northern Chile flows the cold Humboldt Current, and because cold air near the sea cannot rise to build rain clouds, it breeds fog but almost never a downpour, one main reason the Atacama is drier than anywhere else beyond the polar regions. The sea there sits near 16 °C, far cooler than most tropical water, and the Andes and sinking air from high pressure help keep the rain away.

The Atacama's core gets only about 15 millimetres of rain a year, and its lifeless ground is so like Mars that NASA brings rovers there to rehearse missions. One weather station logged just half a millimetre a year for nearly four decades.

What little water the coast receives comes as the camanchaca, a thick sea fog that climbs the cliffs at dawn and burns off as the sun rises, making the Atacama the largest fog desert on Earth. Villagers hang mesh fog catchers, atrapanieblas, across the ridges to comb drinking water from it, and big arrays near Huasco have yielded tens of thousands of litres a day, between 10,000 and 50,000. The village of Chungungo once ran 94 such nets to supply about 300 people.

Across the Atlantic, the cold Benguela Current runs up the coast of southern Africa and creates the Namib. The Namib has been dry for some 55 to 80 million years, and many call it the oldest desert in the world. Fog, not rain, is its main water on more than 180 days a year, and its dunes rise to about 300 metres.

Fog off the Benguela drove so many ships aground on Namibia's northern shore that their hulks, together with the bones of whales and seals, gave it the name the Skeleton Coast. Portuguese sailors called it the Gates of Hell, and the San people named it the Land God Made in Anger. Some wrecks now lie far inland as the dunes advance.

Deep in the Namib lies Deadvlei, a white clay pan ringed by giant dunes. Its camel-thorn trees died some six or seven centuries ago, once the advancing dunes had cut off the river that fed them. Yet the dead trees still stand whole, because the air is so dry that the fungi and bacteria that make wood rot cannot survive there. The sun has simply scorched them black.

continental-drift-and-plate-tectonics.context_blurb:
Earth's rigid outer shell is cracked into a dozen or so great plates that creep across the hot, slowly flowing rock beneath them, carrying continents and ocean floors along. Where they pull apart, new sea floor is born; where they collide, mountains rise; where they slide past each other, faults grind and the ground shakes. The idea took most of the 20th century to win acceptance.

Slide South America across the Atlantic and Brazil's bulge tucks into West Africa's coast so neatly, even along the edges of the underwater continental shelves, that the best explanation is that the two continents were once one single landmass, later torn apart. Alfred Wegener pointed to that fit in 1912. He called the supercontinent Pangaea, Greek for all Earth, ringed by one world ocean, Panthalassa, and it later broke into a northern and a southern half about 200 million years ago.

Critics called the fit a coincidence, so Wegener turned to fossils. Mesosaurus, a little reptile of freshwater lakes and ponds that could never have crossed a salt ocean, turns up in Brazil and in West Africa, on the two coasts that once touched, and nowhere in between.

A few metres under the top of Mount Everest, the pale limestone holds fossils of trilobites and crinoids, sea creatures that lived only in the ocean, so that rock began as the bed of a warm, shallow sea about 450 million years ago. The plate carrying India has been ramming north into the rest of Asia, crumpling the crust upward, and Everest still rises about 4 millimetres a year.

At Thingvellir in Iceland, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge breaks onto dry land, and visitors can stand in the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates while the two pull apart about 2 centimetres a year. Magma wells up to fill the gap, building new crust.

Around the Pacific runs the Ring of Fire, about 40,000 kilometres long, where heavy ocean floor dives down beneath the plates around it, melting and feeding volcanoes, a process called subduction. Nine in ten of the world's earthquakes strike along it. At its deepest, the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench reaches about 10,935 metres, deeper than Everest's 8,849 metres is tall, so Everest could sink into it with some 2 kilometres of water to spare. In January 1960 the deep-diving craft Trieste carried Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh all the way down.

In September 2005, in Ethiopia's Afar desert, a rift 60 kilometres long split the desert open within ten days, and geologists realised they were watching the floor of a new ocean begin to split apart. Africa is slowly breaking in two there, and one day the Red Sea will pour in.

California's San Andreas Fault is a boundary where two plates, the Pacific and the North American, scrape sideways past one another, so Los Angeles, riding the Pacific side, inches northwest by about 3 to 4 centimetres every year and in about 20 million years will sit right next to San Francisco.

The Hawaiian islands come from a hotspot that stays put while the plate drifts over it, so the sharp bend in the chain of old volcanoes records the moment, about 47 million years ago, when the Pacific plate changed the direction it was moving.

What drove the plates was the last puzzle. In the years after the Second World War, the mapmakers Marie Tharp and Bruce Heezen charted a great rift valley running along the ridge in the middle of the Atlantic. Then in 1963 two British scientists, Vine and Matthews, showed that the magnetism of the sea floor lies in mirror-image stripes on both sides of the ridge, proving that new sea floor forms there and spreads away in both directions. Wegener's drifting continents had their engine at last, and the theory became plate tectonics.

continents-in-collision-the-great-mounta.context_blurb:
Where two continents slowly crash together, the ground has nowhere to go but up. India's collision with Asia built the Himalayas and is still pushing them higher; older collisions raised the Alps, the Zagros of Iran and the Appalachians. A mountain range is a car crash in slow motion, spread over fifty million years.

India is still ploughing north into Asia at roughly 5 centimetres a year, about the speed at which human fingernails grow. Because India is thick, light continental rock, it cannot sink into the mantle like ocean floor, so for some fifty million years it has been forcing itself in beneath Asia, doubling the thickness of the crust. That doubled crust lifted the Tibetan Plateau, bigger than Western Europe and about 4,500 metres high on average, and gave Tibet its nickname, Roof of the World.

Every one of the 14 mountains on Earth taller than 8,000 metres stands in the Himalaya and the neighbouring Karakoram, all 14 of them raised by this single collision. Nanga Parbat in northern Pakistan, at the western corner of the range where India pushes hardest, is listed by Guinness as the fastest-rising mountain anywhere, climbing about 7 millimetres a year.

Mount Everest's summit was once under water. Its top rock is limestone holding trilobites and sea-lilies, also called crinoids, that lived in a warm tropical sea some 450 million years back. That sea floor belonged to the Tethys Ocean, the sea that once separated India from Asia, until their collision closed it some 50 million years ago and crumpled its bed into the peaks.

A 2024 study found that nearly half of Everest's present rise of about 2 millimetres a year comes from a river cutting away rock nearby: about 89,000 years ago the Arun River joined the Kosi and gouged out so much stone that the lightened crust is springing upward.

The same engine is running elsewhere. In western Iran the Arabian plate is shoving into Eurasia by some 25 millimetres each year, and the squeeze is folding up Iran's Zagros Mountains. It is a live collision of continent against continent, the same engine that built the Himalayas. In the Alps, the summit of the Matterhorn above Zermatt is not European rock at all but a slab of the African plate, carried hundreds of kilometres north and stranded on top when Africa crushed the Alps upward. Geologists call the stranded slab the Dent Blanche nappe, and it travelled at least 500 kilometres from Africa's old edge.

The soft green Appalachians of the eastern United States rose about 300 million years ago as Pangaea came together, and models suggest that in their youth they stood as tall as today's Himalayas, before erosion wore them down. Before the Atlantic existed, the same chain continued straight on into the mountains of what is now Scotland and Scandinavia, and eastern Greenland too, until the opening ocean tore it in two.

coral-reefs-and-the-heat-that-bleaches-t.context_blurb:
A coral reef is built by tiny animals, coral polyps, which live in colonies and lay down skeletons of limestone. Over thousands of years those skeletons pile into reefs that hold some of the richest life on Earth. The polyps depend on a partnership with even smaller lodgers, and that partnership breaks down when the sea grows too warm.

Off Queensland in northeastern Australia, the Great Barrier Reef runs about 2,300 kilometres through the Coral Sea, the largest structure ever built by living creatures and big enough to be seen from space.

A coral animal is pale and almost see-through; its brilliant golds, greens and pinks come from microscopic algae called zooxanthellae living inside its tissue, which use sunlight to make food for the coral. When the water stays too hot, stressed corals across a whole reef expel these algae at once and turn bone-white, an event called coral bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead yet; if the water cools in time, the algae can return.

When a marine heatwave struck in 2016, it killed somewhere between roughly 30 and 50 percent of the coral in the reef's northern section in a single event. Reefs can recover from one hot year, but not when a second strikes before they heal, and 2017 brought another.

The Maldives, about 1,192 islands in the Indian Ocean strung along 26 rings of coral, is built entirely of coral and is the lowest country on Earth, with its highest natural point only about 2.4 metres above the sea.

A ring of coral islands around a lagoon, with open ocean all round and no island in the middle, like Enewetak in the Pacific, is called an atoll. Most of the world's roughly 440 atolls lie in the Pacific. Charles Darwin, sailing on the Beagle, reasoned that each atoll began as a reef fringing a volcano, and that the volcano was gradually sinking while the coral kept building upward to stay in the sunlit shallows. In 1952, drillers on Enewetak hit volcanic rock about 1,400 metres down, and the team put up a sign: Darwin was right.

Off Belize, the Great Blue Hole, a perfect dark-blue circle about 300 metres across and 125 deep in Lighthouse Reef, began as a limestone cave on dry land during the ice ages, when the sea was far lower, and was flooded when the oceans rose. Stalactites found inside prove it was once a dry cavern. Jacques Cousteau made it famous in 1971.

crater-lake.context_blurb:
In the Cascade Range of southern Oregon lies a lake so blue it looks like a pool of ink. It fills the hollow left when a great volcano, Mount Mazama, blew apart and collapsed about 7,700 years ago. The Klamath people were living nearby when it happened, and they still tell a story of it.

When Mazama emptied its underground chamber of magma, its summit fell in, leaving a caldera, a basin far larger than the small pit around a volcano's vent. The blast poured out roughly 50 cubic kilometres of magma, about 40 times as much as Mount St. Helens did in 1980, the largest eruption in the Cascades in a million years. Its pale ash still forms a marker layer across the Pacific Northwest.

No river flows into Crater Lake, so it is filled only by rain and snowmelt, mostly from the deep winter snows, and its whole volume takes about 150 years to renew. With almost no mud or algae, it is one of the clearest lakes on Earth. At 1,949 feet, or 594 metres, no lake in the United States is deeper. Scientists lowering a white disc into the water could still see it about 100 feet down, around 30 metres, and in 1997 they recorded 142 feet. Sunlight sinks deep and only the blue light scatters back, giving the lake its famous colour.

After the collapse, new eruptions built a cinder cone on the caldera floor that rose above the water, and in 1885 William Gladstone Steel named it Wizard Island because it looked like a sorcerer's pointed hat.

Since at least 1896 a whole hemlock log called the Old Man of the Lake has floated upright, standing straight up like a post with about 1.2 metres above the surface. The cold, pure water has preserved the wood, which is over 450 years old, and in one summer it was tracked drifting at least 62 miles around the lake.

The Klamath tell of Llao, spirit of the underworld, who lived beneath the mountain, and Skell, spirit of the sky, who fought him. In their account the battle ended when Skell hurled the mountaintop down onto Llao and sealed him deep below, where the lake now lies. Because the Klamath were living here when Mazama fell, many believe the story preserves a real memory carried across thousands of years.

cremona-the-town-of-stradivarius-violins.context_blurb:
Cremona is a small city on the plain of northern Italy where, between about 1550 and 1750, a few families of craftsmen invented and perfected the modern violin, viola and cello. The greatest of them, Antonio Stradivari, worked here for most of a very long life. His instruments still set the standard, and nobody can fully explain why.

Antonio Stradivari, who lived from about 1644 to 1737 and hardly ever left Cremona, made violas and cellos too, but it is his violins that the world calls the finest ever made. Any instrument from his hands is called a Stradivarius. Inside each one he glued a paper label, in Latin, saying that Antonio Stradivari of Cremona made it in such-and-such a year. His workshop stood on a square in the centre of town, now called Piazza Roma.

Over some 75 years he made around 1,100 instruments, and after three centuries of wars, fires and hard use, about 650 survive. A single one can sell for millions.

In 2011 the Lady Blunt, a violin he made in 1721, sold for a record 15.9 million dollars, and its owner, the Nippon Music Foundation, gave every penny to relief for Japan after that year's earthquake and tsunami. The violin is named for Lady Anne Blunt, the granddaughter of the poet Byron.

The most celebrated of all, the 1716 Messiah, now in the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, still looks almost new because it has hardly ever been played. A violinist joked that it was like the Messiah: everyone expected it, but it never appeared.

Why do they sound so good? One leading theory points to the Little Ice Age, a long cold spell in Stradivari's lifetime, when spruce in the high Alpine forests grew slowly and made unusually dense, even-grained wood. Tree rings trace his spruce to the Val di Fiemme in the Italian Alps. A rival theory looks to chemical treatments of the wood instead, and neither is proven.

Cremona had other masters. The great violinist Niccolò Paganini prized a 1743 violin by Stradivari's rival Giuseppe Guarneri above all others and called it the Cannon, for the huge power of its sound.

In a blind test held in Paris in 2012, ten top soloists wore welder's goggles so they could not see the instruments, and most of them chose a brand-new violin over the old Stradivari ones as their favourite. Later listening tests found audiences could not reliably tell old from new either, so the famous secret has never been proven.

cuneiform-and-the-clay-tablets-of-sumer.context_blurb:
In the river plain of southern Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, the Sumerians invented one of the first writing systems on Earth late in the 4th millennium BCE. Scribes pressed marks into soft clay with a cut reed, and many of those tablets have outlasted 5,000 years. The script was used for some three thousand years, then forgotten for nearly two thousand more.

Mesopotamia had almost no stone and little wood to spare, but endless river mud, so its scribes wrote on wet clay, shaping a tablet, marking it while damp and then drying it in the sun or baking it hard. Pressing the corner of the reed into the clay left a little triangular mark, and the script is named cuneiform from the Latin cuneus, a wedge, because every sign is built from wedges.

Before writing, bookkeepers counted goods with small clay tokens shut away in a hollow ball of clay, and writing seems to have begun when they pressed each token's shape into the outside of the ball so they could check the count without breaking it. Soon they skipped the tokens and drew the shapes straight onto flat tablets.

The oldest tablets, from the city of Uruk around 3300 BC, are temple accounts, and among the very first things anyone wrote down were the daily bread and beer handed out to workers, the twin staples of Sumer. Writing was invented for bookkeeping, not poetry. Sumerian scribes counted in sixty rather than in tens, because sixty splits evenly in so many ways, and that is why a minute has 60 seconds, an hour 60 minutes and a circle 360 degrees.

The script was first made to write Sumerian, the everyday tongue of the people of Uruk, but a script is only a set of signs, so over three thousand years many unrelated peoples, the Babylonians among them, borrowed the same wedges for their own languages.

Paper and papyrus crumble, but some half a million clay tablets survive. The reason is surprising: when enemies burned down the cities, the flames baked the tablets hard like pottery in a kiln. The great library of Nineveh survived precisely because it was set on fire.

That library belonged to the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, who gathered more than 30,000 tablets, his scribes hunting down and copying old writings in every province. He was proudest of a rare skill for a king of his day: he could read the old scripts himself, including the already ancient Sumerian, when most kings relied on scribes. His library held the fullest copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh, written on 12 tablets. The eleventh tells of a great flood sent by the gods to drown the world, survived by one man in a huge boat, a story like Noah's but written down long before Genesis.

When George Smith, who had trained as an engraver and taught himself to read the wedges, deciphered that tablet at the British Museum in 1872, he grew so excited that he began pulling off his clothes and ran around the room shouting. He had studied the script on his lunch breaks.

Reading the script again had taken heroic work. Around 500 BC the Persian ruler Darius the Great ordered a huge inscription cut into a limestone cliff at Behistun, some 100 metres above the ground. In the 1830s and 1840s the scholar Henry Rawlinson copied it sign by sign while dangling on ropes against the sheer rock, with a nimble local boy helping on the worst stretch. Darius had his boast carved in three languages side by side, and one of the three scripts, Old Persian, was nearly an alphabet, so scholars cracked it first and used it to unlock the others. Behistun became the Rosetta Stone of cuneiform.

The script still had tricks. One sign could stand for a whole word or for a sound. Some signs were never spoken at all: determinatives, silent markers that told the reader whether the next word named a place, a god or something made of wood, so that a town would not be mistaken for a person.

cusco.context_blurb:
In the Andes of Peru, some 3,400 metres above sea level, lies Cusco, the old seat of the Inca emperors. When the Spanish arrived in 1533 they tore down temples and built churches and mansions on top of the Inca walls, yet those walls still line the old streets. The city's stones, roads and festivals still tell how the Inca ruled.

The Inca called their capital Qosqo, traditionally translated as the navel, because to them Cusco was the navel of the world, the still centre of their empire. From its main square four royal roads ran out to the four quarters of the realm, and the Inca called their empire Tawantinsuyu, the four parts together.

Travellers who fly in from sea level often get dizzy and breathless in the thin air, and for thousands of years Andean people have chewed coca leaves, or brewed them as tea, to ease altitude sickness.

By tradition, the emperor Pachacuti remade Cusco in the 1400s in the shape of a puma, with the hilltop fortress of Sacsayhuamán as its head and the meeting of two rivers as its tail. The Inca had no iron tools, no wheel and no draft animals, so they built Sacsayhuamán's giant limestone walls, some blocks over 100 tonnes, with nothing but stone hammers and the muscle of their workers. A Spanish chronicler wrote that not even a coin could slip between two blocks.

In an alley of the old town, one greenish block in the wall of an Inca palace is famous for its twelve fitted corners, each cut to lock into its neighbours without mortar. It appears on postcards all over Peru.

The holiest temple, Coricancha, the golden enclosure, had walls faced with sheets of gold and a garden of plants and animals made of gold and silver. The Spanish stripped it, much of the gold going to the ransom of the captured emperor Atahualpa, and built the church of Santo Domingo on its walls. In the earthquake of 1950 that church cracked and fell, but the Inca walls beneath it held, because their dry-fitted stones, cut to lean slightly inward, can shift during a quake and settle back into place instead of breaking.

The Inca bound their empire together with some 40,000 kilometres of stone roads. News sped along them carried by teams of relay runners, the chasquis, each sprinting his stretch at full speed and handing off to the next. Where a road crossed a gorge they hung a rope bridge, and the last one still in use, Q'eswachaka over the Apurímac River, is rebuilt by hand every year from braided mountain grass.

The Inca had no writing at all, so their officials kept the census, taxes and storehouse records on knotted, coloured cords called quipu, where the type and position of each knot gave units, tens and hundreds.

Every 24 June crowds fill the field below Sacsayhuamán for Inti Raymi, the great Inca festival of Inti, the god of the sun, which the Spanish banned for centuries and Peruvians revived in 1944.

cusco-and-sacsayhuaman.context_blurb:
Above Cusco, the old Inca capital high in the Peruvian Andes, rise the walls of Sacsayhuamán, a vast stone complex that may have been both fortress and sacred precinct. Its giant blocks fit together so perfectly, without mortar, that visitors stand and stare. How the Inca shaped and moved them has puzzled people for centuries.

To the Inca, Qosqo was the navel of the world, and old records say they laid it out in the shape of a crouching puma, with Sacsayhuamán on the hill as its head. The fortress's three great terrace walls zigzag up the ridge in sharp angles, long imagined as the puma's bared teeth.

The joints are so tight that guides still show tourists that not even a sheet of paper will slide between two blocks. In 1553 a Spanish chronicler wrote that not even a small silver coin would fit.

Every 24 June thousands crowd the grassy esplanade beneath the fortress for Inti Raymi, the Inca festival of the sun, with a royal parade honouring Inti, the sun god.

In the city, on a lane called Hatunrumiyoc, crowds gather around a grey block set in Inca Roca's palace wall that locks into its neighbours on twelve separate sides, the famous Twelve-Angled Stone.

From Cusco's central square ran the Qhapaq Ñan, the greatest road network of the ancient Americas, about 40,000 kilometres of royal roads over snow peaks, deserts and rainforest. It linked land that now belongs to Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Colombia.

When the earthquake of 21 May 1950 wrecked over a third of the city, the Inca walls beneath came through untouched, because Inca masons made their walls lean slightly inward, with interlocking blocks and doorways wider at the base, so the stones lock tighter as the ground shakes.

Some people insist that only aliens or some forgotten advanced machine could have cut these stones. The evidence says otherwise. Inca workers shaped every block by pounding it with harder river cobbles used as hammerstones, and the faces still carry thousands of tiny dents from the blows. The largest block, perhaps 128 to 200 tonnes, was dragged about 35 kilometres from its quarry by hundreds of workers on ramps and log rollers, with no wheels or draft animals.

In the city below, the Qorikancha, the Temple of the Sun, had a sacred garden where the corn, flowers and some twenty life-size llamas with their herders were all made of gold and silver, according to Spanish chroniclers. The Spanish stripped it to pay the ransom of the captured emperor Atahualpa.

cyrillic-and-the-brothers-of-thessalonik.context_blurb:
Hundreds of millions of people, from Moscow to Belgrade, write in the Cyrillic alphabet. It grew out of the work of two Greek brothers from the Byzantine world who set out in the 9th century to bring Christianity to the Slavs. To do it, they invented a brand-new alphabet, and the one we call Cyrillic came a little later.

The brothers, Cyril, born Constantine, and Methodius, born Michael, grew up in Thessaloniki, the great port of northern Greece, where their father served as a Byzantine officer. They are honoured as the Apostles to the Slavs.

In 862 they journeyed north to the Slavs of Great Moravia, in the heart of Europe. A monk who called himself Hrabar later wrote that before they came, the Slavs had no letters of their own and kept records with strokes and incisions, rough tally marks and scratches.

Since Greek and Latin letters could not spell many Slavic sounds, around 863 the brothers designed letters made of swirls, rings and crosses, an alphabet called Glagolitic, from glagol, which means the word.

Cyril died in Rome early in 869, and the neater script named after him was actually created later by his followers at the Preslav school, in the First Bulgarian Empire, where the Bulgarian tsar Boris I had taken them in. The oldest dated Cyrillic inscription, from 921, was found nearby. The name honours Cyril; he did not make it.

The Preslav scholars took most of the letters from formal Greek book-writing, but for sounds Greek lacked, such as sh, zh and ch, they borrowed shapes from the Glagolitic alphabet. So the brothers' first alphabet still hides inside every Cyrillic page.

Cyrillic soon pushed Glagolitic aside across most of the Slavic world, but in Croatia priests and clerks on Adriatic islands such as Krk kept writing Glagolitic until the early 19th century, almost ten centuries after the brothers created it.
