dallol-and-the-danakil-depression.context_blurb:
In the Afar region of northern Ethiopia, the land sinks into the Danakil Depression, one of the lowest, hottest and strangest places on Earth. Here the crust is slowly tearing apart. Pools of acid steam among crusts of salt in impossible colours, lava churns in an open crater, and Afar miners still cut salt by hand as their ancestors did.

At Dallol, steaming pools of neon green, yellow and orange sit on twisted salt, a landscape so alien that scientists study it as a stand-in for Mars. The Danakil around it is the hottest place on Earth by year-round average, near 35 °C, and its floor lies about 120 metres below sea level.

The colours are painted by minerals, not living things: as scalding brine wells up and dries, dissolved iron and sulphur, along with copper, crystallise out in bands of green, gold and orange. Magma only a few kilometres down heats the water so fiercely, and fills it with so much sulphur, that some pools reach a pH below zero, about as acidic as battery acid.

Beneath the depression the salt runs as deep as two kilometres, laid down as an arm of the Red Sea flooded the sinking basin again and again and then dried away in the desert sun. For centuries Afar miners have cut that salt into flat slabs called amole, loaded about forty onto each camel, and carried them to the highlands, where the slabs served Ethiopians as money.

The Danakil sits on the Afar Triple Junction, where the African, Arabian and Somali plates are pulling apart a centimetre or two each year, and geologists expect that in millions of years the sea will pour in and the basin will become a whole new ocean.

A short trek away stands Erta Ale, the smoking mountain in the Afar language. Its lava lake has stayed molten since 1906 or earlier, longer than any other, and such open lakes of lava are so uncommon that in 2019 there were only about eight on the entire planet.

damascus.context_blurb:
Damascus, the capital of Syria, grew up in an oasis where mountain water meets the desert at the eastern edge of the Mediterranean world. It has been a city for thousands of years, and in the 7th century it became the capital of the Umayyad caliphs, rulers of the first great Islamic empire. Its old streets still follow a Roman plan.

Jericho was founded earlier, but its people abandoned it again and again, while Damascus was a thriving settlement by 2000 BC and has never been emptied since, so it has a strong claim to be the oldest continuously inhabited city in the world. Aleppo and Byblos are its chief rivals for that title.

The Barada River, fed by mountain snowmelt in the Anti-Lebanon range, fans out across the plain into the Ghouta, the ring of watered orchards and fields that has kept the city alive since ancient times. Damascus sits about 680 metres up and some 80 kilometres from the sea.

At the heart of the old city stands the Umayyad Mosque, begun in 706 by the caliph al-Walid I on ground already holy for millennia, where Hadad the storm god, then the Roman Jupiter and then Christian worshippers had each had their temple or church. About 12,000 labourers built it, and gold mosaics of a green, watery paradise covered some 4,000 square metres of its walls. Inside, a small domed shrine is said to hold John the Baptist's head, and Christians and Muslims, who honour him as the prophet Yahya, pray there side by side. Several other places also claim the relic; the shrine rests on tradition, not proof.

The old Roman main avenue, about 1,500 metres long, is the Street Called Straight, where in the Book of Acts a disciple named Ananias is sent to find Saul of Tarsus, newly blinded, who would become the apostle Paul.

The city also gave its name to a legendary steel. Blades rippled with watery patterns were forged and traded here, though the raw steel came from India and Sri Lanka. By about 1900 the craft had stopped, and the exact method was lost and has never been fully recovered. Scholars still argue about just how the old smiths did it.

damascus-steel-the-lost-watered-blades.context_blurb:
Between about the 9th and 17th centuries, smiths in the Islamic world forged sword blades famous for their beauty and their edge. Across the polished steel ran dark, rippling bands like flowing water. The blades carried the name of the Syrian city where many were sold, but their secret came from far away, and in time it was forgotten.

The rippling pattern was part of the metal, forged into the blade from within, made by microscopic bands of hard carbide crystals locked into the steel. It was not paint added afterwards. The Arabic word damas behind the name also means watered, a perfect fit for those ripples, which is why the metal is still called watered or damask steel.

Syria made no such steel itself: it imported little cakes of steel called wootz, made far to the east in India and Sri Lanka, and Damascus smiths forged them into swords. In Sri Lanka, smiths sealed iron with carbon-rich bamboo and leaves in clay pots and let the monsoon winds blow their furnaces hot enough to melt it into steel unusually rich in carbon. The word wootz comes from a Tamil word meaning to melt.

The blades cut so well that legends grew around them. The most famous tale claims a true Damascus blade could slice a wisp of silk that simply drifted down onto its edge, though no one ever proved it.

As the supply of wootz dried up, the craft faded, and by about 1900 the knowledge of how to make true Damascus steel had died out and been forgotten. The last eyewitness account of the old process was recorded in 1903. In the 1990s the metallurgists John Verhoeven and Alfred Pendray recreated the pattern and found that a trace of vanadium in the Indian ore had been a hidden key.

In 2006 Peter Paufler's team in Dresden examined a 17th-century sabre under a powerful microscope and reported carbon nanotubes inside the steel, a claim other scientists still dispute. Long before, the great scientist Michael Faraday had tried to crack the secret and guessed wrong.

death-valley.context_blurb:
In eastern California, between steep mountain walls, lies Death Valley, the lowest, driest and hottest place in North America. Its floor sinks below sea level and its summer air can top 50 °C. The pioneers who named it expected to die there, yet the valley hides snow, wandering stones and sudden carpets of flowers.

In 1849 a party of Gold Rush families took a shortcut and were stranded for weeks until William Manly and John Rogers, both still young, walked out and returned with food, and despite the grim name one of them gave the valley as they left, just one of the party had died.

On 10 July 1913 the thermometer at Furnace Creek read 134 °F, or 56.7 °C, and the world's weather authority, the WMO, still lists it as the hottest air temperature ever measured on Earth. Some experts think the reading ran a little high, and the hottest readings of sun-baked ground are a separate record held elsewhere.

Badwater Basin, 282 feet below sea level, is the continent's lowest point on dry ground, yet just 15 miles away rises Telescope Peak, an 11,049-foot summit often capped with snow. Its floor is nearly 200 square miles of white salt that cracks into repeating hexagons as briny groundwater rises, evaporates and shrinks the crust. The salt is all that is left of an Ice Age lake.

Storms do blow in from the Pacific, but four mountain ranges stand in the way, and each one forces the clouds up and wrings out their rain and snow, so the air that reaches the valley is dry. That makes Death Valley a rain-shadow desert, with under two inches of rain a year.

No river carved the valley: the crust of the whole region is being stretched apart, and the valley floor keeps sinking a few millimetres deeper each year as fresh faults crack the ground.

On Racetrack Playa, rocks weighing up to 600 pounds sit at the ends of long trails across the dry lakebed, as if they had walked. In 2014 scientists filmed the answer: on rare winter nights a shallow pond freezes into thin sheets of ice, and a light breeze pushes the floating panels, which shove the rocks across the mud.

After an unusually wet winter, the bare floor bursts into sheets of yellow Desert Gold, because the flowers wait out the dry years as seeds lying dormant in the soil. Big superblooms came in 1998, 2005 and 2016.

delhi-the-city-of-seven-cities.context_blurb:
Delhi, on the Yamuna plain of northern India, is called the city of seven cities, because ruler after ruler built a new capital beside the old ones instead of reusing them. Hindu kings, sultans, Mughal emperors and the British all left monuments here, and more than a thousand years of history stand side by side among its traffic and gardens.

Its most famous tower is the Qutb Minar, begun in 1199 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak, which rises 72.5 metres in bands of red and grey sandstone, ringed with balconies, the tallest brick minaret on Earth. In 1369 lightning shattered its top, and Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq repaired the crown, turning its old fourth storey into two, which gave the tower its five storeys.

Beside it stands the Quwwat-ul-Islam, Delhi's first mosque, begun in 1193, and an inscription over its gate states that its stone came from 27 Hindu and Jain temples pulled down to build it. The reused columns still show their old carvings of lotus flowers, bells and chains.

In the same courtyard stands a dark iron pillar about 7 metres tall and over 6 tonnes in weight, made in the Gupta era some 1,600 years ago. Ordinary iron standing outdoors that long would have rusted away, but this pillar has barely rusted at all. The metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur found the secret: the iron is unusually rich in phosphorus, which over time grows a thin protective film that heals itself, so an impurity, not purity, protects it. For centuries visitors believed a wish would come true if they stood with their backs to the pillar and stretched their arms around it until their fingertips met. So many hands rubbed it that a fence now guards it.

In the 1600s the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan made Delhi his capital and built the Red Fort beside the Yamuna, a palace-fortress of red sandstone whose walls run about 2.4 kilometres around halls and gardens. In its Hall of Private Audience, golden letters proclaim that if paradise exists anywhere in the world, this very hall is that paradise, and the verse says it is this three times over. There stood the Peacock Throne, a throne of solid gold, seven years in the making, that blazed with some 26,733 gems, including the Koh-i-Noor diamond. It was later carried off and broken up.

Humayun's Tomb, built between 1565 and 1572 as the first great garden-tomb in India, holds over a hundred members of the Mughal royal family and court, which earned it the nickname Dormitory of the Mughals. It stands in a charbagh, Persian for four gardens: a walled garden divided into four quarters by walkways and water channels that stand for the four rivers of paradise. Modelled on Timur's tomb in Samarkand, its white double dome rising over red sandstone led on to the greatest tomb of all, the Taj Mahal at Agra.

delphi-the-oracle-at-the-navel-of-the-wo.context_blurb:
High on a mountainside in central Greece, ringed by tall cliffs, lie the ruins of Delphi. For about a thousand years, kings, generals and ordinary Greeks climbed here to ask the god Apollo about the future, and the answers they received could launch wars and found cities. The Greeks believed this was the very centre of the world.

They called the spot the omphalos, the navel, so Delphi was the world's navel, marked by a carved stone shaped like a dome. Myth said Zeus released two eagles from the far ends of the earth, each speeding toward the other, and where they met, above Delphi, he set down the stone. The stone in the museum today is a Roman copy.

The temples and treasuries climb in terraces up the southern slopes of Mount Parnassus, high above the Gulf of Corinth.

Before it was Delphi the place was called Pytho, because legend said Apollo had killed a great serpent there, Python, that guarded the spring. From that serpent came the title of the priestess who spoke for Apollo: the Pythia, one of the most powerful women of the ancient world. Questions could be put to her on only one day each month.

Her answers were famous for their double meanings. When King Croesus asked whether to attack Persia and heard that a great empire would fall, he marched, lost, and the empire destroyed was his own kingdom of Lydia, conquered by Cyrus the Great. The historian Herodotus told the story.

The ancients said the Pythia sat on a three-legged seat over a cleft in the floor of the temple, breathing fumes that clouded her mind. In the 1980s and 1990s the geologist Jelle de Boer and the archaeologist John Hale found two faults crossing beneath the temple and proposed that earth movements released ethylene, a sweet-smelling gas once used to put patients to sleep. A spring near Delphi has shown traces of it, but the theory is still debated.

Over the doorway of Apollo's temple were carved short sayings of wisdom, the most famous being Know thyself, and beside it Nothing in excess. Every visitor read them on the way in.

denali.context_blurb:
In the heart of Alaska, the snowy bulk of Denali towers more than 20,000 feet over the forests and tundra, the highest peak in North America. It climbs almost straight from low ground instead of from a high plateau, and it stands so far north that its summit is one of the coldest places on the planet. For a century maps called it Mount McKinley; in 2015 it officially regained its old name.

The name comes from the Koyukon people, who have lived in the valleys around the mountain for countless generations, and in their language Denali means the High One.

In 2015 the US Geological Survey measured the peak with modern GPS and set its official height at 20,310 feet, ten feet less than the 1952 figure, not because the mountain shrank but because the measurement got sharper.

Of the Seven Summits, the highest peaks on each continent, Denali is the most northerly, at about 63 degrees north, just below the Arctic Circle. In December 2003 a station high on the mountain recorded a wind chill of about minus 118 °F, the lowest ever recorded in North America.

Denali's air is even thinner than its height suggests, because the atmosphere is squashed thinner over the polar regions than at the equator, so its summit feels like a far higher peak in the tropics. Climbers there struggle for breath as if they stood hundreds of metres higher.

From the lowland at its foot to its summit, Denali rises about 18,000 feet, more than Everest's own climb from base to top, because Everest starts from an already high plateau. Everest reaches higher above the sea, but it rises only about 12,000 to 15,000 feet above its own base.

Denali is still growing: along the great Denali Fault, the Pacific plate is grinding beneath the North American plate, pushing the whole Alaska Range upward. In another two million years the squeeze may lift it about a kilometre more.

devils-tower.context_blurb:
On the prairie of northeastern Wyoming, a colossal stump of grey rock stands about 265 metres high, its sides fluted with giant columns. Several Plains peoples hold it sacred and call it Bear Lodge. Geologists have puzzled over how it formed, and filmmakers made it one of the most recognisable shapes on Earth.

In Steven Spielberg's 1977 film Close Encounters of the Third Kind, a man haunted by the tower's shape builds its shape at supper out of his mashed potatoes, and the aliens' mothership lands there at the end.

On 24 September 1906, using a brand-new law that let presidents protect natural wonders, Theodore Roosevelt made Devils Tower the first national monument in the United States.

Its columns formed the same way as those of the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland: as a thick mass of molten rock cools, it shrinks and cracks apart into long four- to seven-sided columns. Here they reach up to about 600 feet tall.

The rock hardened underground about 40 million years ago inside softer layers of sediment, and over millions of years erosion stripped that soft rock away, leaving the hard core standing in the open. The tower was uncovered, not built up. It looks like an old volcano, but no eruption ever happened here: the surrounding rocks contain no volcanic ash at all, which an eruption would have left. Geologists still argue over exactly what kind of underground intrusion it was.

In a Kiowa story, seven girls fleeing a giant bear climbed onto a low rock that rose higher and higher, while the bear's claws raked the grooves down its sides, and the girls were carried up into the sky to become the Pleiades, the star cluster called the Seven Sisters. The name Devils Tower came from an 1875 expedition whose interpreter reportedly mistranslated the Lakota name, and many tribes ask that Bear Lodge be restored.

drainage-basins-and-the-continental-divi.context_blurb:
Every raindrop that lands on a continent is headed somewhere. Ridges and mountains sort the water into great natural regions, each draining to a single river mouth or lake, and the highest ridges decide which ocean the water will reach. In the Americas, one long ridge splits whole continents between the Pacific and the Atlantic.

The whole area of land that sends its water to a single river system is called a drainage basin, or watershed, and America's Mississippi collects the runoff of 31 states, nearly half the nation, and delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico.

The Continental Divide runs along the crest of the Rockies and on down the Andes, and rain falling on its western side flows to the Pacific Ocean, while water on the eastern side ends up in the Atlantic, much of it through the Gulf of Mexico. Where it crosses Colorado, the Divide reaches its North American summit on Grays Peak, 14,278 feet high.

At Triple Divide Peak in Montana, meltwater from one summit runs to three seas: one creek to the Pacific, one to the Gulf of Mexico, and a third north across Canada by the Nelson River into Hudson Bay.

At Two Ocean Pass in Wyoming's Teton Wilderness, a creek climbs right onto the Divide and splits in two: one half flows as Atlantic Creek some 3,488 miles to the Gulf of Mexico, the other as Pacific Creek 1,353 miles to the Pacific. It is said a fish could swim across the Continental Divide here.

In southern Wyoming the Divide splits and loops around the Great Divide Basin, an endorheic basin, sealed off from every ocean, where rain and snow simply pool and evaporate.

The biggest drainage basin on Earth belongs to the Amazon, about 7 million square kilometres, roughly 40 percent of South America, spread across nine countries. In Africa, the mighty Congo River loops twice across the equator on a journey of some 4,700 kilometres, draining a vast rainforest, and empties into the Atlantic Ocean at the Gulf of Guinea.

In southern Venezuela the Casiquiare channel breaks away from the upper Orinoco and carries part of its water about 320 kilometres into the Rio Negro, joining the Orinoco to the Amazon, the largest natural link between two great river basins. Alexander von Humboldt confirmed it in 1800.

In 2016 Canada's retreating Kaskawulsh Glacier switched its meltwater away from the Slims River, which flows north, and into a neighbouring river that runs to the Gulf of Alaska, the first river capture scientists ever watched as it happened. Within a single year the Slims ran nearly dry. Geologists think the Casiquiare may slowly be capturing the upper Orinoco in the same way.

drumlins-and-eskers-streamlined-hills-an.context_blurb:
During the last ice age, great ice sheets crept across much of northern Europe and North America. When they melted, they left behind shapes that still mark the land: smooth whaleback hills and long winding ridges of gravel. Read them correctly and they become a map of where the vanished ice once flowed.

Boston's Breed's Hill, where the Battle of Bunker Hill was fought in 1775, is a drumlin, a smooth, egg-shaped hill that a passing ice sheet moulded from the rubble it dragged beneath itself. The word comes from an Irish word for a little ridge, and Boston sits on more than a hundred of them.

In Clew Bay on Ireland's west coast, the sea flooded a field of drumlins after the ice age, leaving a scatter of round green islands, and a local saying claims there is one island for every day of the year.

A drumlin works like a frozen compass: its blunt, steep end faces back toward where the ice came from, and its long gentle tail points the way the ice flowed, so a whole field of them records the direction of the vanished glacier. Between Rochester and Syracuse in New York lie roughly 10,000 drumlins, shaped by the great ice sheet about 18,000 years ago.

An esker is a long, winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel laid down by a river that flowed in a tunnel beneath the glacier, so that when the ice was gone, the old riverbed remained as a raised bank. In Sweden, the Uppsala esker runs about 250 kilometres, straight through the city of Uppsala.

Because eskers stand raised and dry above bog, they made natural roads. In Ireland the chain called the Eiscir Riada carried the Great Way between Dublin and Galway. Old Irish legend says that when Conn and Mug Nuadat fought at Magh Léna some eighteen centuries ago, the ridge served as the line that split Ireland in two between rival kings, Conn of the Hundred Battles in the north and Mug Nuadat in the south.

In eastern Finland the Punkaharju esker winds 7 kilometres along a narrow neck of land between the lakes Puruvesi and Pihlajavesi, so slender in places that a road and a railway squeeze along its crest side by side. Tsar Alexander I admired it on a visit in 1802 and asked that it be preserved, and in 1843 Finland protected it, making it one of the earliest protected natural areas in the world.

dubai.context_blurb:
Dubai sits on the sun-baked shore of the Persian Gulf, in the United Arab Emirates. Within living memory it was a small creek-side port whose wooden dhows traded with India and East Africa. In one lifetime it became one of the most furiously built-up cities on Earth, with towers shooting straight out of the sand.

Its crown is the Burj Khalifa, a needle of steel and glass 828 metres high, which took the title of world's tallest building when it opened in 2010 and has never lost it. It was renamed for Sheikh Khalifa of Abu Dhabi, who lent Dubai ten billion dollars to finish it.

Dubai even builds its own land. From 2001, dredgers piled sand and rock from the seabed into Palm Jumeirah, an island shaped like a palm tree, with a trunk, sixteen fronds and a curved breakwater around them. Every frond is lined with beach, so the island gave the city hundreds of kilometres of extra shoreline.

Before the towers and before oil, the town lived off the sea floor. Its wealth was pearls, which divers called ghawas prised from the oyster beds of the Gulf. A diver dropped about forty feet on one gulp of air and went down again and again all day, until in the 1930s the Great Depression and Japan's new cultured pearls wrecked the trade.

The Gulf itself is a warm, shallow arm of the Indian Ocean, barely 36 metres deep on average and ringed by desert. Under that fierce sun, heavy evaporation pulls water off its surface faster than rain and rivers can refill it, and the salt left behind makes the Gulf saltier than the ocean outside. When Dubai struck oil in 1966, its ruler, Sheikh Rashid, knew the oil would run dry and poured the money into trade.

dubrovnik.context_blurb:
Dubrovnik is a small walled city on Croatia's Adriatic coast, its old town a maze of glossy stone lanes and orange roofs packed inside a ring of medieval stone. For about 450 years it was a tiny sea-trading republic whose merchants rivalled the great ports of Italy and whose citizens kept their freedom with brains rather than battles.

An old city wall, complete and unbroken and nearly two kilometres around, still circles the old town, and you can walk its whole top with orange roofs below you on one side and open sea on the other. It stood in for King's Landing in the television series Game of Thrones.

On the landward side the wall rises as much as 25 metres and is up to six metres thick. The city's proudest boast is that no hostile army ever broke through it, from Saracen raiders in the 800s to the shells that fell on Dubrovnik in 1991 and 1992.

Inside, the main street, the Stradun, runs about 300 metres straight between the city's two great gates. It is paved end to end in white limestone, and centuries of feet have buffed it until it gleams like glass. After an earthquake shattered the city in 1667, its people rebuilt the houses along it in one matching baroque style.

From 1358 to 1808 the city was the Republic of Ragusa, a merchant state whose ships traded across the whole Mediterranean. Squeezed between Venice and the Ottoman Turks, Ragusa fought no great wars; it kept its freedom through shrewd diplomacy and paid tribute to any empire strong enough to threaten it. English still remembers its fleet: an argosy, a great merchant ship, takes its name from Ragusa.

The republic's whole creed fit in one Latin word, Libertas, meaning Liberty, which flew on its flag and is carved over the gate of Fort Lovrijenac, the fortress guarding the city from the sea.

Beneath it all lies limestone, which water slowly dissolves. Along this coast whole rivers drop into sinkholes, run through hidden caves and burst out again near the sea. Geologists named that kind of landscape karst, after the Kras plateau farther up this same Adriatic shore, and now use the word for caves and sinkholes all over the world.

easter-island-rapa-nui.context_blurb:
Easter Island, which its own people call Rapa Nui, is a speck of volcanic land in the far southeastern Pacific, one of the loneliest inhabited places on Earth. Polynesian voyagers settled it roughly a thousand years ago and carved hundreds of giant stone ancestors there. It belongs to Chile today, and the Rapanui still live on it.

Those giants are the moai: about 900 stone figures with jutting brows and long bodies. The Rapanui raised them in rows on long ceremonial stone platforms near the shore, each called an ahu. Most look inland, their backs to the ocean, watching over their makers' villages.

Nearly all of them, about 95 in every 100, came from one quarry: Rano Raraku, an old crater whose soft volcanic tuff carves easily with stone tools. Hundreds of half-made statues still lie on its slopes, some never cut free of the bedrock.

Statues sunk deep in that slope made the island famous for its giant heads. Then archaeologists dug around several of them and found whole statues underneath, with full torsos and arms buried by centuries of rubble and washed-down soil.

The island covers only about 164 square kilometres, and Chile lies some 3,500 kilometres east. Its nearest inhabited neighbour is tiny Pitcairn Island, about 2,075 kilometres away.

The grandest row stands at Ahu Tongariki, the island's biggest platform, where fifteen moai line up shoulder to shoulder. Thrown down long ago, then swept inland by a tsunami in 1960, they were raised again in the 1990s by a team led by Claudio Cristino and Patricia Vargas.

For centuries the moai seemed to have empty eye sockets. Sergio Rapu Haoa's team solved the riddle in 1979 from a broken eye found at Anakena beach. Once a statue stood on its ahu, it received inlaid eyes, with whites made of white coral and a pupil of black obsidian or red scoria.

How could a people without wheels, metal tools or animals to pull loads shift statues of ten tonnes and more? Rapanui oral tradition said the moai walked. In 2012 Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo tested that story: 18 people with three ropes rocked an upright 4.35-tonne replica from side to side, so that it waddled forward on its own base, and walked it 100 metres in 40 minutes. It is one tested idea among several; no single method is proven for every statue.

Some moai wore a pukao, a dark-red stone cylinder set on the head like a topknot and weighing up to about 12 tonnes. That red rock came from Puna Pau, a small crater of soft red scoria apart from the main quarry.

Later the old order broke down and the moai were toppled. The Rapanui turned to a new faith built around the creator-god Makemake: the Birdman cult, Tangata manu. Each year at Orongo, a cliff-top village on Rano Kau's crater rim, chosen young men climbed down the sea cliffs and swam on reed floats to the islet of Motu Nui to wait for the season's first sooty tern egg. The man whose swimmer brought one back became the sacred Birdman for a year.

The island also produced rongorongo, which may be one of only a handful of scripts on Earth invented with no outside model: lines of little carved people, birds, fish and plants on wooden tablets that no one has ever deciphered. Each line runs the opposite way to the one before and is also upside-down, so after finishing a line the reader turned the whole tablet upside-down to begin the next.

Why did the age of the moai end? The writer Jared Diamond made famous the idea of ecocide: the islanders, he argued, felled their own forest to the last tree. Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo disagree, arguing that Polynesian rats brought by the settlers ate the palm seeds so the forest could not regrow, and that the real catastrophe came from outside: Peruvian slave raids in 1862 and 1863, and the smallpox the few survivors carried home. Historians still argue over it.

egyptian-hieroglyphs-and-the-rosetta-sto.context_blurb:
For some three thousand years, the pharaohs' Egypt carved its holiest words in hieroglyphs, little pictures of owls, eyes, feet and reeds that cover the temple walls of Karnak and Luxor. Then the knowledge died and the walls fell silent, until a black stone slab, the Rosetta Stone, and a French scholar, Jean-François Champollion, gave them back their voice.

People long assumed each picture stood for one whole idea, and that mistake kept the script locked. In fact Egyptian used more than a thousand signs, and one picture could work in several ways. It could stand for a whole word, act as a silent helper that sorted out the meaning, or stand for a spoken sound, just as a letter does in our alphabet.

The last hieroglyphs anyone can date were cut on 24 August 394 CE at Philae, an island temple near Aswan on Egypt's southern frontier, by a priest named Nesmeterakhem. Soon nobody alive could read the signs, and for about 1,400 years travellers gazed at the carvings without understanding a word.

The key turned up in July 1799, during Napoleon's invasion of Egypt. French soldiers of Napoleon's army were strengthening a fort near Rosetta, a town in the Nile Delta, when their officer, Pierre-François Bouchard, spotted a heavy black slab carved with three kinds of writing.

The slab repeats one decree three times. Its top band is hieroglyphs and its middle band Demotic, the everyday Egyptian script, and nobody could read either. Its bottom band is ancient Greek, because a Greek-speaking dynasty, the Ptolemies, ruled Egypt at the time, and scholars could read Greek perfectly well. It was a crib: the same words in a known language, for working backward into the unknown ones.

The first crack came from royal names. On temple walls a pharaoh's name always sits inside an oval loop tied off at one end, called a cartouche. A Greek king's name such as Ptolemy had to be spelled out sound by sound, so the loops showed exactly where sound-signs were hiding. The Englishman Thomas Young linked the loops to royal names, but went no further.

The stone never went back. When the French army surrendered at Alexandria in 1801, it had to hand the slab over. Colonel Tomkyns Hilgrove Turner shipped it to England, and by 1802 King George III had placed it in London's British Museum, where it is still the most-visited object of all.

On 14 September 1822 Champollion saw that the Egyptians mixed picture-signs and sound-signs even in their own words. By his brother's account he dashed to his brother's workplace, shouted that he had it, and then collapsed from the shock and lay in bed for days.

Egypt's priests had issued the decree in 196 BC, granting the thirteen-year-old Ptolemy V a divine cult and the temples relief from taxes. Its last lines explain why the stone exists at all: a copy, in all three scripts, was to be set up in hard stone in every temple of the first, second and third rank.

Champollion had an edge his rival lacked. Since boyhood he had studied Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language, written in Greek letters and still chanted in the services of Egypt's Coptic Christians. Because he knew how its words sounded, he could hear the pharaohs' speech behind the pictures.

One last trick at Karnak: lines may run left to right, right to left or top to bottom, whichever suited the wall. The owls, hawks and little people show where a line starts, because they all face its beginning, so you read toward their faces, walking into the oncoming parade.

el-nino-and-la-nina-the-pacific-that-shi.context_blurb:
Across the tropical Pacific, a vast pool of warm water shifts back and forth every few years, and when it moves, the weather of half the planet moves with it: floods in one place, drought in another. The two phases of this natural rhythm are El Niño and La Niña.

For generations Peru's fishermen noticed a warm current that crept along their coast late each year and peaked around Christmas, so they named it El Niño de Navidad: El Niño, the Christ Child, after the newborn Jesus. Today the name covers the warm phase of the whole cycle.

In a normal year the trade winds, steady easterlies, blow across the tropical Pacific from the Americas toward Asia, dragging sun-warmed surface water west. The water heaps up near Indonesia, where the sea stands roughly half a metre higher than off Peru, while off Peru cold deep water wells up to replace what the wind blew away.

Every few years the trade winds go slack, and the heaped-up warm water slides back east toward South America. It spreads over the sea off Peru like a lid, and the cold water rising from below is shut off completely.

That cold upwelling feeds immense schools of anchoveta, long the biggest fishery for one kind of fish anywhere. Without it the fish starve and scatter. In 1972 a great El Niño made the fishery collapse, and the catch crashed from about 12 million tons toward 4 million.

El Niño has a cold twin, La Niña, Spanish for the little girl, when the trade winds blow harder than usual, the upwelling off South America grows fiercer, and the eastern Pacific turns colder than normal. The swing is the Pacific's natural rhythm, separate from long-term global warming.

The winds belong to a giant loop of air. Air climbs above the warm pool near Indonesia, travels east at great height, drops back down where the eastern ocean is cool, and blows home along the sea surface as the trade winds. The British scientist Gilbert Walker mapped that loop in the 1920s, so it is called the Walker circulation.

Through long-distance links called teleconnections, one strong El Niño changes weather around the globe in a single season. It usually brings drought and raging bushfires to Australia and Indonesia, while it drowns Peru and the southern United States in floods.

In the Atlantic it does something surprising. El Niño strengthens the wind shear there, fast winds high up that rip the tops off growing storms. So an El Niño year usually quiets the Atlantic hurricane season, and fewer hurricanes form. Over the Pacific it does the reverse.

Once begun, an El Niño feeds itself: warmer water in the east weakens the trade winds, and weaker winds let still more warm water spread east. In 1969 the Norwegian-American meteorologist Jacob Bjerknes worked out this loop between ocean and air, and it carries his name: the Bjerknes feedback.

From 1876 to 1878 a monster El Niño made the monsoon rains fail across India and upset the rains in China and Brazil, so the crops withered. Famine took somewhere between 19 and 50 million lives. Historians debate the toll and the human decisions that worsened it, but the climate trigger is settled.

Written weather records are young, so how do we know El Niño is ancient? Scientists drilled cores from old coral heads on remote atolls such as Palmyra and Kiritimati, far out in mid-Pacific. A coral colony adds a new band of limestone skeleton every year, and the chemistry of each band records that year's sea warmth and rainfall, so warm, rainy El Niño years leave a clear mark in coral heads thousands of years old.

ellora-kailasa-temple.context_blurb:
At Ellora, in western India, a long cliff of dark volcanic basalt is honeycombed with temples and monasteries cut straight into the rock. The most astonishing is Cave 16, the Kailasa temple, made for King Krishna I of the Rashtrakuta dynasty some twelve centuries ago. It looks like a temple of stacked stone, but it is one single piece of the mountain.

Nobody stacked a single block. The carvers began at the very top of the cliff and cut straight down, freeing a three-storey temple by removing every bit of rock that was not temple, the exact reverse of ordinary building. Their only tools were iron hammers and chisels, along with picks and wedges: no cranes, no machines, no explosives. Over about twenty years they chipped out and hauled away some 200,000 tonnes of basalt. Because the temple is one continuous stone, a single wrong cut could never be patched or replaced.

The temple is a stone copy of a mountain. Mount Kailash, a peak in the Himalayas, is revered by Hindus as the home of the god Shiva, and the temple carries the mountain's own name and is dedicated to him. It is the largest single monolithic rock excavation in the world, the biggest structure ever carved from one continuous piece of stone, and it rises taller than a four-storey building.

The rest of the cliff tells another story. Its 34 caves were carved by three faiths sharing the region, Buddhists, Hindus and Jains, with 12 Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain caves side by side in the same rock face. Ellora is often held up as a picture of religious harmony in ancient India.

On an outer wall of Kailasa is one of the finest sculptures in Indian art. Ravana, the demon-king with ten heads, is pinned under Mount Kailash and heaves with all his arms to shake it loose. Above him Shiva sits perfectly calm, and in the story he holds the whole mountain down with nothing but one toe.

Around the temple, cut from the same rock, stand five small detached shrines. Three of them honour Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati, goddesses who personify India's holiest rivers.

Last, look at the base. The whole temple seems to ride on a herd of full-size stone beasts carved around its plinth. Life-size elephants carry most of the load, and striding among them, shouldering the mountain-temple too, are lions. Like the gateway, the columned galleries and the two free-standing victory pillars, they were left standing as the rock around them was cut away. Nothing at Kailasa was ever assembled.

endorheic-basins-water-with-no-way-out-t.context_blurb:
Most rain that falls on land runs down to the sea in the end. But about 18 percent of Earth's land drains nowhere: its rivers end in closed hollows called endorheic basins, where water can escape only by evaporating into the air. Whatever salt and minerals the water carried in stay behind and pile up, so these basins hold salt lakes, salt flats and white crusted deserts.

The Jordan River pours into the Dead Sea, between Israel and Jordan, and nothing flows out, so the lake has grown about ten times saltier than the ocean. Water that salty is so dense that it pushes a bather up to bob high on the surface like a cork, and people famously lie back and read a newspaper without sinking.

High in the Bolivian Andes, ancient lakes dried away and left Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, some 10,582 square kilometres of crust as flat as a table. When a thin film of rain lies across it, the salt flat becomes the world's largest mirror, with sky above and sky below, and visitors seem to walk on clouds.

The biggest closed basin of all holds the Caspian Sea, the largest lake on Earth, bordered by five countries and holding roughly 3.5 times as much water as the five Great Lakes combined. Its only way out is evaporation, which leaves it brackish.

Because the Dead Sea has no outlet and its region gets less than 50 millimetres of rain a year, its shore has sunk to about 430 metres below sea level, the lowest stretch of dry ground anywhere on Earth.

In Utah, Ice Age Lake Bonneville dried up, and its old floor is now the Bonneville Salt Flats, a blinding white crust. The salt is so hard and level that racing drivers have chased world land-speed records there since 1914, and jet-powered cars have passed 600 miles per hour.

Lake Chad lies on the dry southern edge of the Sahara, in the Sahel, where four countries meet. It is only about two metres deep at most, barely more than a person's height, so a person could nearly wade across it, and it had almost no water in reserve. A run of dry years, plus water drawn off upstream for irrigation, shrank it by about 95 percent from the 1960s to the 1980s.

In the 1840s the explorer John C. Frémont named a huge region of Nevada and Utah the Great Basin, because no drop of water that falls there ever reaches the ocean. There rain evaporates, sinks into the ground or gathers in closed lakes such as Great Salt Lake.

Some basins have been drained by people. The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake on Earth, lies in Central Asia. From the early 1960s, Soviet central planners diverted its only two rivers, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, to irrigate cotton fields across the desert, and the lake began to die.

The fishing town of Moynaq watched the shore retreat tens of kilometres. Its fishing fleet was left to rust on the dry seabed, the trawlers stranded 30 to 90 kilometres from any water, and they became the world's best-known picture of a vanished sea. Its exposed bed is now a toxic desert, the Aralkum.

The Okavango River in Botswana never reaches the sea either. It fans out into the Kalahari Desert as an inland delta, where nearly all its water vanishes into air and sand. Yet the delta is greenest in the dry winter. The reason is that floodwater from Angola's summer rains arrives months late: the surge travels about 1,200 kilometres downriver and then spreads slowly across the floodplains, so it floods them just when the Kalahari is driest.

Closed basins can also break. During the Ice Age, meltwater filled Lake Bonneville higher and higher until, some 17,500 years ago, the water found a low gap in the northern rim and poured through. The overflow became the Bonneville Flood, a colossal torrent that roared toward the Snake River with almost 5,000 cubic kilometres of water in less than a year, one of the largest floods in Earth's history.

estuaries-and-tidal-bores-where-river-me.context_blurb:
Where a river reaches the sea, two waters meet: fresh water flowing down and salt water pushed up by the tide. These meeting places shelter some of the richest life on Earth, and in a few special river mouths the tide does something spectacular, charging upstream as a wave.

Chesapeake Bay, stretching some 200 miles along the American east coast, is an estuary, a partly enclosed body of water where a river's fresh water mixes with the salty tide into half-and-half water called brackish. The mixing traps nutrients, so blue crabs and oysters thrive, and estuaries rank among the richest habitats on Earth.

The biggest average tides on Earth fill the Bay of Fundy, on Canada's Atlantic coast, where the funnel-shaped bay sets the water sloshing in rhythm with the tide and lifts it an average of 11.7 metres at Burntcoat Head, with rare extremes near 17 metres. At low water, boats sit stranded on the seabed mud.

Chesapeake Bay was not always a bay. During the last ice age it was a river valley, where the Susquehanna wound through dry land toward a distant coast. When the ice age ended, melting ice sheets made the sea rise, and some 10,000 years ago the Atlantic flooded in and drowned the valley. A coast drowned this way keeps the branching outline of the old river channels.

Geographers call a drowned river valley like this a ria, from the Galician word for river, and the classic examples are the Rías Baixas of Spain's Galician coast, whose long fingers of sea branch inland like the limbs of a tree. Because rivers carved them, rias keep that branching shape; a fjord, carved by a glacier, is steep and U-shaped instead.

In a few rivers the incoming tide is squeezed into a wave that races upstream against the current: a tidal bore. The biggest on Earth is the Silver Dragon on China's Qiantang River, up to 9 metres tall and charging upriver at 40 kilometres an hour.

On the Amazon the bore is called the pororoca; at the spring tides of March and September it can stand 4 metres tall and run as far as 800 kilometres inland. Its name, from the Tupi language of Brazil, is often taken to mean the great roar, because you hear the wave minutes before you see it. In 2003 the surfer Picuruta Salazar rode one wave about 12.5 kilometres, standing for 37 minutes.

Why do the Severn in England and the Qiantang get bores when thousands of other tidal rivers do not? A bore needs two things together: a large tidal range, usually over about 6 metres, and a channel that is shallow, narrowing and funnel-shaped, which squeezes the rising tide until it rears up into a wave. Without the funnel, the same tide just rises quietly.

etna-stromboli-and-the-word-volcano.context_blurb:
Off the toe of Italy, the island of Sicily and its small neighbours hold some of the most famous active volcanoes on Earth. Mount Etna, on Sicily's east coast, is Europe's largest and most active volcano. Just to the north, in the Aeolian Islands, Stromboli has been erupting almost without pause for thousands of years, and a third island gave the world the word volcano itself.

Etna stands about 3,400 metres tall, but no map can fix that number for long. It erupts so often, sixteen times in 2001 alone, that each summit eruption either piles up new lava and ash or blasts part of the top away, so its official height really does rise and fall.

Stromboli's glowing bursts flare every few minutes to hours, night after night, and sailors far out at sea have steered by the red glow for centuries, so they nicknamed the island the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.

Stromboli looks small, rising only about 926 metres above the waves. But its slopes plunge more than 2,700 metres below the sea, so the island is just the sunlit tip of a giant underwater mountain. A vast horseshoe scar on its side, the Sciara del Fuoco, or Stream of Fire, funnels lava and rock straight into the sea.

Its little explosions, brief rhythmic bursts that toss glowing blobs of lava into the air and let watchers look on safely from a nearby ridge, are so typical of the island that volcanologists call every eruption of that kind Strombolian. They are far gentler than the towering ash columns of the biggest eruptions.

The Romans pictured another Aeolian island as the chimney of the underground forge of Vulcan, their god of fire, so they named it Vulcano, and from that island's name comes our word volcano. In their story its rumbles were his hammer beating out weapons and armour. The Greeks had called it Thermessa, source of heat.

Etna has also tested human courage. In 1669 its lava crept toward the city of Catania. Diego Pappalardo, a priest, led roughly fifty men in cutting a trench that turned the flow aside, the first recorded lava diversion, but people from a town toward Paterno saw the lava now heading their way and chased the diggers off. The flow swung back and buried part of Catania.

Long before geology, the ancient Greeks had their own explanation for Etna's shaking and fire. In the myth Zeus defeated Typhon, a fire-breathing monster with a hundred heads, and buried it forever under the mountain, where its writhing makes Etna rumble and smoke. Some said the smith-god Hephaestus used those flames at his forge below.

fado-lisbon.context_blurb:
Fado is the song of Lisbon, Portugal's hilly capital on the Atlantic. It was born in the early 1800s in the city's oldest and poorest quarters, Alfama, Mouraria and Bairro Alto, sung by sailors, bohemians and tavern singers. A lone voice, two guitars and a dark room are all it needs.

The name fado comes from the Latin fatum, fate, so this music of heartbreak and longing, sung by candlelight in Lisbon's old taverns for some two hundred years, is named after fate itself.

Every fado circles one feeling, saudade: a bittersweet yearning for a person or a place that is loved and gone, so tender it is almost sweet, and English has no single word to match it.

The weeping sound beside the singer is the Portuguese guitar, the guitarra portuguesa, small and shaped like a pear, with twelve steel strings in six pairs. Instead of pegs, its strings run to a fan of screws, and the player tunes each one with a watch key, the kind once used to wind a pocket watch. It grew from the English guitar of the 1750s.

Portugal has a second, stricter fado. In the old university city of Coimbra it is sung at night in the stone squares only by men, male university students and graduates wrapped in flowing black capes, following an old troubadour tradition. Lisbon's fado, by contrast, rose from sailors and taverns.

The greatest fadista was Amália Rodrigues, born in Lisbon in 1920, who sold fruit on the docks as a poor girl before her voice carried fado to concert halls around the world. Crowned the Queen of Fado, she became the best-selling Portuguese artist in the history of recorded music. At her death in 1999 Portugal mourned for three days, and in 2001 she became the first woman laid in the National Pantheon.

Legend, not documented history, traces fado back to Maria Severa, a half-Romani singer of the Mouraria whose love affair with the Count of Vimioso scandalised the city. She died of tuberculosis at 26 and lay in a common grave. Fadistas are said to wear a black shawl in mourning for her, the very garment she sang in. In 2011 UNESCO listed fado as part of humanity's intangible heritage.

fatehpur-sikri-the-abandoned-red-city.context_blurb:
Near Agra in northern India stands Fatehpur Sikri, a whole imperial city built in the 1570s by the Mughal emperor Akbar as his new capital. Its palaces, courtyards and mosque still stand almost untouched, because the court lived there for only about fifteen years. It is one of the best-preserved ghost capitals in the world.

Akbar built it on a rocky ridge entirely of the same red sandstone, quarried close by, so the whole capital glows one colour and is nicknamed the red city.

Then the city emptied, mainly because the rocky ridge and the shallow, drying Sikri lake could never supply enough water for a busy court. Around 1585 Akbar also left for frontier wars and moved his court to Lahore, and his perfect city was left behind.

Its grandest monument is the Buland Darwaza, the Exalted Gate, raised around 1575 to celebrate Akbar's conquest of Gujarat. Some 54 metres tall and climbed by 42 steps, it is often called the world's highest gateway. Across its arch runs a Persian line attributed to Jesus, saying that the world is a bridge to cross, not a place to build a house: an eerie motto for a city so soon deserted.

In the summer heat the royal women climbed into the Panch Mahal, five stacked storeys of open colonnades that caught the breeze like a wind-catcher, and its carvers made sure that no two of its 176 columns are alike. They dwindle from 84 on the ground floor to just 4 holding the tiny rooftop dome.

Why build a capital on a bare ridge at all? In the 1560s Akbar still had no heir, and a Sufi saint who lived up on that ridge, Sheikh Salim Chishti, promised him a son. The boy was born at Sikri in 1569 and named Salim after the saint; he grew up to be the emperor Jahangir. The whole red city rose as an act of thanks.

The saint's small tomb of white marble stands in the great mosque courtyard, its walls carved into lace-like screens called jali. Women hoping for a child tie a thread to the screen and come back to untie it once the wish comes true, echoing the prayer that founded the city.

fes.context_blurb:
Fes, in Morocco, was founded in the 8th century and served for long stretches as the capital of medieval Muslim dynasties in North Africa. Its walled old town, Fes el-Bali, is one of the largest living medieval cities on Earth, a maze of mosques, workshops and homes that has changed little in a thousand years.

Its pride is al-Qarawiyyin, a mosque and school that Guinness World Records and UNESCO recognise as the oldest university still teaching anywhere. Fatima al-Fihri, a merchant's daughter, founded it in 859 and vowed to pour her whole inheritance into it.

The old town's roughly 9,000 lanes are mostly just 1.5 to 3 metres wide, far too narrow for any car, so pack donkeys and handcarts still carry every heavy load. Few cities anywhere have a bigger zone without cars.

At the Chouara Tannery, tanners have softened and dyed hides by hand for about a thousand years. The hides spend days in white vats, in a soak of pigeon droppings, quicklime and cow urine, then go into dyes of poppy, indigo and henna. The stench is so fierce that guides hand each visitor a fresh sprig of mint to hold under the nose.

Al-Qarawiyyin's library, among the oldest libraries still in use, guards a 9th-century Quran written before paper was common there, on gazelle parchment. It also keeps the original manuscript of Ibn Khaldun's history, which the author himself gave to the library in 1396.

Across the lane from the Bou Inania Madrasa hangs Dar al-Magana, a water clock finished in 1357 behind a row of thirteen little windows. Every hour its hidden floats and weights let fall a metal ball into one of thirteen brass bowls, and nobody yet fully understands how the machine worked.

The whole medina depends on one small river, the Oued Fes, and long ago its builders split it into a web of small canals threaded through the lanes, feeding the fountains, turning the mills and filling the tannery vats. One river, carefully divided, serves the entire old city.

fjords-drowned-glacier-valleys.context_blurb:
A fjord is a long, deep arm of the sea squeezed between towering rock walls, often reaching far inland. Fjords cut the coasts of Norway, New Zealand, Greenland, Alaska and Chile, and in places the water inside is deeper than the open ocean beyond. Every one of them is the work of ice.

Norway's Geirangerfjord is the postcard fjord. Down one wall tumble the Seven Sisters, a fall that divides into seven slender ribbons, the tallest dropping free for about 250 metres. On the opposite cliff a lone fall called the Suitor faces them, and legend says he is forever trying to court the seven sisters and will never win them. High on those walls cling Skageflaa and Knivsflaa. They are old mountain farms, perched far up the cliffs, where families once worked the ledges almost cut off from the world; even now you reach them only by boat and a steep climb.

The King of the Fjords is Sognefjord, Norway's longest and deepest, which reaches 205 kilometres into the country and sinks to 1,308 metres, with cliffs rising another thousand metres above the water.

On the far side of the world, in New Zealand's Fiordland, Mitre Peak rises 1,692 metres almost sheer from the surface of Milford Sound, a sight Rudyard Kipling ranked as an eighth Wonder of the World.

The word fjord comes from Old Norse fjörðr, a passage or crossing over water, the same ancient root that gives English the word ferry. Norway's Viking seafarers carried it.

Few inhabited places on Earth get wetter than Milford Sound, with some 6,400 millimetres of rain a year and up to 250 in a single day. Each heavy downpour sends hundreds of temporary waterfalls streaming down the sheer walls, and they dry up again within a day or two of clear weather.

Milford Sound is also misnamed. A true sound is a drowned river valley, but Milford's trough was gouged out by glaciers, so its valley was cut by ice rather than flowing water, and strictly it is a fiord. The mistake stuck, though the region around it is called Fiordland.

Sail into Sognefjord and the depth-sounder surprises you. A glacier grinds less near its snout and dumps a bank of rubble there, a terminal moraine, so a shallow sill bars the fjord's mouth only about 100 metres down, while the basin behind it plunges past 1,300 metres.

Fjords are drowned valleys: a glacier ground its valley floor below sea level, and when the ice age was over and the ice melted, the sea rose and crept up the empty valley, filling it with salt water.

How did ice cut so deep? During the last ice age, sheets of ice as thick as 3 kilometres flowed down Norway's valleys, polishing the bedrock with stones frozen into their base. The ice also froze onto blocks of bedrock and tore them loose, a process called plucking, which let it quarry Sognefjord far deeper and steeper than any river could.

Scoresby Sund in East Greenland is the biggest fjord system anywhere, not a single channel but a branching tree of arms whose longest limb reaches some 340 kilometres inland. Its inner arms drop to about 1,450 metres, and glaciers at its head calve icebergs that drift down to the sea.

Mark every fjord coast, from the thousand inlets of Norway to Patagonia, Alaska and Scotland's sea lochs, and the dots trace the reach of the Ice Age glaciers that flowed all the way down to the sea. That is why fjords cluster on cold, high-latitude shores and never in the tropics.

flamenco-andalusia.context_blurb:
Flamenco is the fiery song, guitar and dance of southern Spain: a voice that wails, a guitar that drives, heels that crack on the floor like gunshots. It grew over centuries out of a mix of peoples, Andalusian, Roma, Jewish and Moorish, and in 2010 UNESCO named it part of humanity's intangible heritage.

Its homeland is Andalusia, Spain's sun-baked deep south of white villages and olive groves around Seville, Cádiz and Granada.

The Roma who forged it, called gitanos in Spain, came originally from northern India and reached Spain in the 15th century, settling largely in Andalusia. There they fused their music with the Arab sounds of Al-Andalus, North African rhythm and Sephardic Jewish song.

At a flamenco night the audience is part of the band. Its hand-claps are called palmas: soft, muffled pops made with cupped hands under quiet singing, and sharp cracks made by snapping two or three fingers into the flat palm for loud, fast dancing.

Guitar, claps and stamping heels all lock into one rhythmic cycle, the compás, which in most styles runs to a demanding twelve beats, and a player who loses count brings the whole thing down.

Each flamenco style, or palo, carries its own mood. The fastest and wildest is the bulerías, born in Jerez de la Frontera and by tradition saved for the end of the night, when everyone joins in a storm of clapping and footwork.

A flamenco dancer may wear the bata de cola, a floor-length dress whose weighted, ruffled train pours out behind her for metres, and she hurls and sculpts it in the air with kicks and turns. Doing that well is a virtuoso skill of its own.

In a famous 1933 lecture in Buenos Aires, the poet Federico García Lorca gave the name duende to the dark, shivering spirit that seizes a flamenco singer only when the singer risks everything, on the edge of death itself. He called it a power rather than a work, a struggle rather than a thought.

The wooden box a flamenco player sits on and slaps is the cajón, which means box or crate, and enslaved Afro-Peruvians invented it on Peru's coast, often from old shipping crates. The guitarist Paco de Lucía met it in Lima in 1977 through the Peruvian percussionist Caitro Soto, took one back to Spain, and it became flamenco's main drum.

florence-brunelleschis-impossible-dome.context_blurb:
Florence, in Tuscany, is where the Renaissance began. Rich with the money of the Medici bankers, the city raised artists such as Donatello, Botticelli, Leonardo and Michelangelo. Above its red roofs swells the great dome of its cathedral, the Duomo, which the goldsmith-turned-architect Filippo Brunelleschi raised by inventing methods no one had tried.

The outer shell is brick, about four million of them, and nearly six hundred years after its completion in 1436 it is still the largest brick-and-masonry dome ever built. Rome's Pantheon is slightly wider, but it was poured in concrete, not laid in brick.

Domes of that age were built over a giant wooden scaffold, called centering, that held the arches up until the top was closed. Brunelleschi's dome was too wide for any forest to prop, so he raised it with no supporting frame underneath, and it held itself up as it climbed, to the amazement of rival masters and watching crowds.

The secret was the way he laid the bricks: in a herringbone pattern, spina-pesce or fish-spine in Italian, which tied every fresh course of brick into the course beneath and steered the load onto the stone ribs. Plain flat rings would have slipped off the ever-steeper wall; instead the brickwork gripped itself as it rose.

A heavy dome pushes outward at its base, like a barrel without hoops. Gothic cathedrals braced that push with flying buttresses, but Florence's officials had banned the style as foreign. So Brunelleschi buried hidden chains inside the masonry: concealed rings of stone clamped with iron, plus a ring of wood, which squeeze the dome inward and keep it from splaying apart.

In August 1944, as German troops pulled out of Florence, they dynamited every bridge over the Arno but one: the Ponte Vecchio, the medieval bridge lined with goldsmiths' and jewellers' shops. Why it was spared is still debated.

The dome is really two shells, a heavy inner one and a lighter outer one, and in the gap between them about 463 steps climb all the way to the lantern at the very top, so visitors can walk up inside the dome itself.

How did he win the job? The painter Giorgio Vasari tells that Brunelleschi refused to show his plans and challenged his rivals to stand an egg upright on a marble slab; when they all failed, he tapped its base flat so that it stood. The trick looked easy only once he had shown them. The tale is probably embellished, since an earlier life of Brunelleschi by his friend Manetti never mentions it.

foehn-and-chinook-the-warm-wind-off-the-.context_blurb:
When moist air is forced up and over a mountain range, it drops its rain and snow on the near side. Then the dry air pours down the far side and arrives warmer than when it started, sometimes raising the temperature by 20 degrees in minutes. Mountain people around the world know this warm wind, and each place has its own name for it.

On the plains of Alberta, east of the Rockies, people call it the chinook, and the Blackfoot named it the snow-eater, because it can strip a snowy field bare in hours, melting some snow and drying the rest straight into the air.

Why is it warm? On the way up the western slopes, the air wrings out its moisture as rain and snow. On the way down it sinks into thicker air, which squeezes it, and squeezed air heats up, so the wind arrives hotter than it began.

The chinook holds the record for the fastest temperature change ever measured: on 22 January 1943, at Spearfish, South Dakota, it rolled off the Black Hills and lifted the thermometer from minus 4 to 45 degrees Fahrenheit in two minutes. Shop windows cracked from the shock, and by about 9:30 that morning it was back down to minus 4.

In Southern California the same kind of wind is the Santa Ana, which roars out of the inland desert each autumn, squeezes the humidity under ten percent and fans wildfires toward Los Angeles. Southern Californians call these the devil winds, and writers from Raymond Chandler to Joan Didion wrote of the edge they put on everyone's nerves.

The original of the whole family blows down from the Alps: the foehn, a warm, dry wind able to clear a valley's winter snow within a day. Old Alpine belief holds it responsible for headaches and dark moods, and judges in Switzerland and Austria once went easier on a crime committed on a foehn day, though doctors have never proved the link.

In western Argentina the Andes squeeze the Pacific winds dry, and the hot, dry blast that falls on the Mendoza and San Juan vineyards is the zonda. It can top 240 kilometres an hour and fill the sky with a yellow haze, and its fierce name went to a supercar, the Pagani Zonda.

Foehn winds even reach Antarctica. Pouring off the Antarctic Peninsula's eastern flank, they can warm the air by up to 17 degrees and leave ponds of meltwater on the ice shelves even in winter. In 2002 such meltwater wedged into cracks in the Larsen B ice shelf and helped break it apart: in a matter of weeks the whole shelf collapsed and shattered into the sea.

from-rift-to-ocean-the-red-sea-and-the-a.context_blurb:
Where two of Earth's plates pull apart, the ground splits into a long valley called a rift. Keep pulling long enough and the sea floods in and a new ocean is born. In northeast Africa you can watch the stages: the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and between them the Afar Triangle of Ethiopia, where three plates are tearing apart one of the hottest, lowest landscapes on Earth.

The Red Sea is a baby ocean: the Arabian Peninsula is splitting from the Horn of Africa at the Red Sea Rift, and given millions more years geologists expect it to widen into a full-sized ocean basin. It began to open in the Eocene epoch and sped up in the Oligocene that followed.

Continents usually drift about as fast as a fingernail grows. But in 2005, in the Dabbahu episode in Ethiopia's Afar region, the rift tore open by about 8 metres in roughly three weeks, as a crack some 60 kilometres long filled with molten rock from below. Satellites caught it happening, the first time such an event had been watched from space.

Most of the ridges where new ocean floor is born lie some two miles under the sea, but in the Afar the spreading seam has risen onto dry land, and Iceland, straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, is the only other place on Earth where you can walk across one.

As the crust stretches and thins, the land sags; the floor of the Danakil Depression sits some 125 metres below the sea. In neighbouring Djibouti, the salt-ringed Lake Assal lies about 155 metres below sea level, the lowest point in all of Africa.

Erta Ale, whose name means smoking mountain, holds in its summit pit a churning lava lake of molten rock at 1,100 to 1,200 degrees that has never frozen over since at least 1906, one of the very few long-lived lava lakes on Earth. Its southern pit is nicknamed the gateway to hell.

The Danakil is the hottest place on Earth by year-round average, and in its heart the salt-mining settlement of Dallol averaged 34.6 degrees Celsius from 1960 to 1966, making it the hottest place where people have lived.

Around Dallol's hot springs the salt flats bloom into terraces of white, green, yellow, gold, orange and red, and the colours come from iron compounds, raw chemistry rather than microbes. The springs are so acidic, so hot and about ten times saltier than seawater that almost nothing lives in them, and scientists study the site as a stand-in for other planets.

g-bekli-tepe.context_blurb:
On a hilltop near Şanlıurfa in southeastern Turkey stand rings of giant carved stone pillars, decorated with foxes, snakes, scorpions and birds. They are about 11,500 years old, older than pottery, metal, writing or farming. Göbekli Tepe has turned the story of civilisation upside down, because here the monument seems to have come before the farm.

Its oldest rings date to about 9500 BCE, so when those pillars first stood, the first stones of Stonehenge were still some 6,000 years in the future. Put another way, the pyramids of Egypt lay as far ahead of them as they lie behind us.

Only about a tenth of the site has been dug, perhaps less: after decades of work four great rings are uncovered, and ground-scanning radar shows some twenty more still buried in the mound.

Surveyors from Istanbul and Chicago crossed the hill in 1963, noticed stone tops sticking out of the ground, logged them as medieval gravestones and went on their way. Only in 1994 did the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt realise those gravestones were the tips of the oldest monumental temple known.

Its builders were Stone Age hunter-gatherers, people with no farming, pottery, metal, writing or wheel, who quarried and raised limestone pillars weighing up to 10 to 20 tonnes. The old rule said you needed a settled farming town before you could build a monument; Göbekli Tepe, older than any farming village, broke it.

The pillars teem with wild animals: foxes, snakes, scorpions, spiders, vultures, cranes, gazelles and big cats. Yet deer, one of the commonest game animals in the region, are almost missing, which tells archaeologists the carvers chose their beasts for meaning, not simply from what they hunted.

Clear human figures are rare among the carvings. On a narrow pillar nicknamed the totem pole, with a stack of three figures and serpents sliding down its edges, the site's clearest human image shows a woman lying back.

The tall central pillars are people too, in stone shorthand. The T-shaped top is a head and the shaft a body, with arms cut in shallow relief bending around to the front, and at the waist the carvers added a belt and loincloth. On Pillar 18, a fox pelt even hangs from the belt.

The busiest carving, Pillar 43, the Vulture Stone, shows three vultures, a scorpion and one rare human figure that has no head, which is why many archaeologists read it as a scene about death, perhaps of vultures stripping the dead. Its meaning is still argued over.

Why are the carvings so crisp? Klaus Schmidt argued that once the builders were done with a ring of pillars, they buried it under rubble, flint chips and animal bones on purpose, sealing it for 11,000 years. Some researchers think the fill built up more slowly, but either way it preserved the site.

In 2020 Gil Haklay and Avi Gopher showed that the centre points of three big enclosures, B, C and D, sit at the corners of an almost perfect equilateral triangle about 19.25 metres on a side, each within about 25 centimetres. The three rings were planned together, by people with no writing at all.

ggantija-and-maltas-megalithic-temples.context_blurb:
Malta is a small island nation in the Mediterranean, south of Sicily. On it and its little sister island, Gozo, stand some of the oldest free-standing stone buildings on Earth, raised by Neolithic farmers whose names are lost. Maltese legend said only giants could have built them, and the greatest still bears the name Ggantija, place of giants.

Ggantija on Gozo went up around 3600 BC, built of huge upright stones, which makes it roughly a thousand years older than Egypt's pyramids, and older than Stonehenge too. Only Göbekli Tepe in Turkey is known to be older.

Folklore, not history, says the giantess Sansuna built Ggantija single-handed, carrying the blocks with a baby on her shoulder and living on nothing but broad beans and honey. The story explains the name, not how the temple was truly built.

How did real people move limestone blocks of more than 50 tons, some nearly 5 metres long, with no wheels and no cranes? Hundreds of small round stone balls lie scattered around the temples, and archaeologists think the builders set the giant blocks on them and rolled them along like ball-bearings.

Malta's builders also dug down. Beneath the town of Paola lies the Hal Saflieni Hypogeum, a hypogeum being an underground chamber carved into solid rock. <<Inside it diggers found a small clay figure of a plump woman lying on her side, probably a mother goddess, known today as the Sleeping Lady.>> She is one of the great treasures of Malta's National Museum of Archaeology.

Cut around 3300 to 3000 BC, the Hypogeum drops three levels into solid limestone, a maze of halls, stairs and chambers hollowed out with nothing but stone and bone tools, because Malta's temple-builders had no metal at all. It is the only known prehistoric underground temple of its kind.

It was a temple for the living and a tomb for the dead: the remains of about 7,000 people were laid there over many centuries, making it one of the largest prehistoric burial grounds ever found.

In one small chamber, the Oracle Room, a deep voice or a drumbeat is amplified into a low hum that resonates through the whole Hypogeum, at a pitch of about 110 hertz, the same found in other ancient chambers such as Newgrange in Ireland. Red ochre spirals still decorate its ceiling.

Mnajdra, a temple high on the sea cliffs of Malta's south coast, works as a Stone Age calendar. At the spring and autumn equinoxes the rising sun shines straight down its central passage, while at the solstices the first light strikes the rims of the two great slabs beside the doorway instead. Its builders aimed it at the sky more than 5,000 years ago, so one temple tracks the whole solar year.

giant-waves-and-where-the-sea-floor-buil.context_blurb:
A few stretches of coast throw up the biggest waves on Earth, again and again, in the very same spots: Nazaré in Portugal, Jaws off Maui, Mavericks in California. Out at sea the swell looks ordinary. The secret that stands it up into a towering wall lies hidden on the seabed.

Off the beach of Praia do Norte, at Nazaré, a submarine canyon, the largest in Europe at about 230 kilometres long and up to 5,000 metres deep, runs to within a kilometre of the beach and delivers the open-ocean swell to shore with almost no loss of energy. On the shallow shelf on either side, ordinary waves lose their power, so the giants rear up at one spot. In October 2020 the German surfer Sebastian Steudtner rode a wave there of 26.21 metres, about as tall as an eight-storey building, which was ratified as the biggest wave anyone has ever surfed.

For centuries sailors told of single monster waves rising out of a normal sea, and scientists dismissed the tales. On the first day of 1995 a laser aimed down from Norway's Draupner platform measured a rogue wave 25.6 metres high, more than twice the height of the waves around it, the first ever caught by an instrument.

At Jaws and Mavericks, as at Nazaré, the seabed's shape fixes where each giant stands up, whatever the weather. At Jaws an underwater ridge trips the swell; at Mavericks a sloping rock ramp slows one part of the wave while deep water beside it races on, bending the crest so it collapses onto one spot.

A tsunami is the opposite kind of wave. Speeding across the deep ocean as fast as a jet airliner, its energy is stretched along a wave hundreds of kilometres long, so out there it stands only about one metre tall and ships pass over it without noticing. Only in shallow water near the coast does it pile up into a killer.

giants-causeway-and-fingals-cave.context_blurb:
On the north coast of Northern Ireland, in County Antrim, the shore is paved with some 40,000 dark stone columns fitted edge to edge, stepping down into the sea like a road. Across the water, on the Scottish island of Staffa, the same columns wall a sea cave. Legend blames two giants; geology tells a story just as dramatic.

Most of the Causeway's columns have six sides, a hexagon, because hexagons pack together with the least wasted space and the shortest cracks as the rock shrinks. Not every one is perfect: some have four, five, seven or even eight sides, and the tallest rise about 12 metres.

The whole pavement formed in one natural event about 60 million years ago, when a thick sheet of molten lava cooled, shrank and cracked from the top down into tall columns, a process called columnar jointing. Drying mud crazes into tiles the same way, only here on a slow, giant scale.

That lava froze into basalt, a dark, heavy, iron-rich volcanic rock, the same stone that makes Iceland's black-sand beaches and the most common rock beneath the oceans. Runny basalt lava spreads far before it cools, into the broad, even sheets that crack into column fields.

No single volcanic cone produced this lava. It welled up from long cracks because a continent was tearing apart: Europe, carrying Ireland and Britain, was pulling away from Greenland and North America, and the stretched crust split open. Into that widening rift the North Atlantic Ocean began to flood, and it still widens by a few centimetres a year.

Fingal's Cave on Staffa runs about 85 metres into the cliff, walled and roofed with columns, and its floor is the sea itself, so visitors come in by small boat, carried on the swell, or scramble along a ledge of broken column tops.

In the best-loved legend, the Irish giant Finn McCool built the causeway, and the much bigger Scottish giant Benandonner came stomping across it to fight him. Finn panicked, but his wife disguised him as a giant baby and tucked him into a cradle, and when Benandonner saw the size of the baby, he imagined how huge its father must be and fled home. He ripped up the road behind him, which in the story is why the columns plunge into the sea and rise again at Staffa.

In the 1800s geologists found the real link: the Causeway and Staffa, some 120 kilometres apart across open sea, erupted from one and the same great outpouring of basalt, which once blanketed the whole region. Erosion stripped away the middle, leaving two matching ends of a road that, in rock at least, really crosses the sea.

Fingal's Cave's Gaelic name means the cave of melody, for the way the swell booms down its columned hall like an organ. In 1829 the seasick 20-year-old composer Felix Mendelssohn heard it, jotted a theme into a letter to his sister Fanny, and turned it into his concert overture The Hebrides, nicknamed the Fingal's Cave overture.
