glacial-erratics-boulders-the-ice-carrie.context_blurb:
Here and there across the northern lands lie great boulders that do not belong where they sit: their rock matches nothing in the ground beneath them. Ice Age glaciers picked them up far away, carried them for miles and set them down when the ice melted. Some are as big as houses.

Geologists call such a far-carried boulder an erratic, from the Latin errare, to wander. The largest known on Earth is Big Rock, on the prairie west of Okotoks, Alberta: about 41 metres long and 16,500 tonnes of quartzite, cracked clean in two.

The Blackfoot tell how the trickster Napi gave the rock his robe, reclaimed it when rain was coming, and was chased across the plains by the angry rolling rock, until a swarm of bats dived at it and split it in two. In the story the bats flattened their faces doing it; the real crack is a natural fracture.

Big Rock is the largest block in the Foothills Erratics Train, a line of matching quartzite boulders that one glacier carried about 930 kilometres south down the Rockies' eastern flank into Montana. The quartzite began as a landslide in the Athabasca River valley.

In New Hampshire the Madison Boulder, more than 5,000 tonnes of granite, can be traced to Whitten Ledge, under two miles away to the northwest, because its rock is an exact match for the Conway granite of that ledge. Matching an erratic to its parent rock turns each boulder into a signpost showing where the vanished ice came from.

On a hillside called Norber, in England's Yorkshire Dales, dark boulders of ancient greywacke stand on little pedestals of paler, younger limestone. Rain slowly dissolves bare limestone, but each boulder sheltered the limestone beneath it, so while the ground around it wore down, the protected stalk was left standing as much as 30 centimetres tall.

Many people long blamed the stranded boulders on a great biblical Flood. On 24 July 1837, at Neuchâtel, the Swiss naturalist Louis Agassiz argued instead that a great ice age had buried the land, pointing to granite from the far-off Alps lying on the Jura's limestone and to bedrock below it that had been polished and scratched. Flood believers such as Charles Lyell held out for a while, but Agassiz's field evidence won.

gondar.context_blurb:
Gondar sits high in the mountains of northern Ethiopia, the heart of an ancient Christian kingdom that was never colonised. From the 1600s into the 1800s it was the seat of Ethiopia's emperors, who filled it with grey stone castles, crenellated walls and round towers, a sight that makes travellers rub their eyes.

Those turrets look so much like a piece of medieval Europe set down on the African highlands that Gondar is called the Camelot of Africa, after King Arthur's legendary court.

For centuries before that, Ethiopia's emperors had no fixed capital: the court roamed the land, living in vast tented camps. Emperor Fasilides ended the wandering in 1636 by settling at Gondar, and it stayed the capital for about two hundred years.

In the little church of Debre Berhan Selassie, built in the late 1600s under Emperor Iyasu I, the whole wooden ceiling is covered with rows of winged cherub angels, about 80 faces, each painted slightly differently and all gazing down, to show that God sees everywhere.

Beside the castles lies Fasilides' Bath, a broad stone pool around an island that carries a little turreted pavilion. It stands dry most of the year and is filled only for Timkat, the Ethiopian Epiphany, on 19 January, when tens of thousands of Orthodox pilgrims plunge into the blessed water to renew their baptism.

Nearby stands a modest stone tomb that Emperor Yohannes I built not for a king or a saint but for his warhorse, Zobel, which he loved too much to forget.

In 1888 a Mahdist army from Sudan sacked Gondar and burned every church except Debre Berhan Selassie, and local tradition says a swarm of bees poured out of it and stung the raiders into flight. Some add that the Archangel Michael stood at its gates with a flaming sword. It is told as legend, not record.

gor-e-island.context_blurb:
Gorée is a tiny island of rock, barely 18 hectares, two kilometres off Dakar in Senegal, West Africa. For centuries Portuguese, Dutch, English and French traders fought over it, and today it is remembered above all as a site of the Atlantic slave trade, and a place of pilgrimage.

In its pink-and-ochre House of Slaves, built around 1776, a narrow upstairs opening is known as the Door of No Return, and beyond it there is nothing but the open Atlantic Ocean: for those sold into slavery, the last African ground before the ships. The curator Boubacar Joseph Ndiaye made the house a museum in 1962.

The name sounds French but is worn-down Dutch: the Dutch, who held the island from 1588, called it Goede Reede, good roadstead, meaning safe water for anchoring ships. The Portuguese had arrived first, in 1444.

Between 1588 and 1814 the island changed hands about seventeen times, because its harbour was the key to the trade of the whole coast south of Cap-Vert: whoever held this speck of rock held the gateway to the Atlantic corner of West Africa.

How many captives passed through this one door is disputed. Guides long said that a million or more did. The historian Philip Curtin, whose 1969 count of the Atlantic trade reshaped the field, called that story phony and argued that only a few hundred people a year were shipped from the island. Most captives in the region, he pointed out, left from busier depots where the Senegal and Gambia rivers meet the sea. Even so, scholars on both sides agree that Gorée holds a real memory, like a tomb of the unknown soldier for a trade that spanned centuries.

When Nelson Mandela came to the House of Slaves after his 27 years in prison, he folded himself into the cramped punishment cell under the stairs, where captives who resisted had been shut, and came out in tears. In 1978 Gorée was among the first twelve UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

granada-the-alhambras-water-palace.context_blurb:
Granada, in southern Spain, was the last Muslim-ruled kingdom in Western Europe. Long after Christian kings had retaken the rest of the peninsula, the small Nasrid emirate held out here. On a ridge above the city its sultans built the Alhambra, a palace-fortress of courtyards, fountains and halls covered in carved plaster calligraphy and geometric patterns.

Its Arabic name, al-Hamra, means the red one, because its walls of rammed earth packed with iron-rich local clay glow reddish, especially at sunset. It stands on the Sabika ridge above Granada.

Water fills the Alhambra's pools and fountains, yet its dry ridge has no stream. The water is snowmelt from the Sierra Nevada: Nasrid engineers diverted the snow-fed Darro river kilometres upstream and carried it by gravity in a canal, the Acequia Real or Royal Canal, then lifted it the final rise onto the plateau. That canal turned a fort that had lived on rainwater cisterns into a garden palace.

In the Court of the Lions, built by Sultan Muhammad V from 1362, the low fountain's basin rests on the backs of twelve lions of white marble, with water spilling from their mouths.

Four slim channels cross the courtyard floor from the fountain toward north, south, east and west, and in the Islamic garden tradition they picture the four rivers that flow through paradise. Christian tradition shares that image of paradise's rivers.

Next door is the Generalife, the summer estate of the Nasrid sultans. Its Water Staircase climbs the hillside in four flights, and its stone banisters are hollowed into channels, so cold Sierra Nevada water runs down the two banisters beside your hand as you climb.

In the Hall of the Two Sisters, the ceiling dissolves into muqarnas, honeycomb vaulting of at least 5,000 tiny plaster cells hanging in tiers from a central peak like the inside of a stalactite cave and opening into sixteen small domes.

On 2 January 1492 the last Nasrid sultan, Muhammad XII, called Boabdil, handed Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella by treaty, so the city surrendered on agreed terms and no army ever stormed the Alhambra. Christian troops moved in quietly, the new rulers kept the palace, and it survives almost intact. Al-Andalus, which began in 711, had lasted almost 800 years.

great-zimbabwe.context_blurb:
In the south of the country that bears its name, the ruins of Great Zimbabwe spread across some 7 square kilometres of granite hills and valleys. From the 1000s to the 1400s it was the capital of a wealthy Shona kingdom on the high plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo, and its curving stone walls are the largest ancient stonework south of the Sahara.

The Shona called such a place dzimba dza mabwe, houses of stone, and when the country won independence in 1980 it took the name Zimbabwe straight from these ruins.

Its walls hold no mortar at all: the masons shaped millions of granite blocks and fitted them so tightly that their snug fit and their own weight have held them for more than 600 years.

The oldest part, the Hill Complex, sits on a rocky hilltop of giant granite boulders and was settled from about the 11th century. Instead of clearing the boulders away, the builders wove their walls in and around them, so stone wall and living rock rise as one.

Below it stands the Great Enclosure, a dry-stone ring about 250 metres around with walls up to 11 metres high. By the ground it covers, it is the second-largest ancient structure in Africa, and only the pyramids of Egypt are bigger.

Enter by its one narrow gate and a curving lane called the Parallel Passage, some 55 metres long between the outer wall and an inner one, leads you to the foot of the Conical Tower. The tower is a solid cone of stone about 9 metres tall, with no door, window or room inside, and the leading idea, debated rather than proven, is that its shape copies a grain bin, a symbol of the king's power to feed his people.

The walls are mostly plain, but high on the Great Enclosure's outer ring runs a famous band tens of metres long, a zig-zag chevron made purely by setting the granite blocks at angles, like herringbone. Many read it as a sign of water and fertility, though that is interpretation.

Eight soapstone birds, each on a tall stone pillar, once perched on the walls; they represent the bateleur eagle, a good omen and spirit-messenger between the living and the ancestors in Shona belief. One now spreads its wings on Zimbabwe's flag and coat of arms.

With no metal tool hard enough to cut granite, the masons are thought to have split it with fire: they heated the rock in a blaze, then doused it with cold water so it cracked along the grain into brick-like slabs.

European visitors long refused to believe Africans had built the city. In 1871 the German explorer Karl Mauch shaved a splinter off a wooden roof beam, judged it to be Lebanese cedar like the wood of Solomon's Temple, and declared the ruins the palace of the biblical Queen of Sheba. He was wrong on every count: the builders were the ancestral Shona.

The city lay hundreds of kilometres inland, yet it grew rich trading its gold and ivory to Kilwa and Sofala on the Swahili coast. Dug from its floors, porcelain from China and glass beads from Persia prove that it traded across the Indian Ocean.

The old myth had a long, ugly life. After 1965, Rhodesia's white-minority government required every article that credited Africans with the city to give equal space to claims that Phoenicians, Portuguese or the Queen of Sheba built it. The archaeologist Peter Garlake, who proved the Shona built it, was forced out of the country in 1970.

groundwater-the-hidden-rivers-under-our-.context_blurb:
Beneath our feet lies a hidden sea. Rain soaks down through soil and rock and fills the tiny spaces between grains, in water-bearing layers called aquifers. Some of that water has waited underground for thousands of years. It feeds springs and secret rivers, and farms and cities across the world pump it up to live.

About 99 percent of Earth's unfrozen fresh water is not in rivers or lakes at all but soaked into rock and sand underground, filling its pores the way water fills a sponge. This groundwater supplies about half the world's drinking water.

In Palawan, in the Philippines, the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River runs 8.2 kilometres through a limestone mountain and pours out into the sea, the longest underground river on Earth that boats can travel. Because it meets the sea, tides reach inside the mountain, and a thin layer of fresh water floats on salty water below.

Where an aquifer meets the surface, groundwater bursts out as a spring. At Florida's Silver Springs, one of the largest in the world, the water is so clear that the glass-bottom boat was invented there to let tourists look straight down; boats have carried sightseers since 1878.

Florida's Wakulla Springs once gushed a record 1.2 billion gallons in a single day, fed by the longest underwater cave known in America. Since 1850 divers have hauled mastodon bones and the remains of at least ten other extinct mammals from its sandy floor.

In Australia's dry outback, desert mound springs bubble up from the Great Artesian Basin, a vast underground store of water beneath about a fifth of the continent, the largest and deepest artesian basin on Earth. Rain that fell on far-off highlands seeps through the rock for thousands of years, then rises by its own pressure, with no pump; the word artesian comes from Artois in France.

The Ogallala Aquifer under the American Great Plains waters about a third of the crops the United States irrigates from the ground, and most of it is fossil water stored since the last Ice Age that barely refills. Once drained, it would need over 6,000 years to recover.

Libya lies almost wholly inside the Sahara, yet its Great Man-Made River pipes water to the coast through 2,820 kilometres of buried tubes 4 metres wide. The water is pumped from the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer, an ancient store deep beneath the Sahara, filled tens of thousands of years ago when the desert was green, and it will not come back.

gyeongju-the-museum-without-walls.context_blurb:
Gyeongju, in southeastern South Korea, served the kings of Silla as their capital from 57 BCE until 935 CE, and Silla went on to unify the Korean peninsula. So much of that kingdom still stands among the modern streets that the whole town feels like an open-air collection of treasures.

In its downtown parks rise grassy hills as big as houses, 23 in Daereungwon park alone, and they are not hills at all but royal burial mounds of Silla kings and queens, some about 1,500 years old. Hundreds more rise between houses, roads and rice fields.

Silla was called the land of gold, and its kings went to their graves in gold crowns, belts and rings. Each royal tomb was a wooden chamber buried under a deep cap of piled stones, then earth, with no doorway a robber could tunnel through. So while almost every other ancient royal treasure was looted, its crowns, belts and jade beads survived.

In 1973 archaeologists opened the mound now called Cheonmachong, the Heavenly Horse Tomb, and among some 11,500 treasures found a painted birch-bark mudguard showing a white flying horse, the Cheonma, one of the very few Silla paintings to survive.

In a field stands Cheomseongdae, a bottle-shaped granite tower raised for Queen Seondeok in the 630s, from which Silla astronomers watched the sky; it is the oldest observatory still standing in East Asia. It is a calendar in stone too: about 362 blocks, near the number of days in a lunar year, in 27 layers, for Seondeok, Silla's 27th ruler.

High on Mount Toham, the Seokguram Grotto, begun in 751, shelters a serene granite Buddha aimed due east, so that he looks out at the first light of sunrise over the East Sea. Its builders used no mortar; carved stone rivets lock its domed roof together.

Lower down the mountain is Bulguksa temple, completed in 774, with two stone pagodas, one plain and one richly carved. When workers opened Seokgatap, the plain pagoda, in 1966, they found the Great Dharani Sutra, printed from carved wooden blocks around 704 to 751 CE, among the oldest printed texts on Earth, though scholars still debate its exact date. The ornate pagoda, Dabotap, appears on South Korea's 10-won coin.

So many tombs, pagodas, temples and carved Buddhas still stand across the open valley that Gyeongju is nicknamed the museum without walls.

ha-long-bay.context_blurb:
Ha Long Bay, on the northern coast of Vietnam, is an emerald sea crowded with steep limestone towers rising straight from the water, some as tall as 400 metres. Sailing among them feels like drifting through a forest of stone.

More than 1,600 islands and islets fill the bay, scattered over about 1,500 square kilometres.

The name Ha Long means descending dragon. In legend a Mother Dragon and her young came down from heaven at the Jade Emperor's command to guard the land against invaders, spitting jewels of jade and emerald into the sea; the jewels turned to stone and rose as islands that walled out the enemy ships.

The real story is karst: over millions of years slightly acidic rain ate a thick bed of limestone down into steep pinnacles, and then rising seas after the last Ice Age drowned the valleys between them, leaving only the tops above water.

One slender pillar, Dinh Huong, the Incense Burner, is so loved that it appears on Vietnam's 200,000-dong banknote. A nearby pair of rocks, Trong Mai, the Fighting Cocks, is a symbol of Vietnamese tourism.

Among the Bo Hon islands, a slim gap in one tower opens into a cavern about 500 metres long and 30 metres high, hung with giant stalactites, which French explorers mapped in 1901 and named the Cave of Surprises. In Vietnamese it is Sung Sot, Surprise Cave.

Some islands hide still lakes in their hearts, drowned sinkholes ringed by sheer cliffs, and the only way in is to paddle a small boat through a low tunnel in the rock. At Ba Ham Lake, inside Dau Be island, the tunnel runs about 152 metres with a ceiling barely 1.5 to 2.8 metres high, and it can be passed only at low tide.

hangul-the-alphabet-korea-designed-on-pu.context_blurb:
Hangul is the alphabet of Korea, and unlike almost every other writing system on Earth, it did not grow slowly over centuries. One man designed it on purpose: King Sejong the Great, who unveiled it to his court in 1443 and published it in 1446. Before that, writing Korean meant mastering thousands of Chinese characters that only a rich elite had time to learn.

Sejong could read Chinese like every nobleman, but he made Hangul so that ordinary people, commoners and women among them, could at last read and write for themselves; more than 99 in every 100 could not read the borrowed characters.

Modern Hangul needs just 24 basic letters, 14 consonants and 10 vowels, where the old system demanded thousands of characters. Sejong's original set had 28.

The scholar Jeong Inji boasted that a wise man could learn the whole script in one morning, and even a slow learner in ten days. The line is often credited to Sejong himself, but it was Jeong Inji's.

Hangul is the only major alphabet whose letters are diagrams of speech. Each consonant is a little picture of your mouth and tongue making its sound. The square letter for m shows closed lips, the letter for n shows the tongue tip touching the ridge behind the teeth, and the letter for k shows the back of the tongue blocking the throat. The linguist James McCawley called it the cleverest writing system ever devised.

The vowels hide a whole cosmos in miniature: every one is built from three marks, a round dot for heaven, a flat line for earth, and an upright stroke for a standing human being between them.

Not everyone cheered. In 1444 the senior scholar Choe Manri petitioned Sejong to scrap the new letters, warning that only barbarian peoples such as the Mongols and Jurchens invented their own scripts, so a Korean one would drag Joseon down to the level of the barbarians to the north. For centuries elite scholars sneered at Hangul as the vulgar script.

In 2009 the Cia-Cia people of Buton Island, in Indonesia, whose language had never been written, adopted a modified Hangul, the first non-Korean language to take it as its main script.

hanoi-old-quarter.context_blurb:
Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, grew up on the Red River in the north of the country and has been one of its great cities for a thousand years. At its heart lies the Old Quarter, a dense tangle of narrow lanes and shop-houses beside a green lake, where scooters, street cooks and old temples all crowd together.

The Old Quarter is nicknamed the 36 Streets, and many of its lane names begin with Hàng, merchandise, followed by the goods once sold along that lane by the guild that clustered there. So Hàng Bạc is Silver Street, Hàng Thiếc is Tin Street and Hàng Mã is Paper-Offerings Street, names that have outlived their trades.

At the edge of the quarter, a bright red wooden footbridge, Cầu Thê Húc, whose name means Perch of the Morning Sunlight, arches over Hoàn Kiếm Lake to Ngọc Sơn Temple on Jade Island. The temple honours the 13th-century general Trần Hưng Đạo.

Hoàn Kiếm means Returned Sword. In legend Emperor Lê Lợi used a magic sword lent by the Dragon King to throw the Ming Chinese out of Vietnam; later, while he boated on the lake, a giant golden turtle, the god Kim Quy, surfaced and carried the blade back to its owner. Real giant softshell turtles lived in the lake; the last famous one died in 2016.

Lý Thái Tổ founded the city as his capital in 1010 and named it Thăng Long, City of the Ascending Dragon, because, by tradition, he saw a golden dragon rise over the Red River as he arrived. The founding date is history; the dragon is legend.

Legend says the new citadel walls kept crumbling until the king prayed at the shrine of Long Đỗ, guardian spirit of the city. A white horse then appeared and galloped a wide circle around the site, and walls built along its trail held firm. That shrine, Bạch Mã, the White Horse Temple, is the oldest in the Old Quarter.

Old Quarter shop-houses are tube houses, with a street front of just two to four metres but stretching back 20 to 60 metres, because the tax on a house was set by how wide it stood along the street. The narrow front was the shop, and the family lived down the long tail and on the upper floors.

The name Hà Nội, chosen by Emperor Minh Mạng in 1831, means inside the river, because it sits cupped in a bend of the Red River on its broad delta. The low, flood-prone city is ringed with dikes, raised earth walls that hold the river back.

harar.context_blurb:
Harar is an old walled Muslim city in the highlands of eastern Ethiopia, which for centuries guarded a crossroads of the caravan trade. Behind its stone wall lies a tight medieval maze of lanes, mosques and brightly painted houses, and outside the wall, every night after dark, something happens that you will see nowhere else.

The old town is called the Jugol, after the single stone wall, about 3.5 kilometres around and pierced by just five historic gates, that squeezes the whole town into barely one square kilometre. Inside, 368 narrow, twisting alleys make it so dense that people simply call it a maze.

Many Muslims rank Harar fourth among Islam's holy cities, after Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem, though that ranking is widely held rather than universal. Inside its one square kilometre stand 82 mosques, three of them from the 10th century, and 102 saints' shrines, which is why its Arabic name means City of Saints.

Every night just outside the wall, a hyena man feeds wild spotted hyenas strips of raw meat by hand, sometimes from a stick held in his own mouth. Yusuf Mume Saleh began the custom around the 1950s or 1960s, reportedly to stop the hyenas raiding his goats, and his son Abbas Yusuf carries it on.

Harari townhouses, called gey gar, have brightly painted rooms built around a raised sitting platform, and their wall niches are filled with brightly coloured woven baskets, the town's famous craft.

For centuries Harar shut out outsiders, and local legend warned that the city would be lost once a Christian came through its gates. Richard Burton, the English explorer, slipped in during January 1855 in the disguise of a Muslim trader, the first European on record inside. Harar did not fall, and Burton had already used disguise to reach Mecca.

The dazzling French poet Arthur Rimbaud, who wrote his poetry as a teenager and gave it up by about 21, spent 1880 to 1891 inside Harar's walls as a caravan trader dealing in coffee, hides and musk. A grand house in the town is now the Rimbaud museum.

harris-tweed-the-cloth-protected-by-law.context_blurb:
Harris Tweed is a thick, hard-wearing woollen cloth from the Outer Hebrides, the storm-lashed chain of islands off Scotland's northwest coast: Lewis and Harris, the Uists, Benbecula and Barra. Fashion houses around the world sell it, yet it is still made the old cottage way, and the law guards it like no other cloth.

Long before outsiders called it Harris Tweed, the Gaelic-speaking weavers of Lewis and Harris had their own name for it, clò-mòr, meaning the big cloth.

By law, Harris Tweed must be handwoven by the islanders at home, on looms driven by foot treadles, with no factory and no electricity.

When mainland mills began selling cheap machine-made imitations under the Harris Tweed name, the islanders fought back. In 1909 they registered a trademark, the Orb, a globe topped with a cross, and inspectors still stamp it on each length once they confirm it was handwoven in the Outer Hebrides. It is the oldest British certification mark still in use.

Then in 1993 the cloth got its own Act of Parliament, the Harris Tweed Act, a UK law passed for this one fabric alone. It requires wool that is pure and virgin, dyed and spun on the islands, and woven by hand in islanders' homes.

Most home weavers on Lewis and Harris still work the Hattersley loom, a single-width English-built treadle loom that has been the island standard for about a century, powered only by the weaver's feet on the pedals.

The old tweeds' deep reds and purple-browns came from crottle, a lichen that islanders scraped from the rocks and boiled with the wool, leaving the cloth with a faint earthy scent.

havana.context_blurb:
Havana, the capital of Cuba, was founded by the Spanish in 1519 beside a superb natural harbour on the island's north coast. For centuries it was the gathering point for Spain's silver convoys home to Europe, and pirates and rival empires coveted it. Its old quarter of faded colonial mansions and stone forts still guards the narrow harbour mouth.

Along the shore runs the Malecón, an 8-kilometre sea wall and promenade begun in 1901, where families stroll and fish on calm evenings. When winter cold fronts blow in, waves thunder clean over it and flood the road behind.

In the 1500s pirates and French privateers sacked Havana repeatedly. So Spain sent the Italian engineer Battista Antonelli to build El Morro, a huge stone castle begun in 1589 at the harbour mouth, with its sister fort, La Punta, across the channel. A lighthouse added in 1846 still marks the entrance.

Every night the Spanish stretched a great iron chain across the narrow channel from El Morro to La Punta, closing the port from dusk to dawn and snagging any ship that tried to force its way in.

And every night at nine o'clock a cannon is fired from La Cabaña, the fortress above the harbour mouth, as it has been for more than three centuries; in colonial times the shot warned that the city gates were closing. A matching gun at six each morning announced their opening.

Twice a year the treasure fleet gathered the silver of Spain's American empire in Havana's bay, then sailed for Spain in one heavily armed body. That is why the Crown ringed this one harbour with stone forts.

Spain's Crown honoured Havana in 1592 with the official title Key to the New World and Rampart of the West Indies, since this harbour controlled the route between Spain's American empire and Europe. A golden key still appears on the city's coat of arms.

hip-hop-the-bronx.context_blurb:
Hip-hop was born in the 1970s in the Bronx, one of New York City's five boroughs, then a poor and battered place. At block parties, in rec rooms and in public parks, young people built a whole culture out of turntables, microphones, dance and spray paint, and within fifty years it had spread to every corner of the world.

The most famous origin is a party on 11 August 1973 in the rec room of 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, a building in the West Bronx, where DJ Kool Herc played two turntables. His teenage sister, Cindy Campbell, threw it to pay for new back-to-school clothes, charging 25 cents for girls and 50 for boys. Hip-hop grew in several Bronx places, but in 2021 Congress recognised this building as its birthplace.

Herc noticed that the dancers went wildest during the short, drum-heavy stretch in each record called the break, so he set the same record spinning on two turntables at once and switched between them to loop the break over and over. He called the trick the Merry-Go-Round, and a conga-heavy track called Apache became known as hip-hop's national anthem.

When the DJs carried the music outdoors to parks and schoolyards, they found power by prying open the base of a street lamppost and wiring their sound systems into it.

While Herc spun, his friend Coke La Rock grabbed the microphone and hyped the dancers with shout-outs and rhymes over the beat, and he is widely credited as hip-hop's first MC, the first to perform what became rapping. MC stands for Master of Ceremonies.

Certain dancers saved their wildest moves for the looped break, dropping to the floor to spin, flip and freeze, and the dance they made is called breaking; Herc named its dancers b-boys and b-girls. Rival crews took each other on, one move at a time.

Grandmaster Flash, a younger DJ from the Bronx, turned the turntable into a science with his Quick Mix Theory, using a fingertip on the record and the crossfader to chop out a sliver of a record and repeat it in perfect time. To make it work he also invented the DJ slipmat.

Grand Wizzard Theodore was about 12, around 1975, when he pressed his hand on a spinning record as his mother told him to turn the music down, rubbed it back and forth against the needle, and so invented the scratch.

Breaking spread across the world, and at the 2024 Paris Games breaking was made an official Olympic sport, the first street-born dance to win that honour; Japan's Ami Yuasa and Canada's Philip Kim took the first golds.

Lance Taylor had led fighters for the Black Spades gang, among the biggest in the Bronx; as Afrika Bambaataa he founded the Universal Zulu Nation, steering that energy into peaceful culture, a movement that carried hip-hop around the world.

Bambaataa insisted hip-hop was a whole culture and named its four elements: DJing, MCing, breaking and graffiti. His Zulu Nation later added a fifth, knowledge.

hiroshima-the-city-that-came-back.context_blurb:
Hiroshima is a city on the southwest coast of Honshu, Japan. On 6 August 1945 the United States dropped on it the first atomic bomb ever used in war, killing tens of thousands of people at once and tens of thousands more through injury and radiation sickness. The city rebuilt itself and became a worldwide symbol of peace.

At its heart stands one broken building, kept exactly as the blast left it: a hollow brick shell under a bare metal frame, the Genbaku Dome, which means the Atomic Bomb Dome.

It stood only about 160 metres from the point beneath the explosion, but the bomb burst some 600 metres up, almost straight overhead, so the shockwave pressed down through its walls and columns from above instead of striking them from the side. That is why its shape held while the city around it was flattened.

It had opened in 1915 as the Hiroshima Prefectural Commercial Exhibition Hall, a bold European design with a copper dome, drawn by the Czech architect Jan Letzel. He died in Prague in 1925, twenty years before his cheerful hall became the world's most famous ruin.

The city nearly tore the shell down after the war, but kept it braced and unrepaired as a warning, and in December 1996 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site, a reminder of the force humankind can unleash and a symbol of hope for peace.

In the Peace Park, the Children's Peace Monument is topped by a bronze girl lifting a folded paper crane high above her head. It honours Sadako Sasaki, a toddler of two in 1945 who later fell ill with leukemia and folded cranes by the hundreds, hoping, as an old story promises, that a thousand of them would earn her a wish; she died aged 12. Children around the world still send cranes by the thousand.

On 9 August 1945, just three days later, a Hiroden streetcar was running again between Koi and Tenma-cho, carrying stunned survivors for free. Two cars damaged that day, numbers 651 and 652, still carry passengers.

Experts warned that nothing would grow there for decades. By spring 1946, trees less than a kilometre from the blast pushed out new leaves and fresh green buds, living proof the city would recover. These hibaku jumoku, survivor trees, still grow there, and the oleander, which flowered fiercely in the ruins, became the city's flower.

hoi-an.context_blurb:
Hoi An is a small town on the central coast of Vietnam, on the Thu Bon River. From about the 15th to the 19th centuries it was one of the busiest trading ports in Southeast Asia, where Japanese, Chinese, Dutch, Portuguese and French merchants all kept houses. Western traders knew it as Faifo.

Its best-loved landmark is the Japanese Covered Bridge, a wooden bridge with its own roof, over four centuries old, with a tiny temple built right into the middle of the span. By legend, the carved monkey at one end and the dog at the other mark the zodiac years when building began and ended.

On the 14th day of every lunar month, the eve of the full moon, the town turns off its electric lamps, so silk lanterns light the lanes and paper ones float down the Thu Bon carrying wishes. The lanterns become the only glow on the brightest night of the month.

Then the Thu Bon slowly filled the harbour with mud and silt until big ocean-going ships could no longer dock, so trade moved about 30 kilometres north to the deeper port of Da Nang. That decline saved the town: left almost untouched for centuries, Hoi An was listed by UNESCO in 1999 as a superbly preserved trading port.

holy-confluences-and-the-lowest-river-on.context_blurb:
Where two rivers meet, many faiths see something holy: two waters becoming one. The most famous meeting of rivers is at Prayagraj in northern India. Far to the west, the Jordan River runs down a crack in the Earth to the lowest ground on the planet.

At Prayagraj the pale, silty Ganges meets the clearer, blue-green Yamuna, and the two colours stay apart in a crisp seam for a while before mixing: a confluence, the meeting and joining of two rivers.

Its name, Triveni Sangam, means the meeting of three rivers, though only two can be seen; in Hindu belief the third is the Sarasvati, a lost, mythical river that joins them invisibly from below.

Legend says that when gods churned the ocean, drops of amrita, the nectar that grants immortality, fell from a pitcher at four places on earth, and Prayagraj is one of them. There pilgrims gather for the Kumbh Mela, and in 2025 the Maha Kumbh drew about 660 million people to bathe at the Sangam, the largest peaceful gathering ever.

The Jordan, only about 250 kilometres long, runs down the Jordan Rift Valley, part of the Great Rift system, where two tectonic plates, the Arabian and the African, are slowly pulling apart and the trench floor keeps sinking below sea level.

On its way south the river widens into the Sea of Galilee, also called Lake Tiberias or the Kinneret, about 210 metres below sea level, the lowest freshwater lake on the planet.

At last the Jordan ends in the Dead Sea, whose shore, about 430 metres below sea level, is the lowest dry land on Earth, and whose water is roughly a third salt, so dense that bathers bob on top and simply cannot sink. It is too salty for fish or plants.

hong-kong-the-vertical-city.context_blurb:
Hong Kong is a cluster of islands and a slice of mainland at the mouth of the Pearl River in southern China. For about 150 years it was a British colony, until it returned to China in 1997. Steep green mountains drop straight into a deep harbour, and between them the city has nowhere to go but up.

With almost no flat land, Hong Kong built upward, and Guinness World Records counts 669 buildings there at least 150 metres tall, the most skyscrapers of any city on Earth.

Above the city rises Victoria Peak, 552 metres high. The Peak Tram, opened in 1888, was Asia's first funicular, a cable railway up a slope as steep as 48 percent, its two cars joined by a cable so that one rises as the other descends.

At eight o'clock each night some 40 towers around Victoria Harbour flash beams, lasers and searchlights in time to music for ten minutes in A Symphony of Lights, which Guinness lists as the largest permanent light-and-sound show in the world.

The name Hong Kong, heung gong in Cantonese, means Fragrant Harbour, because in Ming and Qing times boats from the harbour near Aberdeen carried away bundles of agarwood incense and other fragrant woods.

Kowloon Walled City was once among the densest places people have ever lived: about 33,000 people packed into some 350 towers on a single block, built with no architects and no building codes. Its towers were laced together by bridges, shared stairs and roofed passages, so that, people boasted, you could cross the whole block from north to south without once touching the ground. Hong Kong pulled it down in 1993 and 1994 and opened a classical Chinese garden, Kowloon Walled City Park, on the site in 1995.

Ride the Peak Tram up after dark and the skyscrapers outside seem to lean far over, as though they were about to topple. In 2013 Chia-huei Tseng of the University of Hong Kong showed that the tilted seats and the straight window frames trick the brain about which way is up.

Victoria Harbour is deep and sheltered because it is a ria: after the last Ice Age, rising seas flooded the old river valleys between Hong Kong's hills. That calm, deep water lets the largest ships anchor beside the city and turned Hong Kong into a great natural port.

hotspots-the-island-chains-a-drifting-pl.context_blurb:
A hotspot is a plume of unusually hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth that stays more or less in one place while a tectonic plate slides over it. Like a candle under a moving sheet of paper, it burns through again and again, building a chain of volcanoes. Hawaii is the textbook case.

The Pacific plate creeps northwest over the Hawaiian hotspot at 5 to 10 centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow, and over millions of years that steady creep drags each island off the plume while a fresh one rises.

Today the plume lies under the Big Island, and its Kilauea is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth; its lava flowed for some 35 years, from 1983 to 2018, one of the longest eruptions ever recorded. Kilauea is young, only a few hundred thousand years old.

Kauai, some 5 million years old and the oldest main island, lies furthest northwest; its fires went out long ago, and rainfall has sculpted it into gorges and razor ridges.

As the plate hauls each volcano off the hotspot, it cools, goes quiet and slowly sinks, worn down until it drowns as a flat-topped seamount or a ring-shaped coral atoll. In some 85 million years it has made at least 129 volcanoes, and only a few still rise above the sea.

Beyond Hawaii the chain runs on underwater for about 6,200 kilometres, more than 80 dead volcanoes reaching almost to Russia, and because the hotspot stayed put while the plate slid over it, the trail records, like a fossil, where the Pacific plate has travelled.

At the young end, south-east of the Big Island and some 35 kilometres offshore, the undersea volcano Kamaehuakanaloa, once called Loihi, is already erupting with its summit about 975 metres underwater. Some ten to a hundred thousand years from now it should break the surface as Hawaii's newest island.

The Galápagos ride a hotspot too, but there the islands get younger toward the west, and Fernandina, less than 700,000 years old, lies directly above the plume as the chain's most active volcano. The older eastern islands have drifted off and gone quiet.

Far to the northwest the chain makes a sharp elbow dating from 47 to 50 million years ago, where the volcanoes turn to run almost due north as the Emperor Seamounts, and for decades scientists read it as the moment the plate changed its direction of travel, swinging by roughly 60 degrees.

Newer research argues that the plume itself was drifting south, by hundreds of kilometres, before about 47 million years ago, so many scientists now think the elbow records both a moving plate and a moving plume. Even textbook geology still has unsolved puzzles.

Where the Emperor chain ends, Meiji Seamount, the oldest surviving link at some 82 million years, has reached Russia's Kuril-Kamchatka Trench, where the Pacific plate dives beneath Kamchatka and drags the old seamount down into the Earth to be destroyed. Geologists call that diving subduction.

Hotspots burn through continents too: as North America drifted southwest over a plume, it left a line of dead calderas some 500 miles long across Idaho's Snake River Plain, and today that hotspot sits beneath Yellowstone in Wyoming.

India slid over the Réunion hotspot some 66 million years ago, and floods of runny basalt buried much of the west of the country, the lava piling up more than 2 kilometres deep: the Deccan Traps. They erupted just as the dinosaurs died out, though most scientists name the Chicxulub asteroid as the main killer. The same plume still builds the island of Réunion.

hue-imperial-citadel.context_blurb:
Hue sits on the Perfume River in central Vietnam. From 1802 to 1945 it was the imperial capital of the Nguyen dynasty, and at its heart lies a huge walled and moated citadel of palaces, gates and courtyards. Much of it was wrecked in the Battle of Hue in 1968, during the Vietnam War, and parts have been restored.

The river, the Song Huong, really is fragrant: each autumn blossoms from fruit orchards in the hills far upstream fall into the current and drift down, scenting the water as it passes the city.

In 1804, after reunifying Vietnam, Emperor Gia Long began a walled citadel at Hue and modelled its palace-city on Beijing's Forbidden City, adapted to Vietnamese feng shui with its back to Ngu Binh Mountain and its face to the river. His son Minh Mang finished the core in the 1830s.

At the centre, behind its own wall, lay the Forbidden Purple City, the emperor's private household, where only the emperor, his family and his personal eunuch servants could live. The eunuchs alone were trusted to serve so close to the imperial women.

In 1803 Gia Long had the Nine Holy Cannons cast from the melted-down bronze weapons of the Tay Son dynasty he had just overthrown, four named for the seasons and five for the elements. Though meant as eternal guardians of the throne, not one has ever been fired.

Every Nguyen emperor built himself a garden-tomb among the pines outside the city. Tu Duc completed his in 1867 and then moved in, using it as a retreat for years while he was still alive, boating on its lake and writing poetry in its pavilion.

Yet Tu Duc was never buried there: tradition says he lies in a secret grave somewhere else, and that the 200 or so servants who carried out the burial were all beheaded on their return, so no one could reveal the spot. It is legend, not record, and the grave has never been found.

hurricane-typhoon-cyclone-one-storm-thre.context_blurb:
Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are giant spinning storms of thunderclouds wheeling around a centre of low pressure. They form over warm tropical seas, and they can flatten coasts, drown deltas and reshape whole regions. Seen from space, they all look alike.

And they are alike: one kind of storm, a tropical cyclone, given different names by region, a hurricane over the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific, a typhoon over the northwestern Pacific near the Philippines, and a cyclone over the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

At the centre lies the eye, a calm, often cloud-free circle of sinking air, typically 30 to 65 kilometres across, ringed by the eyewall, where the winds are fiercest and the rain heaviest. Hurricane Hunter pilots punch through that wall into sudden stillness.

Their only fuel is warm ocean water, warmer than about 26.5 degrees Celsius, so they starve and fade within hours once they move over land or cooler seas.

Most people fear the wind, but NOAA finds that water causes nearly 90 percent of tropical-cyclone deaths, and the single biggest killer is the storm surge, a wall of seawater the storm shoves ashore.

The Saffir-Simpson scale sorts Atlantic hurricanes into categories 1 to 5 by one number only, the peak wind speed, not by damage; a Category 5 has sustained winds above 157 miles an hour.

The deadliest tropical cyclone on record, the Bhola cyclone of November 1970, drove a surge about 10.5 metres high up the Bay of Bengal into the low delta of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, because the bay's shallow funnel squeezes the water higher as the coast narrows. Between 300,000 and 500,000 people are thought to have died.

In October 1979 Typhoon Tip grew to about 2,220 kilometres across, the biggest tropical cyclone anyone has measured, and it also set the world record for the lowest air pressure at sea level. Air Force planes flew about 60 reconnaissance flights into it.

In 1935 a Labor Day hurricane, the first Category 5 storm known to hit the United States, battered the Florida Keys, swept a relief train off its tracks, and destroyed the Overseas Railroad to Key West, which was never rebuilt as a railway. More than 400 people died, many of them stranded World War I veterans.

Super Typhoon Haiyan struck the central Philippines in 2013 with winds near 315 kilometres an hour and a surge about 7.5 metres high that flattened the coastal city of Tacloban. About 6,300 people died.

The South Atlantic's cool water and strong upper winds were thought to make hurricanes impossible there, until March 2004, when Hurricane Catarina formed and struck southern Brazil's Santa Catarina state, which gave it its name. It is the first and so far only one confirmed there.

A cyclone needs the spin of the Coriolis effect, which fades to almost nothing at the equator, yet in December 2001 Typhoon Vamei formed only about 1.5 degrees north of it, near Singapore, nearer the equator than any other tropical cyclone on record.

ice-age-megafloods-and-vanished-lakes.context_blurb:
At the end of the last Ice Age, as the great ice sheets over North America melted, meltwater piled up into enormous lakes, some held back by walls of ice. When those dams broke, megafloods roared across the land: torrents bigger than any river flowing today, which tore out canyons in days and left scars you can still see from the air.

In Utah, the vanished Ice Age Lake Bonneville left its own mark. Its dried, cracked floor is now the Bonneville Salt Flats, a hard white crust nearly five feet thick, famous for setting world land-speed records since the 1910s.

In Montana, Glacial Lake Missoula held some 500 cubic miles of water behind a dam about 2,000 feet tall, and that dam was a tongue of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet plugging the Clark Fork valley. Because ice floats and leaks, the dam failed and re-formed again and again, at least 25 times, and every failure loosed a megaflood.

The city of Missoula now sits on the drained lake floor, and level shorelines cut by its waves still line the mountains around it, faint horizontal terraces where the water stood for long spells.

Over roughly 2,000 square miles of eastern Washington, those floods stripped the soil down to black basalt, and the maze of dry rock canyons they left, the Channeled Scablands, was carved by brief, violent floods in a matter of days, not over slow ages.

At each flood's peak, the water raced across the land at up to 65 miles an hour, carrying roughly the flow of 13 Amazon Rivers at once. Only from an aeroplane did geologists see that the long, evenly spaced ridges marching across parts of the Scablands, as tall as 50 feet, are giant ripples that rushing water left behind, the same marks a stream leaves in sand.

Dry Falls, a dry horseshoe of cliffs 400 feet tall and some three and a half miles across, was a waterfall at the floods' peak, roughly five times the width of Niagara and among the greatest on Earth by flow. Today not a drop runs over it.

J Harlen Bretz first made the case for fast, giant floods in 1923, and for about 40 years colleagues who believed landscapes change only slowly ridiculed him, until photographs taken from aircraft and from space in the 1970s showed the flood channels plainly. In 1979, aged 96, he won geology's top prize, the Penrose Medal.

Farther east, water from the shrinking Laurentide Ice Sheet gathered into Lake Agassiz, named for the scientist Louis Agassiz, which spread over 440,000 square kilometres of central North America, bigger than all the Great Lakes combined. Its silty bed is now the rich farmland of the Red River Valley, and Lake Winnipeg is a remnant.

The 15-ton Willamette Meteorite, the largest found in the United States, first landed near the Montana border; it was frozen into glacier ice, carried hundreds of miles inside an iceberg on a Missoula flood, and dropped in Oregon's Willamette Valley when the ice melted.

Then, some 12,900 years back, with the planet warming, the north fell back into hard cold for more than a thousand years. Scientists call it the Younger Dryas, after an Arctic wildflower whose pollen reappears in mud from that time. One debated idea is that Lake Agassiz burst into the sea and its cold fresh water stalled the ocean's warm currents.

Lake Bonneville rose until, some 17,500 years ago, it overtopped Idaho's Red Rock Pass, which crumbled, and the Bonneville Flood roared down the Snake River, carving canyons and stranding house-sized boulders.

icebergs-how-they-calve-and-drift.context_blurb:
Icebergs are mountains of fresh water adrift in salt seas: chunks that break, or calve, off the ends of glaciers and ice shelves and float out to sea. Antarctica sheds the biggest; in the north most come from Greenland and drift down the chilly Labrador Current.

Ice is a little lighter than seawater, so a berg must sink about nine-tenths of its bulk to float and only about a tenth shows above the surface, which is why a small sign of a much bigger hidden problem is called just the tip of an iceberg.

An iceberg is glacier ice, snow pressed down on land over thousands of years, so unlike sea ice, which is the ocean's own surface frozen into a salty crust each winter, a berg is fresh water you could melt and drink. The word comes from the Dutch ijsberg, ice mountain.

Floating ice counts as a true iceberg only when it measures over 15 metres or so, and the smallest, most dangerous pieces, no bigger than a truck and barely clearing the waves, are growlers, named for the hiss of air escaping as they melt. Low and dark, they slip past radar when the sea is rough.

The berg that doomed the Titanic in 1912 began life on Greenland's glaciers, probably the Jakobshavn Glacier near Disko Bay, and rode the Labrador Current south past Newfoundland, along the stretch called Iceberg Alley. After the disaster, nations founded the International Ice Patrol in 1914 to track drifting bergs.

The largest bergs are Antarctica's flat-topped tabular giants, and B-15, which split off Antarctica's Ross Ice Shelf in March 2000, measured about 295 by 37 kilometres, some 11,000 square kilometres, as big as Jamaica.

Most bergs look white because fresh glacier ice is packed with tiny air bubbles that scatter light. After thousands of years, though, the ice's own weight squeezes the bubbles out, so the dense ice soaks up red and yellow light and glows deep blue: a blue berg is ice thousands of years old.

iceland-where-two-continents-pull-apart.context_blurb:
Iceland sits in the middle of the North Atlantic, on a seam where two of Earth's great plates are pulling apart. The island is literally splitting in two, and new land keeps welling up from below. Volcanoes, glaciers, hot springs and fissures crowd together here as almost nowhere else.

Magma keeps rising under the country, which has some 30 active volcanic systems, and in the last five centuries this little island has produced about a third of all the lava erupted on Earth.

When Fagradalsfjall, on the Reykjanes peninsula, erupted in March 2021 after some 800 quiet years, it caused no panic; instead some 700,000 visits were counted across the eruptions of 2021 to 2023 as people hiked out to see molten lava from just a few steps away.

The world's longest mountain range runs almost entirely under the oceans, and Iceland is where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a spreading seam on the sea floor, rises high enough to become dry land. Iceland also sits over a hotspot, and both feed its volcanoes.

Along it the North American and Eurasian plates drift apart about 2 centimetres a year, so Iceland grows a little wider each year, its western half riding with North America and its eastern half with Eurasia.

At Thingvellir National Park the rift lies open on land: a path drops through the Almannagjá gorge, with the North American plate's cliff to one side and Eurasia's to the other. Thingvellir also hosted the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments, founded in 930.

In the same rift lies Silfra, a flooded crack where divers glide between the two plates, and its glacial meltwater, filtered for decades through porous lava, gives more than 100 metres of visibility, said to be the clearest water on the planet.

When a volcano buried beneath a glacier, such as Grímsvötn beneath the Vatnajökull ice cap, melts the ice from beneath, the water collects in a secret lake under the ice and then breaks out in a violent flood that Icelanders call a jökulhlaup, a glacier run. In 1996 one peaked at about 500,000 cubic metres per second.

In April 2010 Eyjafjallajökull erupted under its glacier and threw glassy ash high into the sky. Winds carried it over Europe, airlines grounded flights for days, and more than 100,000 flights were cancelled, the biggest disruption to flying in Europe since the Second World War.

Just after midnight on 23 January 1973 a fissure tore open on Heimaey, barely a kilometre from the sleeping town, and within roughly six hours almost all 5,300 islanders had been taken off the island aboard the fishing boats of the island, which by luck were in harbour that night.

As the Eldfell eruption went on for months, a wall of lava crept toward the harbour mouth, and townspeople and crews pumped about 7.3 million cubic metres of seawater onto it, up to 1,000 litres a second, cooling it solid. They saved the harbour, and the hardened lava even improved it as a new breakwater.

teaches.747a2d1a84: At Thingvellir National Park the rift lies open on land: a path drops through the Almannagjá gorge, with the North American plate's cliff to one side and Eurasia's to the other.
teaches.6cbbe75c1c: In the same rift lies Silfra, a flooded crack where divers glide between the two plates, and its glacial meltwater, filtered for decades through porous lava, gives more than 100 metres of visibility, said to be the clearest water on the planet.
teaches.f7d1a4fa11: When a volcano buried beneath a glacier, such as Grímsvötn beneath the Vatnajökull ice cap, melts the ice from beneath, the water collects in a secret lake under the ice and then breaks out in a violent flood that Icelanders call a jökulhlaup, a glacier run.
teaches.2b0ce892bd: In April 2010 Eyjafjallajökull erupted under its glacier and threw glassy ash high into the sky. Winds carried it over Europe, airlines grounded flights for days, and more than 100,000 flights were cancelled, the biggest disruption to flying in Europe since the Second World War.
teaches.66ed6af684: Just after midnight on 23 January 1973 a fissure tore open on Heimaey, barely a kilometre from the sleeping town, and within roughly six hours almost all 5,300 islanders had been taken off the island aboard the fishing boats of the island, which by luck were in harbour that night.
teaches.0d91727c5a: As the Eldfell eruption went on for months, a wall of lava crept toward the harbour mouth, and townspeople and crews pumped about 7.3 million cubic metres of seawater onto it, up to 1,000 litres a second, cooling it solid.

iguaz-falls.context_blurb:
Iguazú Falls thunders over a long curved cliff on the border of Argentina and Brazil, deep in subtropical rainforest. Instead of one broad sheet, the river breaks over the edge into a long chain of separate cascades divided by green rocky islands, and walkways let visitors wander among them.

Strung along an arc of about 2.7 kilometres are roughly 275 separate falls, though the count shifts with the water, from about 150 in the dry season to nearly 300 in flood.

The arc is nearly three times as wide as Niagara, which is also the shorter drop, so when Eleanor Roosevelt, the American First Lady, first saw Iguazú in the 1940s, she is said to have sighed, Poor Niagara!

At the centre of the arc, about fourteen falls pour together into one U-shaped chasm and plunge about 82 metres, flinging up a column of mist that never settles: the Garganta del Diablo, the Devil's Throat. From the metal walkway on its rim you watch about half of the whole river's flow vanish into that single gorge.

The Guaraní people named the river long before Europeans came: in their language y means water and ûasú means big, so Iguazú simply means big water.

A Guaraní legend says a jealous serpent-god of the forest wanted the girl Naipí, and when she fled downriver by canoe with her love, Tarobá, the furious god sliced the river in two, opening the cliff so the lovers would fall forever.

The falls star in The Mission, a 1986 film about Jesuit missionaries living with the Guaraní, which opens with a captured priest lashed to a cross and sent over the cataract; it won the Palme d'Or at Cannes and an Oscar for its cinematography.

Great dusky swifts hunt insects in the mist all day, then fly straight through the curtain of water to nest on bare rock ledges hidden behind the cascade, where predators cannot follow.

The hard black lip the river leaps from is flood basalt, the upper layer of lava sheets piled up to 1,000 metres deep across the Paraná Plateau, a formation called the Serra Geral.

Like Niagara, Iguazú is creeping upstream: water washes out the softer rock beneath the hard basalt lip, the overhang collapses, and the whole cliff retreats about 1.4 to 2.1 centimetres a year, a migration geographers call headward erosion.

isfahan.context_blurb:
Isfahan, in the heart of Iran, was the capital of the Safavid Persian Empire. Around 1600 Shah Abbas the Great made it his seat and filled it with blue-tiled domes, palaces, bridges and gardens, and most of his city still stands, among the most beautiful in the Islamic world.

A Persian proverb boasts, in the words Isfahan nesf-e jahan ast, that Isfahan is half the world.

At its heart lies Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Image of the World, laid out by Shah Abbas from 1598 to 1629 and about 560 by 160 metres, framed on all four sides by mosques, a palace and the gate of the bazaar; few public squares anywhere are bigger.

The shahs also played polo there, watching from the terrace of the Ali Qapu Palace, and the original stone goalposts from those games still stand at the square's north and south ends.

On the square's east side the little Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, a jewel of tilework, has no minaret and no courtyard, because it was the shah's own private family mosque and needed neither to call nor to hold the crowds.

The Si-o-se-pol, a Safavid bridge of 33 stone arches nearly 300 metres long across the Zayanderud, built from 1599 to 1602, could also hold the river back as a dam, ponding the water upstream. At dusk people still gather in its arcades.

Shah Abbas II's garden pavilion of about 1647 is called Chehel Sotoun, Forty Columns, though its porch has only twenty slender wooden columns; by tradition the other twenty are their reflections in the long pool out front.

To cover the great blue dome of the Shah Mosque quickly, Safavid craftsmen used haft-rangi, seven colours: they painted many colours onto each square tile and fired them together, far faster than cutting and fitting pieces of single-colour mosaic.

isostatic-rebound-the-land-still-rising.context_blurb:
A thick ice sheet is heavy enough to push the Earth's crust down into the soft, dense mantle beneath, the way a hand presses into a mattress. When the ice melts, the crust slowly springs back over thousands of years. Geologists call this isostatic rebound, and in lands that lay under the last Ice Age's ice it is still going on.

On Sweden's High Coast the land rises faster than anywhere else known: an ice sheet about two miles thick pressed it down, and now that the ice has melted the crust is springing back, about 300 metres in ten thousand years and still some 8 millimetres a year.

Around Hudson Bay, where the Laurentide Ice Sheet lay thickest until about 8,000 years ago, the crust is still slightly dented, with a little less mass beneath you, so gravity reads weaker and a scale shows you weigh a hair less than elsewhere. Incomplete rebound explains only part of the gap; slow flow deep in the mantle explains the rest.

Across the gulf at Finland's Kvarken archipelago, the land rises 8 to 9 millimetres a year, so fresh land keeps rising out of the shallow sea, about a square kilometre of new ground each year, with new islands and meadows appearing within a lifetime.

istanbul.context_blurb:
Istanbul, in Turkey, is the great city of two continents. For most of its history it was Constantinople, capital of the Christian Byzantine Empire from 330 and then, after 1453, of the Muslim Ottoman Empire for nearly five centuries more. Byzantine churches, Ottoman mosques and thousand-year-old walls stand layered together on its hills.

The city's European and Asian halves are split by the Bosphorus, a saltwater strait about 31 kilometres long and pinching to about 700 metres at its tightest, crowded with ferries. It is the Black Sea's only natural gate to the open world, linking it through the Sea of Marmara to the Mediterranean.

Greek settlers from Megara founded the first town here, Byzantium, around 660 BC; Constantine the Great refounded it as the Roman capital in 330 and it became Constantinople. The name Istanbul, from a Greek phrase meaning to the City, became official only in 1930.

Its greatest building is Hagia Sophia, which Emperor Justinian raised in under six years and finished in 537; its dome is so wide and ringed with so many windows that it seems to float on light. For nearly a thousand years it was the largest cathedral on Earth.

Hagia Sophia has lived four lives: an Orthodox cathedral from 537, a mosque once Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453, a museum from 1935 under Turkey's new secular republic, and a working mosque again since 2020.

Under the streets lies the Basilica Cistern, Justinian's 6th-century reservoir, where 336 marble columns rise from shallow water, and two of them stand on huge carved heads of Medusa the Gorgon, dragged from an older Roman building, one upside down and one on its side. No one knows for certain why.

Mehmed the Conqueror began the Grand Bazaar in the 1450s, and today its roofed maze of about 61 streets and more than 4,000 shops draws a quarter of a million people or more every day.

On the northern shore rises the Galata Tower, raised in 1348 by settlers from Genoa, and a beloved legend from 1638 tells how Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi glided all the way across the Bosphorus to the Asian shore on home-made wings.

For a thousand years the triple Theodosian Walls, a moat and two lines of ramparts, turned back every attacker. Then Mehmed II, still a young man, broke through in 1453 with a giant bronze cannon about 9 metres long, cast for the siege by the founder Orban and dragged into place by teams of oxen.

The sultans governed for almost four centuries from Topkapı Palace, which Mehmed the Conqueror began in 1459 on Seraglio Point, where the Bosphorus meets the Sea of Marmara, until they moved to a new palace in 1853.

Sultan Ahmed I built his mosque across the square from Hagia Sophia with six minarets, the same number as the Great Mosque of Mecca, and legend says he settled the scandal by paying for a seventh minaret at Mecca. Its tens of thousands of blue İznik tiles earned it the name the Blue Mosque.

jaipur-the-pink-city-and-its-stone-sky-m.context_blurb:
Jaipur, in the desert state of Rajasthan in northwestern India, was founded on 18 November 1727 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II of the Kachhwaha Rajputs, who named it the City of Jai. He built it to a plan, filled it with palaces, and crowned it with an observatory of giant stone instruments.

Step into the walled old town and every building wears the same terracotta pink, the traditional colour of welcome, which is why Jaipur is called the Pink City.

For a royal guest in 1876, Ram Singh II had the whole old town washed pink: Albert Edward, the visiting Prince of Wales and Britain's future King Edward VII, on his royal tour of India. Jaipur has stayed pink ever since.

Jai Singh's great passion was astronomy, studying the stars; he built huge stone observatories in Jaipur, Delhi and other cities.

Most old Indian cities grew into tangles of lanes, but Jai Singh's planner, Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, drew Jaipur on paper first as a grid of nine rectangular blocks, two for the palace and state buildings and seven for the people, cut by main streets about 34 metres wide. In 2019 UNESCO listed the walled city.

Jai Singh's open-air observatory, the Jantar Mantar, finished in 1734, holds 19 instruments built not as small handheld tools but as huge masonry ramps, bowls and towers, and astronomers climbed them as if they were buildings to take their readings with the naked eye.

Its biggest instrument, the Samrat Yantra, rises about 27 metres and keeps local time accurate to a couple of seconds, which makes it the world's largest sundial; its shadow creeps about a hand's breadth every minute, so you can watch the sun move.

The pink Hawa Mahal, built in 1799, let royal women watch the street unseen through 953 tiny latticed windows, and it is called the Palace of Winds because a breeze squeezed through so many small gaps speeds up into a brisk draft that cools the rooms.

Its architect, Lal Chand Ustad, gave it a tall, tapering, pyramid-like front deliberately, so that it would recall the crown of Lord Krishna.

Above Jaipur in Amber Fort lies the Sheesh Mahal, or Mirror Palace: thousands of little curved mirrors, each set over coloured foil, cover its walls and ceiling, so the light of a single candle glitters across the whole hall like a sky full of stars. The fort, begun by Raja Man Singh I, is reflected in Maota Lake below.

jazz-new-orleans.context_blurb:
Jazz was born in New Orleans around the turn of the 20th century, out of the city's rich mix of African, Caribbean, French, Spanish and American traditions. Brass-band marches, blues, ragtime, church spirituals and Creole songs all poured into it, and out came a new music of off-beat rhythm and improvised solos that travelled up the Mississippi and around the world.

When a brass band comes down the street, the band and the family up front form the main line, and the dancers who join behind them with parasols and handkerchiefs are the second line, which anyone may join.

A New Orleans jazz funeral has two halves: on the way to the grave the band plays slow dirges, and after the burial it cuts the body loose and swings into joyful music, most famously When the Saints Go Marching In, for the dancing march home.

The music's roots go back to slavery. Under the French slave code, Sunday was a day of rest, and Congo Square became effectively the one spot in the country where enslaved people were free to gather, beat drums, sing and dance outdoors, keeping alive the rhythms that later seeded jazz. There they played drums, gourds and banjos beside European fiddles and tambourines, and the most celebrated dance, which set the whole crowd stamping together, was the bamboula, named for the bamboo-headed drum that drove it.

Louis Armstrong was eleven when he shot off his stepfather's pistol to celebrate the New Year in 1912; he was sent to the Colored Waif's Home, where the teacher Peter Davis handed him a cornet, the trumpet's stubbier cousin, and made him bandleader.

From 1897 to 1917 the city's legal red-light district, Storyville, named for the alderman Sidney Story, gave early jazz pianists their steadiest work in its saloons and brothels. When the Navy shut it down in 1917, many musicians headed north by riverboat, bringing jazz to Chicago.

On a 1926 recording of Heebie Jeebies, the story goes, Armstrong's lyric sheet fell to the floor, so he kept singing in made-up syllables, and the hit record spread scat, wordless improvised singing that treats the voice like a horn. Armstrong did not invent scat, and the dropped-sheet tale may be a legend he enjoyed telling.

In the 1920s, on the records he cut with the bands he called the Hot Five and the Hot Seven, Armstrong almost single-handedly made the improvised jazz solo the centre of the music, building his lines on a song's chords rather than just its melody.

Jelly Roll Morton, who began playing piano in Storyville's brothels at fourteen, boasted that he had invented jazz in 1902; critics mocked him, but his Jelly Roll Blues of 1915 really was one of the first jazz compositions ever published.

The earliest jazz record to reach the shops was Livery Stable Blues, cut in February 1917 by the Original Dixieland Jass Band, a white New Orleans group, a novelty in which cornet, clarinet and trombone imitated barnyard animals for laughs. It became a national hit, though Black New Orleans musicians had been making the music for years.

Buddy Bolden, a cornet player of about 1900, blew so loudly that listeners claimed his horn carried clear to the far side of town when the air was calm, and fans crowned him the first King of jazz, yet no recording of him has ever been found. His career ended in 1907 with a mental collapse, and he died in an asylum in 1931.

jerusalems-old-city-quarter-by-quarter.context_blurb:
The walled Old City of Jerusalem is less than one square kilometre of pale golden stone, yet few places on Earth are held so sacred by so many. Jews revere it as the city of David and of the vanished Temples, Christians as the place where Jesus was crucified and, they believe, rose again, and Muslims as the city of Muhammad's Night Journey.

Within the walls lie four neighbourhoods, the Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian Quarters, each home to its own people and shrines; the Muslim Quarter is the largest and the Armenian the smallest.

At the Western Wall, the Kotel, the holiest place where Jews gather to pray, worshippers have for centuries tucked folded slips of paper bearing prayers into the gaps between its huge stones.

The golden walls look ancient, but the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent raised them in just five years, from 1537 to 1541: about 4 kilometres around and some 12 metres high.

Through the twisting lanes runs the Via Dolorosa, the Way of Sorrows, about 600 metres long, which Christian tradition marks as the path Jesus walked carrying his cross; pilgrims stop to pray at its 14 Stations of the Cross, the last five inside the Holy Sepulchre, the great church where the route ends.

On the raised platform at the city's heart stands the Dome of the Rock, built around 691 by Abd al-Malik, an Umayyad caliph, the oldest Islamic building still standing; its golden dome has become the symbol of the city. It shelters the Foundation Stone, a slab of bedrock that Jews, Christians and Muslims all hold sacred.

Across the deep Kidron Valley to the east rises the Mount of Olives, whose slope facing the city has been a Jewish burial ground for about 3,000 years, with some 150,000 graves stepping down the hill. At its foot lies the Garden of Gethsemane, with olive trees believed to be centuries old.

In the eastern wall, facing that valley, stands the double-arched Golden Gate, also called the Gate of Mercy, bricked up in 1541 and sealed ever since; in Jewish tradition the Messiah is to come through it into the city from the Mount of Olives.

The Western Wall was never a wall of the Temple itself: around 19 BCE Herod the Great raised an enormous artificial platform around the sacred hill to enlarge the Temple Mount, and the Wall is a surviving retaining wall holding up one side of it.

Around 700 BCE, with the Assyrians advancing, King Hezekiah's engineers drove a tunnel over 500 metres through the rock to bring the Gihon Spring's water inside the walls. The Siloam inscription, which the workers carved and which was found in 1880, records how two teams dug toward each other, cut from opposite ends and met in the middle.

Six Christian communities share the Holy Sepulchre, the church over the traditional site of Jesus's tomb, and quarrel over it, so for centuries two Muslim families have kept its door: the Joudeh family holds the iron key, and the Nuseibeh family unlocks and locks it each day. Tradition traces the arrangement to Saladin in 1187.

Under the Status Quo of 1757, nothing in the church may change unless all six communities agree, so a plain wooden ladder propped on a ledge above the main doors has not moved in roughly 300 years: the Immovable Ladder.

jingdezhen-chinas-porcelain-capital.context_blurb:
Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi province in southeastern China, has made porcelain for more than a thousand years: thin, white, ringing ware that Europe's kings coveted for centuries and could not copy. From the 14th century its kilns fired porcelain for the emperors themselves.

Jingdezhen's kilns were so many that Père d'Entrecolles, a French Jesuit who lived there, wrote in 1712 that, arriving at night, you would think the whole town was on fire, one great furnace with many vents.

So much of this porcelain reached Europe that English speakers named it after the country it came from, first China dishes, then China-ware, and by the 1650s simply china.

Italians called it porcellana, their word for a cowrie shell, because the ware's smooth, glossy surface looked like that little shell, and from it comes our word porcelain.

The pure white body comes from a clay dug at Gaoling, High Ridge, a hill and village near Jingdezhen, and potters everywhere now call it kaolin, after the hill. The word reached English in 1727 through d'Entrecolles' letters.

Jingdezhen had it all close at hand, fine clay, porcelain stone and pines to feed the kilns, and it sent its brittle ware out by boat on the Chang River, far more safely than by jolting cart.

European potters kept failing, and a Jingdezhen merchant told d'Entrecolles why: Chinese potters called kaolin the bones of porcelain and the ground porcelain stone its flesh, and the Europeans were trying to make a body of flesh with no bones to hold it up.

The emperor kept his own imperial kiln at Jingdezhen, and the five-clawed dragon belonged to him alone; by Ming times painting it for anyone else counted as treason, and tradition says that under the Qing such a painter could be killed with his whole family. Four claws marked the princes.

The second ingredient is petuntse, also called China stone: in the fire it melts into glass and binds the clay into hard-paste porcelain, and the best deposits in China lay right next to the town.

A single imperial order of 1433 called for 443,500 pieces, over 440,000, in dragon-and-phoenix designs, every one meant to be given away to court officials and envoys from abroad.

Around 1004 the Song emperor Zhenzong loved the town's thin white ware so much that he had pieces marked with his reign-era title, Jingde, and renamed the town Jingde-zhen, Jingde town, a rare Chinese city named for an emperor's reign.

Europe's rulers poured fortunes into the hunt for the porcelain secret, which they called the Arcanum, and d'Entrecolles, from his home by the kilns, sent back in 1712 the first detailed Western account of the recipe. Germany's Meissen works had already made hard-paste porcelain from local kaolin a few years earlier, so his letters spread the secret rather than giving Europe its first porcelain.

k2.context_blurb:
K2 rises on the border of Pakistan and China, deep in the Karakoram range. At 8,611 metres it is the second-highest mountain on Earth, only about 240 metres lower than Everest, but it is far steeper, colder and more dangerous to climb.

After the 1953 American expedition, the climber George Bell called it the Savage Mountain, a mountain that tries to kill you, and the nickname stuck.

Its name comes from a mapping survey of the 1800s: in 1856 the British surveyor Thomas Montgomerie, working on the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, labelled the Karakoram peaks K1, K2, K3 and so on, with K for Karakoram. K1 later took back its local name, Masherbrum, but K2 stood so deep in the range that no common local name reached the mapmakers, so the code stuck.

For decades about one in four climbers who reached K2's summit died on the mountain, a fatality rate above 20 percent, while far fewer die on taller Everest.

Near the top lies the most feared passage in mountaineering, the Bottleneck, a narrow chute of snow and ice around 8,200 metres that runs beneath overhanging cliffs of ice, called seracs, that can break off without warning. On 1 and 2 August 2008 a serac collapse there cut the fixed ropes, and eleven climbers died.

On 31 July 1954 Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli of an Italian expedition led by Ardito Desio made the first ascent by the Abruzzi Spur, the classic route most climbers have followed ever since.

In a storm in 1953, as the American team lowered their sick teammate Art Gilkey, six roped climbers slipped and began to slide, and Pete Schoening held them all by wedging his ice axe behind a boulder, a save known simply as The Belay. Gilkey was later swept away and died.

K2 was the last 8,000-metre peak unclimbed in winter, until on 16 January 2021 an all-Nepali team of ten, led by Nirmal Purja and Mingma Gyalje Sherpa, regrouped just below the top and stepped onto the summit together, singing Nepal's national anthem.
