kabuki-and-noh-japan.context_blurb:
Japan has two great traditional theatres. Noh, from the 14th century, is slow, masked and austere, the drama of the samurai elite. Kabuki, born in the early 1600s, is its loud, colourful younger rival, full of painted faces, dazzling costumes and stage tricks, and it drew crowds of townspeople in the big cities.

Kabuki began around 1603 on the dry, stony bed of the Kamo River in Kyoto, where Izumo no Okuni, a former shrine dancer, and her company of women performed a flashy new dance-drama. In a famous irony, the theatre a woman founded would soon ban women and become entirely male.

The name comes from the kabukimono, flashy young rebels of the early 1600s whose nickname grew from the old verb kabuku, to tilt or lean off-centre, so they were the crooked ones who leaned against every custom. Only later was kabuki written with characters for song, dance and skill.

At a play's most thrilling moment the hero freezes in a mie, every muscle locked, a foot stamped down and his eyes crossed in a fierce glare, as an admirer in the audience calls out his stage name. The great actor Ichikawa Danjuro I pioneered the pose.

Namiki Shozo, a playwright in Osaka, set a mawari-butai into the stage floor around 1758: a huge revolving turntable, more than a century before Western theatres copied it. Playhouses still use it today.

kano.context_blurb:
Kano, in northern Nigeria, ranks among West Africa's oldest cities and is the heart of the Hausa homeland. For a thousand years it stood at the southern end of the caravan routes across the Sahara, and today it is a city of millions, still ringed in places by its great medieval wall.

The wall, the Ganuwa, was built of sun-dried mud, begun under King Gijimasu around 1100 and raised higher by later kings. By 1851 the explorer Heinrich Barth found it about 10 to 11 miles around and as much as 30 feet tall, and after the British conquest of 1903 Frederick Lugard said he had never seen anything like it in Africa.

Beside Kofar Mata, one of the old city gates, lie the Kofar Mata dye pits, where cloth has been dipped in deep clay pits of near-black indigo since around 1498; no older indigo pits are still in use anywhere in Africa. The dye needs just indigo leaves, wood ash and potash, left to ferment for weeks.

King Muhammad Rumfa founded Kano's Kurmi Market in the 1400s, and leather became the city's most prized export: by 1851 Kano sent out some 10 million pairs of leather sandals and 5 million tanned hides a year, carried by camel to Timbuktu, Tripoli, Morocco and beyond.

karnak-and-ancient-thebes-luxor.context_blurb:
Beside the Nile at Luxor, in southern Egypt, on the river's eastern bank, stood ancient Thebes, capital of the pharaohs, and at its heart Karnak, the biggest temple complex anyone has ever raised. Its temples, chapels, gateways and obelisks honour above all Amun-Re, king of the gods, and they sprawl across more than 2 square kilometres.

The Egyptians called it Ipet-isut, the Most Select of Places, their boast that this was the finest, holiest ground in Egypt.

It is not one building but a walled expanse of temples, chapels, courts, gateways and its own sacred lake, so Egyptologists often call it a city of temples.

There was never one plan: Egypt's pharaohs, one after another, about thirty in all, kept adding to Karnak from around 2000 BCE to 204 BCE, each building onto or right over the work of the one before.

In its Great Hypostyle Hall stand 134 stone columns, and the twelve giants down the centre aisle, about 21 metres tall, are carved as papyrus stalks crowned with open papyrus flowers. Papyrus grew thick along the Nile, and its stalks were pressed into sheets to write on. The hall is the largest room of any ancient religious building.

To the priests the dim hall was a stone image of the primeval marsh, the watery chaos from which the creator-god Atum first rose on the mound of creation at the beginning of the world. Its stone roof once kept it in permanent twilight, like a marsh at dusk.

For great festivals priests carried Amun's statue out of Karnak along the Avenue of Sphinxes, about 2.7 kilometres long, to the temple at Luxor, past more than a thousand sphinxes, many with the heads of rams, Amun's sacred animal. Buried for centuries, the avenue reopened in 2021.

Beside the temples lies the Sacred Lake, the largest at any Egyptian temple, dug for Thutmose III, and each day the priests walked down its steps and bathed in it to purify themselves before serving the god.

Nearby stands Queen Hatshepsut's obelisk, about 30 metres tall and over 300 tonnes, cut from one single block of pink granite at Aswan and floated 200 kilometres down the Nile; no taller ancient obelisk still stands in Egypt. Its broken twin lies beside the Sacred Lake.

The First Pylon, Karnak's grandest gateway, about 113 metres wide and the largest in Egypt, was never finished, and against its inner face still stands the long mud-brick ramp the builders used to drag huge stones up as the walls rose.

A pit opened in 1903 in a courtyard now called the Cachette Court held a mass of old statues, some 900 of stone and many thousands of bronze, which the temple's priests had reverently buried there rather than throw sacred images away.

kente-the-ashanti-cloth-of-ghana.context_blurb:
Kente is the blazing strip-woven cloth of Ghana in West Africa, made by the Ashanti and Ewe peoples. Weavers build each cloth from narrow handwoven strips sewn edge to edge, and every pattern and colour has its own name and meaning. Once worn only by royalty, it is now a worldwide symbol of African heritage.

The famous home of kente is Bonwire, in Ghana's Ashanti Region, where weavers have worked their wooden looms for centuries, turning out strips only about four inches wide that are then sewn into one broad cloth.

Ashanti legend says the first weavers learned by watching a spider, the trickster Anansi, spin its web in the forest, and copied its work in silk and cotton. The tale changes from teller to teller, as legend rather than fixed history.

Its older Akan name, nwentoma, simply means woven cloth, and the word kente probably comes from kenten, a basket, because the tight, interlaced weave looks like basketwork.

In kente every colour speaks: gold speaks of wealth, blue of peace, green of growth, red of the blood of the ancestors, and black, rather than standing for mourning, of maturity and the ancestors' spirits. A cloth can be read as much as worn.

The Ashanti kings at Kumasi kept the finest kente for themselves; in the 1700s the Asantehene Opoku Ware I set up a royal weaving workshop, and only kings and chiefs wore the richest cloths, draped toga-style across one shoulder.

The most intricate pattern of all, needing extra heddles on the loom and fetching the highest price, is Adweneasa, which means roughly I have used up all my skill, a name a master weaver gives a cloth only when he has poured every technique he knows into it.

Kwame Nkrumah, who led Ghana to independence in 1957, was not Ashanti, yet he chose kente to represent the whole new country; in 1960 he gave a kente cloth to the United Nations in New York, where a replacement still hangs.

kettle-lakes-where-buried-ice-melted.context_blurb:
As the great ice sheets retreated from North America about 12,000 years ago, they left the land pocked with small round lakes, as if a giant thumb had dimpled it. Most of them are kettles, and each one marks the grave of a lump of buried ice.

Minnesota's slogan boasts 10,000 lakes, and a careful count finds 11,842, most of them small round ponds that share an odd trait: no river flows into them and none flows out, so they fill with rain and groundwater alone.

Each formed when a block of glacier ice, stranded as the ice sheet retreated, was buried under sand and gravel by meltwater streams; when the buried ice finally melted, the ground over it caved in, leaving a rounded, riverless basin called a kettle.

Walden Pond, the pond in Concord, Massachusetts, beside which Thoreau put up his cabin in 1845, is a kettle: small and steep-sided, about 102 feet deep, with no stream in or out, and Thoreau, struck by its clear water, guessed that a secret spring fed it from below.

In Wisconsin's Kettle Moraine, where two lobes of the ice sheet met, the same ice that left pits also heaped up mounds of piled gravel and sand, called kames, some rising 300 feet above the lakes.

From the Dakotas into Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba stretches the Prairie Pothole Region, a belt of shallow kettle ponds called prairie potholes, the birthplace of over half the continent's migrating waterfowl, which earns it the nickname the duck factory.

khiva-the-walled-desert-city.context_blurb:
Khiva is a small oasis city in the desert of Uzbekistan, in Central Asia, once a Silk Road stop, a notorious slave market and the capital of the Khanate of Khiva. Its old quarter, the Itchan Kala, is packed with blue-tiled madrasas, minarets and palaces inside thick mud-brick walls, and at dawn it glows like a stage set.

The Itchan Kala, about 650 by 400 metres inside crenellated mud-brick walls some 8 to 10 metres high, is the largest surviving walled town in Central Asia, the only one that keeps its full circuit of walls.

For Silk Road caravans heading west, Khiva was the last place to fill water skins and feed camels before a brutal 400-kilometre crossing of the Karakum, the black-sand desert, toward Persia.

The fat, blue-and-green-tiled Kalta Minor, whose name means short, was meant to outsoar every minaret in Islam, but its khan, Muhammad Amin Khan, was killed in 1855 while it was being built, and work stopped at just 29 metres.

Khiva's Djuma, or Friday, Mosque is a shadowy hall with a flat roof that rests on a forest of some 212 carved wooden columns in 17 rows, cut from black elm, and a few of them are over a thousand years old.

In 1990 UNESCO gave the Itchan Kala a World Heritage Site listing, the first in all of Central Asia, ahead of the grander domes of Samarkand and Bukhara.

Though the walled town is smaller than many shopping malls, it packs in more than fifty historic monuments, about 20 mosques, 20 madrasas and 6 minarets, plus palaces and tombs, among some 250 old houses.

kilimanjaro.context_blurb:
Kilimanjaro rises alone from the savanna of northern Tanzania, near the Kenyan border: a vast volcano almost 6,000 metres high, the tallest mountain in Africa. Its summit, Uhuru Peak, is called the Roof of Africa, and because it can be hiked rather than technically climbed, thousands of trekkers make the week-long walk up each year.

Everest is taller, but because Kilimanjaro stands alone and rises about 4,600 metres straight from the plains, it is the world's tallest free-standing mountain.

Across the border in Kenya, Amboseli National Park is famous for photographs of elephants and zebras on dusty plains with Kilimanjaro's snowy peak floating on the horizon behind them.

Although the summit lies only about 3 degrees south of the equator, above savanna where the heat bakes the ground, Uhuru Peak wears thick white glaciers and snow all year.

The mountain is built of three volcanic cones, and the youngest and tallest, Kibo, rises to 5,895 metres and holds Uhuru Peak; the two older cones have worn down, one into jagged spires and one into a flat plateau.

In 1889 the German geographer Hans Meyer made the first ascent and named the summit Kaiser Wilhelm Peak, after the German emperor; when Tanganyika won independence in 1961, a torch of freedom was lit on top and the peak became Uhuru Peak, Swahili for freedom.

In 1926 the missionary Richard Reusch found a leopard near the frozen rim of Kibo, at about 5,600 metres, and the cold, thin, dry air had freeze-dried its body into a mummy instead of letting it rot. Ernest Hemingway put it into his story The Snows of Kilimanjaro, and the spot is now called Leopard Point.

Ice cores from the summit record a great drought some 4,200 years back, the one climatologists call the 4.2-kiloyear event, which also helped bring down Mesopotamia's Akkadian Empire, and the ice lived through it. Today about 85 percent of the ice present in 1912 has gone.

Kibo is dormant, not dead: inside its summit crater lies the smaller Reusch Crater, whose ash pit steams with sulphurous vents, and a probe pushed just 30 centimetres under the crater floor read about 79 degrees Celsius.

A week's climb crosses five climate zones, from farmland and rainforest at the base, through heath and moorland, then alpine desert, to the arctic summit, and the moorland zone is the one where giant groundsels and giant lobelias grow taller than the hikers.

The mountain makes its own weather: damp trade winds off the Indian Ocean are forced up its southern flank, cool and drop their water, an effect called orographic rainfall, so that slope is soaked with 2,000 to 3,000 millimetres a year and cloaked in thick rainforest. The summit, in the mountain's own rain shadow, gets barely 100 millimetres.

kilwa-kisiwani.context_blurb:
Kilwa Kisiwani, whose name means Kilwa on the island, is a small island off the southern coast of today's Tanzania, reachable only by boat. Its stone ruins, among the oldest in sub-Saharan Africa, are all that remain of a medieval city that grew rich trading across the Indian Ocean with Arabia, Persia, India and China.

From the 1100s to the 1400s Kilwa was the leading trading city of the East African coast, home to perhaps more than 10,000 people who traded African gold and ivory for luxuries such as Chinese porcelain.

Its mosques and palaces are built of coral rag, blocks of coral limestone cut from the living reef offshore and squared like quarried stone, then finished with coral-lime plaster, the signature building material of the whole Swahili coast, from Kilwa to Zanzibar and Lamu.

No older mosque survives on the East African coast than Kilwa's Great Mosque, which had no open courtyard, and in the early 1300s Sultan al-Hasan raised a great dome over it, the first true dome on the coast and the largest there until the 1800s.

Kilwa had no gold mines; its wealth came from controlling Sofala, the port on the coast of today's Mozambique where gold from the far interior reached the sea, and taking a cut of the gold, ivory and goods heading on toward Arabia and India.

From the 1100s Kilwa struck its own coins, mostly copper, each bearing the reigning sultan's name and a short line of rhyming Arabic verse, a touch almost unheard of on coins of that era. Very few cities south of the Sahara minted their own money.

Husuni Kubwa, the palace Sultan al-Hasan raised around 1310 to 1333 on a sea cliff, had more than a hundred rooms round sunken courtyards and an octagonal bathing pool, and it was the biggest building anywhere south of the Sahara until modern times. Part of it doubled as a warehouse for loading trading ships.

By the founding legend in the Kilwa Chronicle, a Persian prince from Shiraz, Ali ibn al-Hassan, paid the local king enough coloured cloth to ring the site, and when the local king came to take it back, the settlers had already dug away the land bridge, so Kilwa was now a true island beyond his reach.

Kilwa's coins travelled far: archaeologists dug two of them out of the ruins of Great Zimbabwe, the stone-walled kingdom hundreds of miles inland whose gold flowed down to the coast.

kintsugi-japans-golden-mending.context_blurb:
Kintsugi is the Japanese art of mending broken pottery so that the repair shows. Instead of hiding the cracks, the mender makes them shine, so a bowl's history of breaking becomes part of its beauty. The idea grows from wabi-sabi, the Japanese sense that imperfect and impermanent things can be the most beautiful.

The name means golden joinery: the mender bonds the shards with urushi, a lacquer tapped from a Japanese tree, then dusts or mixes the seams with powdered gold, so every old crack becomes a bright gold line.

An old story, legend rather than history, says that in the late 1400s the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa sent a cracked Chinese tea bowl back to China for repair, and it came home merely clamped together with ugly metal staples, which pushed Japanese craftsmen to invent a lovelier mend.

A later rumour, also legend, claims some tea collectors loved the golden seams so much that they smashed perfect pots deliberately, shattering the flawless glaze just to have them mended in gold. It fits mottainai, the Japanese dislike of waste.

knossos-the-minoan-palace-and-the-labyri.context_blurb:
The ruins of Knossos lie on the island of Crete, in Greece: the largest palace of Europe's Bronze Age and the heart of the Minoan civilisation, which flourished from about 2000 to 1400 BC. First built around 1900 BC, it was home to thousands, and its painted walls, pipes and stairways still astonish.

Its plan of some 1,300 interlocking rooms on as many as five floors so bewildered later Greeks that they turned the palace itself into their most famous legend: the Labyrinth.

In the myth, King Minos had his architect Daedalus build that maze beneath the palace to cage the Minotaur, a monster with a bull's head on a man's body.

The sea god Poseidon punished Minos by driving his queen, Pasiphae, into an unnatural love for a white bull he had sent up from the sea, and from that union the Minotaur was born. To feed it, Minos forced Athens to send seven youths and seven maidens as tribute.

The Athenian hero Theseus came to kill it, and Princess Ariadne, Minos's daughter, gave him a ball of thread; he unwound it on his way in, slew the Minotaur and followed the thread back out.

Again and again the palace walls bear a carved double-headed axe, the labrys, and many scholars think Labyrinth first meant House of the Double Axe.

The Bull-Leaping Fresco, painted around 1450 BC, shows young athletes in a real, dangerous sport, somersaulting over a charging bull's horns: one grips the horns, one vaults across its back, one waits behind. By Minoan custom, painters showed women pale and men reddish-brown.

In the queen's rooms, the Dolphin Fresco still shows a school of dolphins curving through blue water among darting little fish, one of the loveliest images in Minoan art.

Those royal rooms also held what may be Europe's oldest flushing toilet, about 3,700 years old: a seat over a drain to the palace sewer, flushed by pouring in a jug of water.

Fresh water ran through Knossos in clay pipes, each one narrowed at the joint where it met the next, which sped up the flow like a thumb over a hose and scoured out the silt so the pipes never clogged.

In the Throne Room a carved gypsum seat, the oldest stone throne in Europe, is flanked by painted griffins, mythical beasts with a lion's body and an eagle's head. Arthur Evans called it King Minos's throne, but many archaeologists now think the room was sacred, a place where a High Priestess appeared in the role of a goddess.

From 1905 to 1930 Sir Arthur Evans reconstructed large parts of the palace in reinforced concrete and repainted its columns red and blue, freezing his own guesses into the ruins. Critics call the result a museum of a museum. It was Evans who coined the name Minoan, after King Minos.

konark-sun-temple.context_blurb:
On the Odisha shore of eastern India, beside the Bay of Bengal, stands the Konark Sun Temple, raised around 1250 for Surya, the Hindu sun god. Its tallest tower fell centuries ago, but what remains is one of the great sculptural wonders of medieval India and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The whole temple, walls, base and terraces, is carved as a giant war-chariot, Surya's cosmic chariot in stone, on which the sun god rides forever across the heavens.

Its platform rolls on 24 huge carved wheels, a long row down each side, and is hauled by seven straining stone horses; the horses are read as the seven days of the week and the wheels as the fortnights of the year, a wheel of time.

Every wheel is also a working sundial: the shadow a spoke casts on the beaded rim tells the hour, the eight broad spokes split the day into three-hour watches, and the fine beads let a careful reader tell the time to within minutes.

The main spire over the sanctum, perhaps over 200 feet tall, collapsed into rubble centuries ago, and what survives almost whole is the great audience hall, the jagamohana, about 39 metres high. Scholars still debate how tall the fallen spire really was.

Sailors from Europe used the dark, weathered temple as a seamark on the Bay of Bengal and called it the Black Pagoda, pairing it with the bright White Pagoda, the Jagannath temple up the coast at Puri.

Scholars blame the spire's fall on poor stone, a sinking foundation or lightning, but an old sailors' legend says a giant lodestone, a natural magnet, sat on the summit, throwing ships' compasses into chaos and luring them ashore, until its removal brought the tower down.

krakatoa-1883-the-loudest-sound-on-earth.context_blurb:
Krakatoa was once a little volcanic island lying between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia, on a chain of volcanoes where one plate of the Earth dives beneath another. In August 1883 it blew itself apart in one of the most violent eruptions in recorded history, with a sound heard across a large part of the planet and a haze that spread around the globe.

The island stood in the Sunda Strait, the narrow sea that divides Java from Sumatra.

The final blast came at 10:02 in the morning on 27 August 1883, and when the smoke and steam cleared, almost the whole island had gone, collapsed into a great crater beneath the sea.

Some four hours after the blast, on Rodrigues Island in the Indian Ocean, nearly 5,000 kilometres away, the police chief wrote down what he took for distant naval guns firing at sea. No sound has ever been heard farther away.

About 64 kilometres from the volcano, the captain of the ship Norham Castle wrote in his log that the explosion had burst the eardrums of more than half his crew.

Of the 36,417 official dead, more than 34,000, about nine in ten, were killed not by fire but by drowning, as the collapsing volcano sent walls of tsunami water up to 42 metres high onto the coasts of Java and Sumatra.

The waves seized the Dutch gunboat Berouw, anchored in the strait, and carried it about 2.5 kilometres inland, leaving it stranded up a river valley some 9 metres above sea level; all 28 of its crew died.

In late December 1927 a new volcano broke the surface from the drowned crater, and Indonesians named it Anak Krakatau, Child of Krakatoa; by 1930 it had become a lasting island.

Its energy, some 200 megatons, was roughly four times that of the Soviet Tsar Bomba of 1961, the biggest nuclear bomb ever set off.

The blast also sent a pressure wave around the atmosphere, and barographs worldwide recorded it seven times over five days, four times going out and three coming back, so it went around the whole planet three and a half times.

For months afterward, sunsets everywhere glowed blood-red from the ash and sulphur aloft, and in American towns such as New York, New Haven and Poughkeepsie the glow looked so like a great fire that people called out the fire brigades. The haze also cooled the next summer by about 0.4 degrees.

Without warning, one December night in 2018, part of Anak Krakatau's flank slid into the sea and raised a sudden tsunami along the Sunda Strait that killed 437 people. The child had echoed its parent 135 years later.

krakow.context_blurb:
Kraków, on the Vistula River in southern Poland, is one of the country's oldest cities and was its royal capital from the 11th century until the court moved to Warsaw in 1596. Above it rises Wawel Hill with its castle and cathedral, and at its heart lies a vast medieval market square.

At the mouth of a cave beneath Wawel Hill sits a bronze dragon, set there in 1972 by the sculptor Bronisław Chromy, and every few minutes a hidden gas nozzle makes it shoot a jet of real flame.

Visitors who cannot wait can make it breathe fire on command by sending it a text message to a special number.

The Dragon's Den beneath it is a genuine cave carved by nature in the limestone of Wawel Hill, hollowed out over thousands of years by slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolving the stone, the process geographers call karst. About 80 metres of its 270 are open to visitors.

In the legend the dragon devoured the townsfolk's flocks and their daughters and killed every knight who charged it, until a humble shoemaker's helper, Skuba, left a sheep stuffed with sulphur outside its lair; the dragon swallowed it, drank from the Vistula to quench the burning thirst, swelled up and burst.

Three huge bones have hung on chains over a door of Wawel Cathedral since at least the 1500s, long called the dragon's bones, but a Jagiellonian University researcher showed in 1937 that they are a whale bone, a mammoth bone and a rhinoceros bone. Legend warns that when they fall, the world will end.

The market square, Rynek Główny, laid out in 1257, runs more than 200 metres on each side, the largest medieval town square in Europe, framed by the Renaissance Cloth Hall and the twin towers of St Mary's Basilica. The Old Town joined the first UNESCO World Heritage list in 1978.

Every hour a live trumpeter plays the hejnal from the higher of St Mary's two towers, toward each of the four compass points, and each time the tune breaks off abruptly in mid-phrase. Polish radio has broadcast the noon call live every day since 1927.

Guidebooks say the call breaks off to honour a medieval watchman shot through the throat by an arrow as he sounded a warning, but historians say that story was popularised by an American children's novel of 1928, Eric P. Kelly's The Trumpeter of Krakow. The broken tune itself is genuinely old.

Kraków survived the Second World War almost untouched while Warsaw was flattened, partly because the German occupiers made it the capital of the General Government, their occupation regime, ruled by Hans Frank from Wawel Castle, and meant to Germanize the city rather than destroy it.

kyoto-the-thousand-year-capital-of-templ.context_blurb:
Kyoto was the imperial capital of Japan for more than a thousand years, from its founding in 794 until the court moved to Tokyo in the 1860s. Spared in the Second World War, it still holds some 1,600 temples of the Buddhists and 400 shrines of the Shinto faith, along with gardens, teahouses and old wooden streets where Japan's classical arts took shape.

In northern Kyoto stands Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion, a three-storey hall whose upper two floors are covered in real gold leaf, mirrored upside down in Kyoko-chi, the Mirror Pond, on calm days.

The hall you see is a 1955 rebuilding: on 2 July 1950 a troubled 22-year-old novice monk, Hayashi Yoken, deliberately set the original ablaze, and it burned to ash. The novelist Yukio Mishima built his novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion around him.

Each of its three floors is built in a different style: the ground floor like a Heian noble's palace, the middle like a samurai house, and the gilded top floor like the hall of a Zen temple in China.

Fushimi Inari, a vast Shinto shrine on the hills south of the city, is guarded by hundreds of stone foxes, the messengers of Inari, god of rice, many holding in their mouths the key to the rice store.

Some 10,000 bright orange torii gates form tunnels up the mountain, and each was paid for by a business or a person to give thanks after the god granted a wish, with the donor's name painted down its back. The densest stretch, the Senbon Torii, holds about 800.

West of the city at Arashiyama, the Togetsukyo, Moon-Crossing Bridge, has spanned the river at the same spot since 836; by tradition a retired emperor named it because the moon looked as though it were strolling from one end to the other.

Kiyomizu-dera's great wooden stage juts thirteen metres out over a wooded hill, propped on tall pillars joined with not one nail, and in Edo times people truly did leap from it; records show roughly 85 out of every 100 jumpers lived. Japanese still speak of jumping from Kiyomizu's stage when someone takes a big plunge, and the government banned the leaps in 1872.

In Kyoto's Gion district, where geisha still slip between wooden teahouses along lantern-lit Hanamikoji street, a full-fledged geisha is a geiko and her apprentice a maiko.

The Path of Philosophy, Tetsugaku-no-michi, a two-kilometre stone path along a cherry-lined canal, takes its name from the philosopher Nishida Kitaro, who walked it in thought every morning on his way to Kyoto University.

Japan's environment ministry picked 100 Soundscapes of Japan in 1996, and the Arashiyama bamboo grove made the list for the creaking and hissing of wind through its giant timber bamboo.

When UNESCO listed Kyoto in 1994, it grouped seventeen scattered sites in and around the city into one World Heritage Site, the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

In early 1945 Kyoto was near the top of the American list of atomic-bomb targets, but the US Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, personally struck it off to save its treasures of Japanese art and religion, and Nagasaki was added in its place. The tale that he spared it because he had honeymooned there is a myth.

teaches.8f993104a8: West of the city at Arashiyama, the Togetsukyo, Moon-Crossing Bridge, has spanned the river at the same spot since 836; by tradition a retired emperor named it because the moon looked as though it were strolling from one end to the other.
teaches.98e82506f6: Kiyomizu-dera's great wooden stage juts thirteen metres out over a wooded hill, propped on tall pillars joined with not one nail, and in Edo times people truly did leap from it; records show roughly 85 out of every 100 jumpers lived.
teaches.111a88084b: In Kyoto's Gion district, where geisha still slip between wooden teahouses along lantern-lit Hanamikoji street, a full-fledged geisha is a geiko and her apprentice a maiko.
teaches.c7ffafa2a3: The Path of Philosophy, Tetsugaku-no-michi, a two-kilometre stone path along a cherry-lined canal, takes its name from the philosopher Nishida Kitaro, who walked it in thought every morning on his way to Kyoto University.
teaches.9a538cca18: Japan's environment ministry picked 100 Soundscapes of Japan in 1996, and the Arashiyama bamboo grove made the list for the creaking and hissing of wind through its giant timber bamboo.
teaches.fcda1a35ad: When UNESCO listed Kyoto in 1994, it grouped seventeen scattered sites in and around the city into one World Heritage Site, the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.
teaches.15e5890668: In early 1945 Kyoto was near the top of the American list of atomic-bomb targets, but the US Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, personally struck it off to save its treasures of Japanese art and religion, and Nagasaki was added in its place.

la-paz-and-el-alto.context_blurb:
La Paz, in Bolivia, fills a deep canyon in the Andes at around 3,600 metres above sea level, the highest seat of government on Earth. On the flat plateau above the canyon's rim sprawls El Alto, a younger city built largely by Aymara migrants, about 400 metres higher still. Everything about life here is shaped by altitude.

Bolivia's capital is split between two separate cities: La Paz has held the president and congress since 1898, while Sucre, a lower colonial city, remains the constitutional capital and houses the supreme court.

Once the only way up was a single zigzag road, until in 2014 the city opened Mi Teleférico, My Cable Car, a network of gondola cable cars that turned a 90-minute crawl into a ride of about 11 minutes, with a cabin leaving every 12 seconds or so.

Its ten lines are named by colour, like a subway map in the sky: Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Orange, White, Sky Blue, Purple, Brown and Silver. Guinness counts it the largest urban cable-car network on Earth.

La Paz turns the usual city map upside down: the wealthy live low, in the Zona Sur around 3,250 metres, because the air down there is warmer and holds more oxygen, while poorer neighbourhoods climb the canyon sides past 4,000 metres.

El Alto International Airport sits on the plain at about 4,058 metres, and no major airport anywhere sits higher; its thin air gives wings less lift and engines less thrust, so every airliner must roll much farther down the runway before it lifts off.

Above the city shines Illimani, highest summit of the Cordillera Real at 6,438 metres, and in Andean belief it is an apu, a sacred mountain's guardian spirit, watching over La Paz.

About 10 kilometres south of the city lies the Valle de la Luna, Moon Valley, a bone-white maze of clay spires and gullies that fast-eroding soft rock has carved into badlands, the same landform found in the Dakotas. Local tales say Neil Armstrong named it, but that story is not documented.

At about 3,600 metres each breath still carries about two-thirds of the oxygen it would at sea level, enough of a drop that newcomers often fall ill with soroche, altitude sickness, within a day, yet millions live here all their lives.

lagos.context_blurb:
Lagos, on the southwestern coast of Nigeria, is the largest city in Africa and still growing fast. It sprawls across islands, sandbars and creeks around a huge coastal lagoon, tied together by bridges, and it is a cultural powerhouse, the birthplace of Afrobeats music and the Nollywood film industry.

When the Portuguese explorer Rui de Sequeira reached this watery maze of islands and creeks in 1472, he called it Lago de Curamo, and lagos is simply Portuguese for lakes and lagoons.

Long before that, Yoruba speakers knew the town as Èkó, and Èkó is still the everyday Yoruba word for the city; its exact meaning, perhaps a farmstead or a war-camp, is debated.

Out on the Lagos Lagoon stands Makoko, a district of wooden houses on tall stilts where people get about by canoe from door to door, nicknamed the Venice of Africa. Its people, many of them Egun from Badagry and neighbouring Benin, live mainly by fishing.

The Third Mainland Bridge runs 11.8 kilometres across the lagoon; opened in 1990, it held the title of Africa's longest bridge until a Cairo bridge overtook it in 1996.

In 1991 Nigeria moved its capital from crowded, coastal Lagos to Abuja, a planned city built from scratch in the centre of the country. Lagos still produces roughly a third of Nigeria's wealth and handles most of its port trade.

Off Victoria Island, engineers are raising Eko Atlantic, a new luxury district on reclaimed land won from the sea, behind an 8.5-kilometre barrier that people call the Great Wall of Lagos. The contrast is stark: Makoko's families live out in the lagoon water, while this city is walled off from the same sea.

lahore-the-mughal-city-of-mosque-and-gar.context_blurb:
Lahore, in Pakistan, was for long stretches one of the great cities of the Mughal Empire, and several emperors preferred it to Delhi and Agra. Its old city holds a huge fort, Persian-style pleasure gardens and some of the grandest mosques in the Islamic world, built in red sandstone and white marble, and it is also a city of poets.

Across a wide plaza from Lahore Fort stands the Badshahi Mosque, the Imperial Mosque, which the emperor Aurangzeb had built of deep red sandstone in just two years, finishing it in 1673; for more than three centuries no larger mosque stood anywhere. Its four corner minarets rise 60 metres.

The fort's main entrance is the Alamgiri Gate, added by Aurangzeb in 1674, its high arch flanked by two huge round, fluted bastions like giant drums.

Inside the fort, Shah Jahan built the Sheesh Mahal, Palace of Mirrors, around 1631, a marble pavilion covered in thousands of little convex mirrors, an art called ainakari, that multiply a single candle flame into a sky of sparks.

Shah Jahan's Shalimar Gardens, finished in 1642, step down the land in three terraces, Farah Baksh, Faiz Baksh and Hayat Baksh, names that praise the gifts of pleasure, goodness and life, laid out as a Persian four-part paradise garden.

Its roughly 410 fountains needed a constant flood of water on the dry Punjab plain, so Ali Mardan Khan, a Mughal noble, had a long canal dug, about 160 kilometres, to bring water down from the foothills of Kashmir.

The fort's outer Picture Wall, about 440 metres long and glittering with glazed tile and fresco from the 1620s, shows elephant fights, camels, polo matches and angels, and among them coil winged dragons from Persian myth. It is often called the largest mural in the world.

Under Sikh rule, after the Mughal empire fell apart, the Badshahi Mosque's vast courtyard was turned into a horse stable for the army, and its cells into soldiers' quarters.

The most richly tiled mosque of the whole Mughal age, sheathed inside and out in cobalt, green and gold, is the Wazir Khan Mosque, built from 1634 to 1641 and paid for by Hakim Ilam-ud-din Ansari, a doctor from Chiniot who rose to serve as the emperor's physician and later ruled Punjab as governor.

lake-baikal.context_blurb:
Lake Baikal is a long crescent of water in southern Siberia, in Russia, lying in a crack in the Earth's crust. It is the oldest and deepest lake on the planet, it holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface, and it shelters creatures found nowhere else. In winter it turns to a sheet of clear ice.

Baikal's crescent stretches more than 600 kilometres, and because its trench is so long and deep it holds about 23,615 cubic kilometres of water, making it the largest freshwater lake on Earth by volume; lakes such as Superior spread wider, but none holds as much.

Most lakes fill with silt and vanish within 10,000 to 20,000 years, but Baikal has held its water for some 25 to 30 million years, which makes it by far the oldest lake in the world.

Its deepest point lies 1,642 metres below the surface, deeper than any other lake, and its floor sits far below sea level in one of the deepest rifts on any continent.

Some 330 rivers and streams feed Baikal, yet only the Angara drains it, carrying its water on toward the Arctic Ocean. In Buryat legend the Angara is Baikal's runaway daughter.

About 80 percent of the lake's roughly 2,600 kinds of animals, from branching sponges to pale deep-water fish, live nowhere else on Earth. Together with its age, depth and volume, this earned Baikal a place on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996.

On Olkhon, the island at the heart of Buryat spiritual life, the twin marble peaks of Cape Burkhan, Shaman Rock, are held in Buryat belief to be the dwelling of the spirit that guards the lake, a place so sacred that ordinary people long kept away.

Though the nearest ocean is over 1,700 kilometres away, Baikal is the one lake on Earth with a seal of its own, the nerpa, the world's only seal that lives entirely in fresh water, probably cut off when Ice Age rivers that once linked the lake to the Arctic dried up.

Deep lakes usually have dead, oxygen-starved bottom water, but powerful seasonal mixing keeps Baikal's water rich in oxygen all the way to its floor, so creatures thrive more than a kilometre down.

Baikal is a rift lake: the Eurasian and Amur plates are pulling apart beneath it, widening the basin about two centimetres a year, and geologists say that if the spreading continues long enough the continent could split and Baikal could become a new ocean.

Since the 1990s satellites have spotted dark rings several kilometres across on the winter ice, and researchers traced them to warm eddies of water spinning beneath the ice and thinning it from below.

In a hard freeze, wind-driven waves lock into jagged, glass-clear shards of ice heaped along the shore, some as tall as twelve metres, and where light passes through them they glow an unearthly turquoise.

Plants rotting on the deep lakebed give off methane, which rises in bubbles that freeze when they meet the ice from below, stacked into milky white discs that hang in the clear ice like strings of pearls.

lake-natron.context_blurb:
In northern Tanzania, down in the East African Rift, lies Lake Natron, a shallow soda lake whose water, seeping from volcanic rock, is loaded with sodium carbonate. It is hot, harsh and caustic, few living things can bear it, and yet it is one of the most important bird nurseries on Earth.

Its deep red and orange colour, bright enough to see from orbit, is alive: salt-loving microbes crowd the brine, and their red pigment dyes the whole lake.

The white salt caked on its shores is natron, mostly sodium carbonate, the very salt the ancient Egyptians packed around bodies to dry and preserve their dead as mummies; the lake is a whole basin of embalming salt.

Chemically its water is a natural lye, as caustic as drain cleaner: packed with soda, its pH sits near 10.5 and can climb above 12, and it can heat toward 60 degrees, hot and harsh enough to burn skin and eyes.

Nick Brandt's photographs of birds and bats from the lake, looking like blackened stone statues, fed a viral claim that the lake petrifies whatever touches it, but that is wrong: the soda slowly crusts over animals that were already dead, sealing them like natural mummies.

Up to 2.5 million lesser flamingos, most of the world's population, nest on low islands of soda crust out in the middle of the lake, and foxes and jackals rarely get near them, because a moat of scalding, caustic soda-water surrounds the islands that no predator will cross.

Just south of the lake looms the volcano the Maasai call Ol Doinyo Lengai, Mountain of God, the only volcano on Earth erupting carbonatite lava, cool enough, at about 500 degrees, to pour out black instead of glowing. Within hours of hardening it soaks up moisture from the air and weathers to white powder that rain washes down to feed the lake.

lake-nyos.context_blurb:
Lake Nyos is a deep lake filling an old volcanic crater in the hills of northwestern Cameroon. Beneath it, magma breathes out gas that seeps up into the cold water at the bottom. On one night in 1986 that hidden gas made Nyos one of the deadliest lakes on Earth.

In August 1986, one night, a huge cloud of carbon dioxide burst from the lake; about half again as dense as air, it hugged the ground, rolled down into the valleys and smothered the sleeping villages, killing 1,746 people and herds of cattle without a wound or a flame.

For years the gas had collected in the cold, deep water, which never mixes with the layers above, until something disturbed the water and the gas burst out in one go, like a shaken soda bottle: a limnic eruption, from the Greek limne, lake. No one is sure what set it off; an underwater landslide or cold rain are the leading guesses.

Since 2001 engineers have sunk long pipes into the deep water; once started, each shoots up a fountain that keeps going on its own, because as the deep water rises the pressure drops, the carbon dioxide bubbles out, and the bubbly column, lighter than the water around it, races upward.

lake-superior-and-the-great-lakes.context_blurb:
North America's five Great Lakes straddle the border of the United States and Canada and drain east through the St Lawrence River to the Atlantic. The greatest of them, Lake Superior, is so wide that from one shore you cannot see the other.

Superior covers about 82,100 square kilometres, more surface than any other freshwater lake, which makes it the world's largest freshwater lake by surface area; by volume it ranks only third.

Together the five lakes hold about one-fifth of all the fresh water on Earth's surface, some six quadrillion gallons.

The lake that holds more water than Superior is Siberia's Lake Baikal, more than 1,600 metres deep, the deepest lake on Earth and the largest of all by volume.

Sailors say this lake does not give back its drowned, and the reason is its cold: below about 200 metres the water stays near freezing, about 4 degrees, all year round, which slows the decay and gas that would normally float a body back up.

Superior's Gales of November, the fierce autumn storms that sink ships, form when cold Canadian air slams into warm, moist air drawn up from the Gulf. The Great Storm of 1913 raged for days with 90-mile-an-hour winds and 35-foot waves; it sent twelve ships to the bottom and took as many as 250 lives.

Their basins are young: during the last Ice Age advancing ice sheets over a mile thick scraped and gouged the bedrock, a process called glacial scouring, and meltwater filled the hollows about 10,000 years ago.

Freed of that weight, the land around Superior is still slowly rising, its north shore faster than its south, so the lake is slowly tipping toward its southern shore: a process called isostatic rebound.

Along the north shore and Isle Royale lies dark basalt 1.1 billion years old, poured out when the continent started to split along a crack some 3,000 kilometres long, the Midcontinent Rift, which then stopped and left North America whole. Its copper-rich veins made Michigan's Keweenaw Peninsula a famous mining district.

lake-tanganyika.context_blurb: Lake Tanganyika, in the East African Rift Valley, is the second-oldest and second-deepest freshwater lake in the world, after only Lake Baikal in Siberia. It stretches for over 670 kilometres along the border of four African countries — Tanzania, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Zambia. Like Baikal, it occupies a long thin crack in a continent that is slowly being pulled apart. Hundreds of species of brightly coloured cichlid fish live in its deep waters, and most of them are found nowhere else.

lake-titicaca.context_blurb: Lake Titicaca straddles the border of Peru and Bolivia high in the Andes Mountains, at over 3,800 metres above sea level. It is the largest freshwater lake in South America by volume and is sometimes called the highest navigable lake in the world. The Uru people live on floating islands built out of totora reeds that grow in the lake. In Andean tradition, the lake is the birthplace of the sun and of the ancestors of the Inca, who stepped out of its waters.

lake-victoria.context_blurb: Lake Victoria is the biggest lake in Africa by surface area and the chief source of the Nile River. It is shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. The lake is relatively young and shallow for its size. It is also one of the stage-sets of one of the most dramatic recent biological disasters: the introduction of the Nile perch as a food fish in the 1950s and 60s drove hundreds of the lake's distinctive cichlid species to extinction or near-extinction, in what biologists call the largest vertebrate mass extinction of modern times.

laki-1783-the-fissure-that-starved-a-nat.context_blurb: In the summer of 1783 a long volcanic fissure in southern Iceland called Laki opened up and poured out enormous quantities of lava and poisonous sulphur gases for eight months. About a quarter of Iceland's population died in the subsequent famine as livestock perished and crops failed. The gases drifted south across Europe, blanketing it in a strange hazy fog, poisoning crops, and sickening or killing many thousands of people. The disruption may have contributed to the catastrophic grain shortages that helped set the stage for the French Revolution in 1789.

lalibelas-rock-hewn-churches.context_blurb: In the highlands of northern Ethiopia, the medieval king Lalibela ordered an entire cluster of Christian churches carved out of the solid red rock of the mountainside. They were not built up with stones; they were cut down into the earth, each one a single huge sculpture with a hollow interior, roof included. Carved in the 12th and 13th centuries, the churches of Lalibela are still active places of worship for the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and Christian pilgrims walk between them along passages dug through the rock itself.

lava-lakes-the-worlds-eternal-fire-pits.context_blurb: A persistent lava lake is a pool of molten rock exposed inside a volcanic crater or vent, continuously replenished from below. They are rare — at any given time only a handful exist on Earth. The best-known are at Erta Ale in Ethiopia, Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mount Erebus in Antarctica, and (intermittently) Kilauea in Hawaii. Looking down into one is probably the single most direct window you can get on the molten interior of our planet.

leshan-giant-buddha.context_blurb: At Leshan in Sichuan, China, where three rivers meet, a Chinese Buddhist monk in the 8th century had the mountainside itself carved into a Buddha. The seated figure is more than 70 metres tall from head to foot — the largest ancient stone Buddha in the world. The project took about ninety years. According to tradition, the sculpting was begun to calm the dangerous rapids where the rivers joined, and tons of carved stone dumped into the current from the works really did change its flow.

lhasa-the-potala-palace-above-the-roof-o.context_blurb: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet, high on a plateau at an elevation that leaves most visitors short of breath. Rising above it on a hill is the Potala Palace, a soaring white-and-red fortress-monastery that was for centuries the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas, the spiritual and (until recent times) temporal leaders of Tibetan Buddhism. The current Dalai Lama has lived in exile in India since 1959. The Jokhang Temple down in the old town is the single holiest site in Tibetan Buddhism.

light-bent-into-an-arc-rainbows-and-the-.context_blurb: A rainbow forms when sunlight bends and reflects inside falling raindrops. White sunlight splits into its separate colours and lines up into a circular arc opposite the Sun — red on the outside, violet on the inside, with every observer actually seeing a slightly different rainbow. On rare occasions moonlight is bright enough to produce the same effect, with much paler colours, which is called a moonbow. Double rainbows have a secondary, dimmer bow outside the primary one, with the order of the colours reversed.

lima.context_blurb: Lima, the capital of Peru, lies in a narrow strip of coastal desert between the Pacific Ocean and the foothills of the Andes. It was founded in 1535 by the Spanish conqueror Francisco Pizarro as the seat of Spain's South American viceroyalty, and for about three centuries it was the richest Spanish colonial city on the Pacific coast. It is one of the driest major cities in the world — annual rainfall is almost zero — but it is kept green by rivers running down from the Andes.

linear-b-and-the-burnt-tablets-of-knosso.context_blurb: Linear B is a Bronze Age script found on clay tablets at Knossos on Crete and at several sites on the Greek mainland. For decades after its discovery nobody knew what language it recorded. In the 1950s a brilliant young English architect named Michael Ventris, working with the classicist John Chadwick, finally cracked it: Linear B turned out to be an early form of Greek, written down roughly a thousand years before Homer. The tablets survived precisely because the palaces that stored them burned down, baking the wet clay inventories into permanence.

lisbon-the-quake-that-shook-the-enlighte.context_blurb: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal, perched on seven steep hills above a great natural harbour on the Atlantic. On the morning of November 1, 1755, All Saints' Day, a massive earthquake — followed by a tsunami and a city-wide fire — levelled much of it and killed tens of thousands of people. The disaster rattled Europe intellectually, inspiring Voltaire's Candide and provoking fierce arguments about the goodness of God and the natural order. The city was rebuilt afterward on a famously orderly geometric grid in the old lower town.

loess-ice-age-dust-builds-a-plateau.context_blurb: Loess is a fine, pale yellow wind-blown dust that was blown off the barren outwash plains in front of ice-age glaciers and deposited downwind in huge thick blankets. It covers large regions of the central United States, central Europe, Ukraine, and above all northern China, where the Loess Plateau is tens of metres deep in it. Loess is extraordinarily fertile, which is one reason these regions have long been agricultural heartlands. It also erodes dramatically into vertical cliffs and gullies when water cuts into it.

london-the-city-on-the-tidal-thames.context_blurb: London, on the River Thames in southern England, began as a Roman trading post, grew into the capital of medieval England, and in the 18th and 19th centuries became the headquarters of a global empire. The Thames right through central London is tidal, which allowed the Royal Navy's sailing ships to come straight up to the docks. London has repeatedly reinvented itself: a great plague in 1665, a great fire in 1666, bombing in the Blitz of 1940-41, and most recently a transformation from grimy post-industrial port into one of the world's financial centres.

luang-prabang.context_blurb: Luang Prabang is a tiny former royal capital of Laos, tucked at the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan rivers in the mountains of the country's north. Its small centre is packed with gilded Buddhist temples and French-colonial shuttered villas on sleepy lanes, and every morning at dawn barefoot saffron-robed monks walk through the streets in a long procession collecting rice from kneeling residents.

machu-picchu.context_blurb: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca royal estate perched on a ridge in the cloud forest high above the Urubamba River in the Peruvian Andes. It is built of beautifully fitted stone terraces and buildings and is thought to have been constructed for the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The Spanish, remarkably, never found it, which is one reason it survived in better shape than most Inca sites. It was brought to international attention by the American explorer Hiram Bingham III in 1911, who was led there by a local farmer.

madagascar-the-isolated-ark.context_blurb: Madagascar is a huge island off the southeast coast of Africa — bigger than France — that broke off from the African mainland tens of millions of years ago and from the Indian subcontinent soon after. In its long isolation, its plants and animals evolved on their own path. Roughly 90% of the species found on Madagascar live nowhere else on Earth, including all the lemurs, the fossa, and bizarre spiky trees like the baobab and the octopus tree. Humans only arrived about two thousand years ago, which is very recent as islands go.

maelstroms-the-seas-great-whirlpools.context_blurb: A maelstrom is a powerful, often permanent whirlpool caused by strong tidal currents being forced through a narrow strait. The most famous ones are off the Lofoten Islands in northern Norway, where strong Atlantic tides race through gaps between the islands and spin up turbulent eddies big enough to pull small boats around. The word itself is Norwegian. Edgar Allan Poe and Jules Verne both wrote tales about them in which seafarers get sucked down into the depths, but real maelstroms, though impressive, do not actually swallow ships.

manaus.context_blurb: Manaus is the largest city deep inside the Amazon rainforest, in Brazil, far up the Amazon River where it meets the Rio Negro. At the end of the 19th century it exploded into a short-lived rubber boom and was briefly one of the wealthiest cities in the world; the rubber barons built a grand pink opera house in the middle of the jungle, imported European marble and chandeliers, and brought over opera companies from Italy. The boom collapsed when rubber seedlings smuggled to Southeast Asia undercut Brazilian prices.

manila-intramuros.context_blurb: Manila, the capital of the Philippines, was founded by the Spanish in 1571 on the shore of Manila Bay. For some 250 years it anchored the Manila Galleon trade — a yearly convoy of Spanish treasure ships that carried silver and goods between Manila and Acapulco in Mexico, linking Asia into the Spanish global empire. At the heart of old Manila stands Intramuros, the stone-walled Spanish colonial quarter. Most of it was flattened during the Battle of Manila in 1945; portions have been restored, portions remain scarred.

mariachi-jalisco-mexico.context_blurb: Mariachi is the traditional Mexican ensemble music that most of the world now hears as the sound of Mexico. It grew up in the state of Jalisco in western Mexico in the 19th century, out of a blend of indigenous, Spanish, and French musical traditions. A typical mariachi group includes violins, trumpets, Spanish guitars, a round-bellied bass guitar (the guitarron), and a small high-pitched guitar (the vihuela), with the musicians dressed in the ornate charro outfit of the Mexican horseman. Mariachi was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2011.

marrakech.context_blurb: Marrakech, in Morocco, was founded in 1070 at the foot of the Atlas Mountains and became the royal capital of successive medieval Berber dynasties ruling an empire that reached from Spain to Senegal. Its old medina is enclosed by red-earth walls, from which the city takes its nickname 'the Red City.' At its heart lies the Jemaa el-Fnaa, a huge market square that empties out during the day and fills with storytellers, snake charmers, musicians, and food stalls at dusk.

mecca-and-the-valley-of-the-hijaz.context_blurb: Mecca, in the dry Hijaz region of western Saudi Arabia, is the holiest city of Islam. It is the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad in the 6th century and the site of the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine around which Muslim worship is organized. Observant Muslims who can afford to are expected to make the pilgrimage, the Hajj, to Mecca at least once in their lifetime; several million do so every year during a specific week of the Islamic lunar calendar. The city is closed to non-Muslims.

mediterranean-climate-the-scattered-five.context_blurb: A 'Mediterranean climate' means hot dry summers and mild wet winters, and the surprising thing about it is that it occurs in only five places on Earth. One is the actual Mediterranean basin. The other four are coastal California, central Chile, the Cape region of South Africa, and the south and southwest corners of Australia. These five scattered pockets, each sitting on the western edge of a continent at roughly the same latitude, have independently grown drought-tolerant shrublands with similar silver-grey leaves — and in modern times they have become the world's five great wine-making regions.

megathrust-the-deepest-trenches-and-the-.context_blurb: Where one tectonic plate dives down beneath another, the long fault running along the top of the sinking plate is called a megathrust. These are the biggest active faults on Earth, and they produce the biggest earthquakes. The largest earthquakes ever recorded, including the 1960 magnitude 9.5 Chile quake and the 2011 magnitude 9.1 Tohoku quake off Japan, were megathrust events. Earthquakes on megathrusts can also lift the sea floor by metres in seconds, which is what sets off the biggest tsunamis.

meissen-how-europe-cracked-chinas-porcel.context_blurb: For centuries Europeans paid huge sums to import Chinese porcelain, which they could not reproduce. In 1708, in the small Saxon town of Meissen near Dresden in modern Germany, an alchemist named Johann Friedrich Bottger — reportedly working under threat of death from the local prince — finally cracked the recipe. Meissen became the first porcelain factory outside Asia, and its characteristic crossed-swords mark is one of the oldest trademarks still in use. Within a generation, European porcelain workshops had spread across the continent.

melbourne.context_blurb: Melbourne is a southeastern Australian city on a bay off the Southern Ocean. It exploded during the 1850s gold rush in the state of Victoria and briefly, in the 1880s, was one of the richest cities on Earth, with grand Victorian boulevards to prove it. It is a famously liveable modern city with the largest tram network in the English-speaking world. For a few decades (1901-1927) Melbourne even served as the temporary capital of Australia, until Canberra was ready.

mesa-verde.context_blurb: Mesa Verde, in southwestern Colorado in the United States, preserves the most spectacular cliff-dwellings ever built by the Ancestral Puebloans. Beginning around 1200 CE, people who had been farming on top of the flat mesa began moving into the natural rock shelters in its canyon walls and building elaborate multi-story stone-and-mortar villages tucked under the overhangs. The largest of these, Cliff Palace, has over 150 rooms. The whole mesa was abandoned by about 1300, in a drought-stricken migration whose destination is now the Pueblo villages of the Rio Grande.

mexico-city-tenochtitlan.context_blurb: Mexico City sits in a high mountain valley on top of the ruins of Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztec Empire that Hernan Cortes and his Spanish-and-Tlaxcalan forces conquered in 1521. The Aztec city was built on islands in a vast shallow lake, laced with canals; the Spanish filled in most of the lake and built their colonial capital on top. The soft lake-bed sediments mean that modern Mexico City is slowly sinking in uneven patches, so cathedrals and apartment towers lean at odd angles.

miyajima-the-floating-torii.context_blurb: Miyajima is a small forested island in Japan's Seto Inland Sea, considered one of the three most beautiful views in Japan. On its shore stands a huge vermilion Shinto gate — a torii — that has been painted so many times its wood is now sealed in colour. At high tide the sea comes right up around it, so the gate seems to float on the water. Deer wander freely on the island; traditionally no births, deaths, or farming were permitted on it, to keep it sacred.

mohenjo-daro-and-the-indus-cities.context_blurb: In the Indus River valley of modern Pakistan, archaeologists in the 1920s uncovered the ruins of one of the world's three oldest urban civilizations — alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia. The Indus Valley Civilization flourished around 2600 to 1900 BCE, with planned grid-pattern cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, standardized bricks, and sophisticated drainage. Its people wrote in a script that still has not been deciphered. Why their cities emptied out after about 1900 BCE is one of the great unsolved puzzles of ancient history.

monasteries-in-impossible-places.context_blurb: Religious communities around the world have a persistent habit of building their monasteries in places that are as hard as possible to reach: on cliff tops, on isolated sea rocks, inside sheer canyons. The great meteora monasteries of central Greece sit atop pinnacles of rock, originally reached only by net and rope ladder. The Taktsang Palphug ('Tiger's Nest') in Bhutan clings to a cliff hundreds of metres above the valley floor. These places are usually chosen for both their physical remove from worldly distractions and the sheer wonder of occupying such sites.

monte-alban.context_blurb: Monte Alban is an ancient city built on the artificially flattened top of a mountain in the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico. It was the capital of the Zapotec civilization from roughly 500 BCE to 750 CE, flourishing in parallel with the Maya further east. Its enormous central plaza is lined with pyramids, palaces, and tombs, including a strange J-shaped observatory oriented to the stars. Carved stone slabs around the site depict rows of mysterious contorted figures that early archaeologists called 'the dancers' and whose real meaning is still argued over.

monterey-bay-kelp-forests.context_blurb: Monterey Bay, on the central Californian coast, is one of the richest marine ecosystems on the North American Pacific coast. A deep underwater canyon reaches almost right up to the shore, pulling cold nutrient-rich water from the depths close to the surface. That nutrient supply feeds enormous underwater kelp forests — great golden-brown fronds of giant kelp that grow upward from the sea floor to the surface, forming a canopy about 30 metres tall. Sea otters, harbour seals, sea lions, and leopard sharks all live among the kelp.

montreal.context_blurb: Montreal is on an island in the St. Lawrence River in the Canadian province of Quebec. It is the largest primarily French-speaking city in the Americas and the second-largest in the French-speaking world after Paris. Founded by the French in 1642, it was conquered by the British in 1760 but kept its French language, Catholic churches, and civil-law system. Below its downtown streets runs an enormous network of underground pedestrian passages linking shops, hotels, and metro stations, built so that Montrealers can survive the long winter without stepping outside.

moraines-the-ridges-of-dumped-rubble.context_blurb: A moraine is a ridge or hummocky expanse of rubble — rocks of every size mixed with sand and clay — that a glacier left behind. 'Terminal moraines' mark the furthest point a glacier reached before it stopped and started melting back. The spine of Long Island in New York, for example, is a terminal moraine from the last ice age. Lateral moraines mark the sides of a glacier's track, and medial moraines run down the middle where two glaciers merged.

moscow.context_blurb: Moscow has been the capital of Russia for most of the last five hundred years. In its exact centre, on a bluff above the Moscow River, stands the Kremlin: a vast walled triangle of cathedrals, palaces, and government buildings that has served as the seat of Russian rulers since the days of Ivan the Terrible. Just outside its walls is Red Square, with the brightly-coloured onion domes of St Basil's Cathedral. Moscow was burned during Napoleon's 1812 invasion, held fast against Hitler in 1941, and ruled by Stalin from the Kremlin for a quarter-century.

mount-everest.context_blurb: Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and Tibet, is the highest point on the Earth's land surface, at about 8,849 metres above sea level. Its summit is in what climbers call 'the death zone' above 8,000 metres, where the air is too thin to sustain life for long. Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and the Sherpa Tenzing Norgay were the first climbers confirmed to reach the top, in 1953; since then thousands have followed in their footsteps, with the mountain growing increasingly commercialized. Hundreds have died on it.

mount-fuji.context_blurb: Mount Fuji, west of Tokyo on the main Japanese island of Honshu, is the highest and most iconic mountain in Japan. It is a nearly perfect, symmetrical, snow-capped volcanic cone, and it has been both climbed by Shinto pilgrims and painted by Japanese artists — Hokusai's famous woodblock series of 'Thirty-Six Views' captures it from every angle — for centuries. It last erupted in 1707. On a clear winter day it can be seen from downtown Tokyo more than a hundred kilometres away.

mount-kailash.context_blurb: Mount Kailash in the far west of Tibet is a sacred mountain for four religions at once — Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and the older Tibetan Bon faith — each with its own tradition about who or what the peak is. Hindus consider it the home of the god Shiva. Pilgrims from all four religions walk the roughly 52-kilometre-long devotional circuit around its base at high altitude, taking a few hard days to do a single lap. The mountain itself has never been climbed; all climbing attempts have been forbidden out of religious reverence.

mount-roraima.context_blurb: Mount Roraima, on the triple border of Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana, is one of the oldest and strangest mountains on Earth. It is a 'tepui' — a flat-topped, sheer-sided table mountain, the eroded remnant of a once-vast sandstone plateau that is now almost two billion years old. Its summit stands as an isolated plateau in the sky, hundreds of metres above the rainforest around it, with its own species of plants and animals that have evolved in isolation. It inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The Lost World.

mount-st-helens-1980-the-sideways-blast.context_blurb: On May 18, 1980, Mount St Helens in Washington State in the United States erupted in one of the most-studied eruptions in modern history. A huge chunk of the mountain's north face collapsed in a giant landslide, which depressurized the magma inside and triggered a lateral blast that flattened forests over hundreds of square kilometres. Fifty-seven people died, including a volcanologist monitoring the mountain. The eruption left a huge horseshoe-shaped crater and a new generation of American geologists who had seen a major eruption up close.

murano-venices-island-of-glass.context_blurb: Murano is a small island cluster in the lagoon of Venice. In 1291, the Venetian government ordered all of Venice's glassmakers to move their furnaces onto Murano — officially to protect the wooden city from kiln fires, but also to keep the glassmakers (and their trade secrets) under control. The Murano workshops dominated European glassmaking for centuries and invented key techniques of clear 'cristallo' glass, enamelled glass, and millefiori. Workers who tried to leave the island with their skills were sometimes hunted down.

mycenae-the-lion-gate-and-the-cyclopean-.context_blurb: Mycenae, in the hills of mainland Greece, was the stronghold of the warrior kingdoms that fought the Trojan War in legend and the real-life center of a late Bronze Age civilization that spoke an early form of Greek. Its massive stone walls are built from blocks so huge that later Greeks assumed only Cyclopes could have moved them, which is still what archaeologists call this style. The main gate is crowned by a carved relief of two heraldic lions — one of the oldest monumental sculptures in Europe.

nan-madol.context_blurb: Nan Madol is a ruined stone city built on top of a coral reef off the Micronesian island of Pohnpei in the western Pacific. Its people, the Saudeleur dynasty, piled up roughly a hundred artificial islets separated by canals, then stacked them with walls of giant basalt logs — natural columns of volcanic rock quarried elsewhere on the island. It flourished from about 1200 to 1600 CE, is sometimes called 'the Venice of the Pacific,' and nobody is quite sure how its people moved the enormous stones into place.

naples-and-the-bay-of-fire.context_blurb: Naples sits on a famous bay on the southern coast of Italy, in the shadow of Mount Vesuvius — the volcano that destroyed Roman Pompeii in AD 79 and could easily erupt again. Just offshore are the volcanic islands of Capri and Ischia; just inland, beneath the suburbs, lie more volcanic calderas that still shift up and down. Naples is the home of pizza (its margherita is the original), it was once the capital of its own kingdom, and its old centre has one of the densest tangles of medieval and Baroque churches anywhere in Europe.

nara-the-first-capital-and-its-great-bud.context_blurb: Nara was the first permanent capital of Japan, established in 710 CE before the court moved on to Kyoto. In this short, intense period it absorbed Chinese models of statecraft and Buddhist architecture. Today the quiet city houses one of the largest wooden buildings on Earth, the Todai-ji, inside which sits an enormous bronze seated Buddha. Hundreds of tame deer wander Nara's park, bowing politely for the biscuits sold to tourists; in Shinto tradition they are considered messengers of the gods.

nazca-lines.context_blurb: On the dry desert plateau south of Lima, Peru, the Nazca people — ancestors of the later Inca — scraped away the dark surface stones to reveal lighter sand underneath, creating a vast gallery of lines and figures spread across hundreds of square kilometres. Some are enormous stylized animals (a monkey, a hummingbird, a spider, a whale) hundreds of metres long; others are long straight lines running toward distant mountains. They were made between roughly 500 BCE and 500 CE. Because they are so big and so flat, their shapes are only fully visible from the air.

new-orleans.context_blurb: New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718 near the mouth of the Mississippi River on the Gulf of Mexico. Over its history it has been French, Spanish, French again, and American, and that layered inheritance shows in everything from its cuisine (gumbo, jambalaya) to its architecture (wrought-iron balconies in the French Quarter) and its Catholic feast-day traditions (Mardi Gras). Much of the city sits below sea level in a shallow bowl, which made the levee failures of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 so devastating.

new-york-city.context_blurb: New York City, on the Atlantic coast of the United States, grew up around one of the finest natural deep-water harbours in the world, which made it an obvious terminus for immigrant ships and transatlantic trade. Its five boroughs — Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island — together hold over eight million people. In the 20th century it emerged as the largest city of the English-speaking world, the headquarters of global finance and advertising, and the symbol of the United States in a thousand films and TV shows.

new-zealand-and-zealandia-the-drowned-co.context_blurb: Geologists now agree that New Zealand sits on the top of its own continent, called Zealandia or Te Riu-a-Maui. The problem is that about 94% of this continent is under the ocean. Only New Zealand, New Caledonia, and a few scattered islands show above the water as the exposed peaks of a drowned landmass. The real continent extends across huge areas of submerged seafloor. New Zealand is also unusual as one of the last large places humans ever reached; Polynesian voyagers arrived there only about 800 years ago.

newgrange-and-bru-na-boinne-the-solstice.context_blurb: In the green rolling fields of the Boyne Valley in Ireland sits Newgrange, a huge grass-covered dome of a tomb built more than 5,000 years ago — older than the pyramids and older than Stonehenge. A long stone passage leads into a cross-shaped burial chamber at its heart. The whole monument was engineered for one astronomical moment each year: for a few minutes around sunrise on the winter solstice, a shaft of light pierces the passage and lights up the inner chamber.

niagara-falls.context_blurb: Niagara Falls, on the border between the United States and Canada, is actually three waterfalls side by side on the Niagara River between Lakes Erie and Ontario. It is not the tallest nor the widest waterfall in the world, but by sheer volume of water tumbling over the edge, it is among the most powerful on Earth. In its two centuries as a tourist attraction, Niagara has drawn tightrope walkers, barrel-riders, honeymooners, and hydroelectric engineers; much of the river's flow is diverted at night to spin turbines.

norse-runes-and-the-jelling-stones.context_blurb: Runes are the angular alphabetic letters that the Vikings and their Germanic ancestors scratched into stone, bone, and wood from about the 2nd century CE through the Middle Ages. Because they had to be cut with a blade across wood grain, the letter shapes are made of straight lines and avoid horizontal strokes. The great Jelling stones in Denmark, raised in the 10th century by King Harald Bluetooth (the king whose nickname was later borrowed for the wireless technology), carry one of the longest and most important royal inscriptions in the runic alphabet.

ocean-gyres-the-garbage-patch-and-the-sh.context_blurb: A gyre is a huge circular current system in an ocean basin. There are five major ones in the world's oceans, driven by winds and the Earth's rotation. The water at the centre of a gyre tends to rotate slowly and accumulate anything that floats — seaweed, driftwood, and now plastic. The 'Great Pacific Garbage Patch,' between California and Hawaii, is the largest known concentration of ocean plastic debris, and the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic is a huge calm patch of ocean where unique rafts of golden sargassum seaweed drift year after year.

old-sanaa.context_blurb: Sanaa, in the mountains of Yemen, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Its old quarter is a dense pack of tall mud-brick tower houses, several storeys each, their upper floors decorated with fired-brick geometric patterns and bands of white gypsum around the windows. Many of these houses are five or six hundred years old and are still lived in by the same families' descendants. The Yemeni civil war that began in 2015 has heavily damaged parts of this fragile old city.

palenque.context_blurb: Palenque, in the forested hills of Chiapas, southern Mexico, is a classic Maya city that flourished from about 300 to 800 CE. Its elegant limestone temples and palace are among the finest achievements of Maya architecture. In 1952, after years of digging through rubble inside the Temple of the Inscriptions, the Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz discovered a sealed stairway leading down into a hidden crypt beneath the pyramid, which turned out to hold the elaborate tomb of a 7th-century ruler named Pakal the Great.

palmyra.context_blurb: Palmyra was a caravan city at an oasis in the Syrian desert, halfway between the Roman and Persian empires. In the 1st to 3rd centuries CE it grew rich as a middleman on the overland silk routes, and its people built an extraordinary skyline of columns, arches, and tower-tombs in a style mixing Greek, Roman, and Persian ideas. Its most famous ruler was Queen Zenobia, who briefly rebelled against Rome. In the 2010s much of its ancient architecture was deliberately blown up by the terrorist group ISIS, which makes the surviving photographs and reconstructions all the more precious.

pamukkale-and-hierapolis.context_blurb: At Pamukkale ('cotton castle') in southwestern Turkey, hot mineral-rich springs cascade down a hillside and deposit layer upon layer of brilliant white calcium carbonate. The result is a staircase of blindingly white terraces holding pools of warm turquoise water — one of the strangest-looking natural landscapes anywhere. On the plateau at the top sits the ruins of Hierapolis, a Greco-Roman spa city whose people came to bathe in these same waters two thousand years ago.

pangaeas-ghost-how-we-know-the-map-moves.context_blurb: The idea that the continents have shifted around the globe over hundreds of millions of years was once ridiculed. The German meteorologist Alfred Wegener laid out the hypothesis in 1912, pointing out how well the eastern coast of South America fits against the western coast of Africa, and how matching fossils and rock types line up across the ocean. His 'continental drift' idea was dismissed because no one could think of a mechanism. In the 1960s, new data from the sea floor revealed the mechanism, and plate tectonics became scientific consensus.

paris-the-city-above-and-below.context_blurb: Paris, on the River Seine in northern France, has been the capital of France for well over a thousand years. Its skyline above the river is still mostly the one laid out in the great 19th-century redesign by Baron Haussmann, whose boulevards cut long straight lines through the medieval maze. Below the streets runs an immense parallel city of tunnels: Metro lines, sewers, ancient limestone quarries, and the famous ossuary where the bones of several million Parisians were quietly moved in the 1780s when the city's cemeteries overflowed.

perito-moreno-glacier-patagonia.context_blurb: The Perito Moreno Glacier, in the Argentine Patagonia on the border with Chile, is one of the most accessible large glaciers on Earth. Walkways let visitors stand right in front of a sheer blue ice wall nearly 60 metres high, where huge slabs of ice regularly crack off and crash into the lake below. Unlike most of the world's glaciers today, Perito Moreno is roughly stable in size, neither clearly advancing nor clearly retreating.
